passages.title: LITERARY NARRATIVE: "What Ready Looks Like" (an original story written for this practice set)
passages.text:
The bakery on Linden Street opened at six, but the work began at midnight. That was the first thing Mrs. Dalca told me when she hired me, the summer I was seventeen, and she said it the way other people mention the weather: a fact to be dressed for, not complained about. I nodded as if midnight were nothing. I had stayed up later than that for worse reasons.

The first week, I was useless in a way I had not known was possible. I measured flour too quickly and scattered it across the counter. I kneaded the dough as if it had insulted me. When the loaves came out of the oven flat and pale, Mrs. Dalca did not scold me. She broke one open, pressed the crumb between her fingers, and handed me half. "Taste what hurry tastes like," she said.

It tasted like nothing. That was the problem.

I wanted to be good at things immediately. At school I had been the kind of student who finished tests first and then waited, tapping a pencil, for everyone else. Speed had always looked like intelligence to me, and slowness like a kind of failure. The bakery did not care what I thought. Dough rose on its own schedule, and no amount of glaring at the proofing baskets made it rise faster.

Mrs. Dalca worked without a clock. She would lift the cloth from a bowl, press a floured finger into the dough, and watch the dent. If it sprang back at once, she covered the bowl again. If it filled in slowly, halfway, she nodded and reached for the scale. I asked her once how she knew how long to wait. She shrugged. "I don't know how long," she said. "I know what ready looks like."

By July I had stopped looking at the wall clock above the ovens. I began to notice other things instead: the sour, almost fruity smell that meant the starter was strong; the way a well-shaped loaf held its seam on the counter; the faint crackle, like distant rain, that came from the crusts as they cooled. None of these were things I could have learned faster by trying harder. They arrived when they arrived, the way the dough did.

On my last night, Mrs. Dalca let me make the rye on my own. I mixed and folded and waited, and when the loaves came out I broke one open the way she had that first week. The crumb was dark and open and smelled of caraway. I handed her half. She chewed for a long time, longer than seemed necessary, and I felt the old impatience rise in my chest. Then she nodded once, the same small nod she gave the dough.

"Now," she said, "it tastes like time."

passages.title: SOCIAL SCIENCE: Passage A is from an essay by an urban ecologist; Passage B is from an essay by a city planner. Both are original texts written for this practice set.
passages.text:
Passage A

For much of the last century, cities treated small streams as problems to be solved. A creek that flooded a neighborhood or carried away sewage was straightened, lined with concrete, and eventually sealed inside a pipe beneath the street. Out of sight, the stream stopped being anyone's concern.

In recent decades, a number of cities have begun to reverse that choice by "daylighting" buried streams: removing the pavement above them and rebuilding a channel open to the sky. Supporters often lead with the ecological case. An open channel, lined with gravel and shaded by plants, can support insects, fish, and birds that a dark pipe cannot. Exposed water also cools the air around it on hot days.

But the most persuasive argument may be the practical one. A pipe has a fixed capacity; when a storm sends more water than it can carry, the excess backs up into basements and streets. A restored stream with a wide, shallow floodplain can spread that water out and slow it down. In this sense, daylighting does not merely decorate a city; it gives the city room to absorb storms that pipes were never built for.

Daylighting is not cheap, and it is not always possible. Where buildings now sit directly above an old stream, the cost of restoration can be prohibitive. Yet the cities that have tried it often report a benefit no engineer predicted: people come. They walk along the water at lunch, bring children to look for minnows, and begin to treat the neighborhood as a place worth caring for. A stream that was once a problem to be hidden becomes, in a sense, a public room.

Passage B

Proposals to daylight buried streams are easy to love. Few people object to the image of clear water running where there was once only asphalt. As a city planner, though, I have learned to ask what such projects cost and what else the same money might do.

The answer is often sobering. Opening a stream through a dense neighborhood can mean acquiring property, rerouting utility lines, and rebuilding streets, work that may cost many times as much as repairing the existing pipe. For the same budget, a city might install rain gardens and permeable pavement across dozens of blocks, capturing storm water closer to where it falls.

Nor is a restored stream automatically a healthy one. Water that runs off city streets carries oil, salt, and litter. Unless the surrounding area is also changed, a daylighted stream may simply put polluted water on display. Some restored channels require years of maintenance before they support the wildlife their designers promised.

None of this means daylighting is never worth doing. Where a buried stream runs beneath an open lot or a park, the costs can be modest and the benefits real. My concern is with treating daylighting as a symbol rather than a tool. A city's first question should not be "How do we bring the stream back?" but "What is the most effective way to manage this water?" Sometimes the answer will be a stream. Often it will not.

passages.title: NATURAL SCIENCE: "The Night Shift" (an original essay written for this practice set)
passages.text:
On a summer afternoon in the desert, a plant faces a dilemma that most of us never consider. To grow, it needs carbon dioxide from the air, which enters through tiny pores in its leaves or stems called stomata. But every open pore is also an exit. Water vapor escapes through the same openings, and in hot, dry air it escapes quickly. A plant that keeps its pores open all day may run short of water; a plant that keeps them shut may run short of carbon.

Many desert plants, including most cacti, have settled this dilemma by changing their schedule. Rather than opening their stomata in daylight, as most plants do, they open them at night, when the air is cooler and more humid and far less water is lost. The carbon dioxide they take in is not used right away. Instead, the plant stores it, chemically bound in an acid, inside its cells.

When the sun rises, the stomata close, sealing the plant against the heat. Only then does the stored carbon go to work. Sunlight powers photosynthesis, and the plant releases carbon from its acid store and builds it into sugars, all without opening a single pore. In effect, the plant has separated two tasks that most plants perform together: gathering carbon at night and using it by day.

Botanists call this strategy crassulacean acid metabolism, or CAM, after the stonecrop family of succulents in which it was first studied. The name is clumsy, but the idea is elegant. A plant using CAM can capture carbon while losing only a small fraction of the water that a typical plant would lose.

The strategy has a cost. Storing carbon overnight takes energy, and the amount a plant can store is limited by the size of its cells. CAM plants therefore tend to grow slowly. Where water is plentiful in the soil, they are usually outgrown by faster-growing neighbors. The very adjustment that lets a cactus thrive in the desert would be a handicap in a well-watered meadow.

Perhaps that is the most useful lesson the cactus offers: an adaptation is not simply an improvement. It is a trade, and whether the trade pays depends on where the organism lives. A strategy that looks like brilliance in one place can look like weakness in another.

passages.title: The Middle Octave
passages.text:
My grandfather tuned pianos for forty years, and for most of those years he refused to own one. "A tuner with a piano at home," he told me once, "is like a baker who eats his own bread. He stops tasting it." So the upright that arrived at his house the spring I turned twelve was a surprise to everyone, including, I think, him.

It had belonged to Mrs. Okafor, whose church had replaced it with an electric keyboard. The movers set it against the dining-room wall, and for a week my grandfather walked past it as though it were a stranger who had come to stay without being invited. He did not lift the lid. He did not, as far as I could tell, even look at it.

On Saturday he called me in from the yard. He had laid his tools out on a dish towel—the tuning hammer, the rubber mutes, the felt strip—in the same order he used in other people's houses. "You'll do the middle octave," he said. I said I didn't know how. "Nobody knows how," he said. "They learn to hear it."

What he meant, I found out, was that a string slightly out of tune with its neighbor doesn't sound wrong so much as restless. Two notes that should agree produce a slow wavering, a beat, like someone breathing just out of step with you. My job was to turn the pin until the breathing stopped. For the first hour I heard nothing at all. Then, near noon, I heard it everywhere: in the piano, in the refrigerator's hum against the clock radio, in the two of us humming the same note while we waited for each other.

My grandfather did not praise me. When I finished the octave he played a single chord, listened, and moved one pin a hair's width with his own hand. Then he put the hammer back on the towel—at my place, not his—and went to make lunch.

I understood years later that he had not needed a piano. He had needed someone to hand his ear to, and an instrument was simply the only way he knew to do it. That afternoon, though, I knew only that the house sounded different, and that when I walked past the dining-room wall, I no longer felt I was passing a stranger.

passages.title: Why Ice Is Slippery
passages.text:
Ask most people why ice is slippery and they will offer an explanation they probably learned in school: the weight of a skater presses on the ice, the pressure melts a thin film of water, and the blade glides on that film. The account is tidy, memorable, and, according to most physicists who have checked the numbers, largely wrong.

Pressure does lower the temperature at which ice melts, but only slightly. Even the narrow blade of a skate, concentrating a person's full weight on a sliver of steel, lowers the melting point by only a few degrees at most. That might matter on a mild afternoon, when the ice is already close to melting. It cannot explain why people slip on sidewalks at fifteen degrees below zero, or why a stationary shoe, pressing far less sharply than a blade, slides just as readily.

A second explanation shifts attention from pressure to motion. When an object slides across ice, friction generates heat, and that heat may melt a thin layer of water at the point of contact. Experiments have supported this idea for fast-moving objects such as skates and sled runners. But friction requires movement, and ice is slippery even at the very first instant of a step, before any appreciable heat could build up.

The explanation that has gained the most support in recent decades was first suggested in the 1850s by the physicist Michael Faraday. Faraday proposed that the surface of ice is never entirely solid. The molecules in the outermost layer, he reasoned, have fewer neighbors to hold them in place than molecules deeper inside, and so they remain loosely bound, behaving more like a liquid than a solid even well below the freezing point. Modern measurements have detected such a layer, though researchers still debate how thick it is, how liquid-like it really is, and how it changes with temperature.

None of this means that pressure and friction play no role. On a rink, all three effects may operate at once, and their relative importance likely shifts with temperature, speed, and the materials involved. What has changed is the order of the story. The surface of ice, it turns out, is slippery before anyone steps on it.

passages.title: Street Trees (paired passages)
passages.text:
Passage A

On a July afternoon, the asphalt of an unshaded parking lot can grow far hotter than the air above it, while the pavement beneath a mature tree a few steps away stays markedly cooler. Multiply that difference across a neighborhood and the effect is measurable: blocks with dense tree canopy are often several degrees cooler than nearby blocks with little shade. For cities facing longer and more frequent heat waves, this makes street trees something more than decoration. They are infrastructure, as essential in their way as storm drains or power lines, and they deserve to be funded like it.

The comparison is not merely rhetorical. A tree, like a water main, delivers its benefits for decades, but only if it survives its vulnerable early years. Cities that count trees as infrastructure tend to budget not just for planting but for watering, pruning, and replacement—the unglamorous maintenance that turns a sapling into shade.

Passage B

Announcements of tree-planting campaigns are a fixture of city politics. A mayor promises a hundred thousand new trees; volunteers dig holes; photographs are taken. Five years later, a sizable share of those trees may be dead, killed by drought, road salt, or simple neglect. And the neighborhoods that most needed shade may have received the fewest saplings to begin with, because planting programs often depend on residents to request trees and to agree to water them.

None of this means planting is a mistake. But a count of trees planted measures effort, not results. The figure that matters is canopy—how much shade actually exists, and where. A city that plants fewer trees but keeps them alive, and that places them deliberately in the hottest, least-shaded blocks, may do more good than one that plants many and tracks none.

passages.title: The Inventory
passages.text:
My aunt Theodora kept records of everything. When the lawyer handed me the keys to her house on Alder Street, he also handed me a ledger bound in green cloth, and in it, in her small upright hand, was an inventory of the house's contents: every chair, every teacup, every one of the eleven clocks, each with the date and price of its purchase. "She made my job very easy," the lawyer said. I thanked him, though it seemed to me, even then, that a person who records the price of every teacup is not making anyone's job easy so much as making sure no one can say she was careless.

I spent the first week checking the ledger against the rooms. The work suited me. I had been, for most of my adult life, the member of the family who could be relied upon to show up with a notebook, and I took a certain pride in finding that the inventory was, as far as I could tell, perfect. The clocks were where she had said they would be. The teacups numbered forty-two. In the pantry, the ledger told me, I would find a copper kettle bought in 1961 for four dollars and fifty cents, and there it was, dented exactly where I would have expected a kettle of that age to be dented.

It was on the eighth day, in the back bedroom, that I found the box. It was a shoebox, unremarkable, pushed to the back of the closet shelf behind a stack of folded blankets, and it did not appear in the ledger at all. Inside were perhaps two hundred letters, all addressed to my aunt, all from the same person, a woman named Celia whose return address changed four times over thirty years. I read the first one standing up. I read the second sitting on the edge of the bed. By the time I looked up, the light in the window had gone from white to orange, and I had not opened the ledger in hours.

I do not intend to describe the letters. They were not mine, and in any case what struck me was less what they said than where they had been kept. My aunt had written down the price of a kettle. She had numbered her teacups. And she had left out of a record so complete that a lawyer could call it easy the one thing in the house she had evidently returned to again and again, for the envelopes were soft at the edges from handling.

I had always thought of the ledger as a kind of self-portrait, and I suppose it was, though not in the way I had assumed. A list can be honest about every item on it and still be a disguise. I put the box back behind the blankets, though I knew I would have to decide, eventually, what to do with it, and I went downstairs and made tea in the copper kettle, and I did not write down anything at all.

passages.title: Ruins on Purpose
passages.text:
In eighteenth-century England, a landowner who wanted his estate to look properly distinguished might commission, alongside the lawns and lakes, a ruin. Not an old building that had fallen down, but a new one designed to look as if it had: a broken tower with an artfully collapsed staircase, a chapel wall with empty windows framing a view of the hills. Builders were sometimes instructed to leave stones scattered at the base, as though they had dropped there over centuries.

To a modern visitor, the practice can seem faintly absurd, even dishonest. We are accustomed to valuing old buildings for their authenticity, for the fact that they were actually there when the events we associate with them took place. A ruin built in 1760 to evoke the Middle Ages appears to offer the feeling of history without the thing itself, the way a souvenir offers the feeling of a trip.

But that judgment assumes the builders were trying to deceive, and there is little evidence that they were. Visitors generally knew which ruins were new; guidebooks said so, and owners were often proud of the fact. What the sham ruin offered was not a false claim about the past but an occasion for a particular state of mind. Writers of the period described the pleasure of contemplating decay: the reminder that all human works, including the grand house a few hundred yards away, would eventually crumble. The ruin was less a history lesson than a kind of philosophical furniture.

Seen this way, the sham ruin tells us less about how the eighteenth century misunderstood the past than about how it used the past. History, for these landowners, was not primarily a record to be consulted but a mood to be cultivated, a backdrop against which the present could feel both important and fleeting. The broken tower did not need to be old to do its work. It needed only to be broken.

It is tempting to feel superior to this attitude, and in some ways we are right to. The modern preservation movement, with its insistence on original materials and documented histories, has saved a great deal that the eighteenth century would have let fall or would have cheerfully "improved." Yet the impulse behind the sham ruin has not disappeared. It survives whenever a new restaurant installs reclaimed barn wood, or a housing development is named for the farm it replaced. We still want the feeling of age; we have simply become more particular about where it comes from.

passages.title: A Compass in the Eye
passages.text:
Each autumn, a young European robin that has never made the journey before leaves its breeding ground and flies hundreds of kilometers south, often at night and often alone. How it finds its way has puzzled biologists for more than a century. Young birds raised in isolation still orient in roughly the right direction when the season arrives, which suggests that at least part of the ability is inborn rather than learned.

Birds are now known to use several cues. They can read the position of the sun, correcting for its movement across the sky during the day; they can use patterns of stars, learning as nestlings which part of the night sky rotates least; and they can sense Earth's magnetic field. The last of these has proved the most difficult to explain. Magnetic fields pass through living tissue almost without effect, so a sense that detects them needs some special mechanism, and for decades no one could say what it was.

One early proposal held that birds carry tiny crystals of magnetite, a magnetic iron mineral, that act like compass needles. Clusters of iron-rich cells were in fact found in the upper beaks of pigeons, and for a time the case seemed strong. Later work showed that many of those cells were not nerve cells at all but immune cells that had accumulated iron for unrelated reasons. The magnetite idea has not been entirely abandoned, but it no longer dominates the field.

The leading alternative is stranger. In the bird's eye, a light-sensitive protein called cryptochrome may form pairs of molecules whose chemical behavior depends slightly on the direction of a magnetic field. If so, a robin might literally see the field, perhaps as a faint pattern laid over its ordinary vision. The hypothesis fits two puzzling observations: in experiments, robins could orient magnetically only when some light was present, and very weak radio-frequency noise, far too weak to move a compass needle, was enough to disrupt their orientation.

None of this has been confirmed in a living bird's eye, and the chemistry involved operates at a scale where measurements are extraordinarily difficult. What researchers can say is that the robin's magnetic sense, whatever its mechanism, appears to be a compass rather than a map: it tells the bird which way is north, not where the bird is. Knowing where to go, and recognizing when it has arrived, may depend on other senses entirely.

passages.title: The Option Nobody Wants
passages.text:
Imagine choosing between two subscriptions to a news site: an online-only plan for $59 a year and a print-and-online plan for $125. Many people pick the cheaper plan. Now add a third option, print only, also for $125, and something strange happens. Almost no one chooses print only, yet far more people now choose print-and-online. An option that almost nobody wants has changed what people pick.

Researchers call this the decoy effect. The decoy is designed to be clearly worse than one option (print-and-online gives everything print-only gives, plus more, at the same price) but not clearly worse than the other. Faced with a comparison that is easy to make, people seem to lean toward the option that wins it, even though the decoy tells them nothing new about whether that option is worth its price.

The effect is troubling for a simple model of choice in which people assign each option a value and pick the highest. Under that model, adding an option nobody chooses should not change which of the remaining options is preferred. That it does suggests that people often evaluate options by comparing them with one another rather than judging each on its own merits.

Not every study has found the effect, however. When options are described by many attributes, or when people already hold strong preferences, decoys often have little influence. Some researchers have argued that the effect appears most reliably in laboratory tasks with simple, numerical descriptions, and that its importance in everyday decisions may have been overstated.

Even so, businesses appear to have taken the lesson to heart. Menus, software plans, and appliance lineups often include an option whose main purpose seems to be making a neighbor look attractive. Whether those decoys work as well in the store as they do in the laboratory is a question the research has not yet settled.

passages.title: What Was Left Out
passages.text:
The first thing Master Brandt taught me was that a map is mostly a list of things left out. I had come to his workshop at fourteen expecting to learn how to draw rivers, and for my first month he would not let me draw anything at all. Instead he sent me out with a surveyor's chain and a notebook, and each evening he asked me what I had decided not to record.

I did not understand the question. I had recorded everything I could: the width of the road, the position of each farmhouse, the bend in the stream below the mill. When I said so, he took my notebook, turned a few pages, and asked how many sheep had been in the field behind the church. I told him I had not counted. "Then you decided," he said, "that the sheep did not matter. You were right. But you did not know you were deciding."

It took me a long time to see what he meant. A map of the parish that showed every sheep would be useless, but so would one that showed only the church. Every line was a choice about what a reader would need, and a mapmaker who made those choices without noticing them would make them badly, leaving off a ford because it was small, or drawing a ruined wall because it was large, without asking which one a traveler would care about.

Brandt himself was not an easy man to work for. He corrected my lettering until I hated the alphabet, and he once made me redraw a coastline four times because, he said, I had drawn the sea instead of the shore. But he never corrected a choice without first asking me why I had made it, and he listened to the answer as if it might change his mind. Occasionally it did.

I have made maps for thirty years now. I still hear his question at the end of each day's work, and I still find, more often than I would like to admit, that I have decided something without knowing it.

passages.title: The Joke That Will Not Cross
passages.text:
Every translator eventually meets a sentence that refuses to cross. Usually it is a joke. A pun depends on two meanings sharing one sound, and the chance that another language will happen to pair the same two meanings in the same sound is close to zero. Faced with such a sentence, the translator has three choices, none of them good: translate the words and lose the joke, keep the joke by inventing a new one, or explain the joke in a footnote and kill it.

Readers tend to assume that the first choice is the honest one. A translation, they feel, should report what the author wrote, not what the translator wishes the author had written. But this assumes that what the author wrote was a set of words. If a character in a novel makes a pun at a funeral, what the author wrote is not chiefly the words of the pun; it is the shock of someone joking at a funeral. A translation that renders the words faithfully and leaves the reader puzzled has preserved the least important part of the sentence and discarded the rest.

The second choice, inventing a new joke, is the one translators argue about most. Its defenders point out that it preserves the effect the author intended: the reader laughs, or winces, at the same moment the original reader did. Its critics answer that the new joke is, after all, the translator's, and that a book full of such substitutions slowly becomes a different book. Both sides are right, which is why the argument never ends. The question is not whether substitution is legitimate but how much of it a book can absorb before its author disappears.

The footnote is the scholar's solution, and it has its uses. In an edition meant for study, a reader may want to know exactly what the original said and why it was funny. But a joke explained is a joke that has already been told and has fallen flat; the reader understands it and does not laugh. For a novel meant to be read rather than studied, the footnote trades the experience of the book for information about it.

I have translated novels for twenty years, and I no longer believe there is a rule. I keep the words when the joke is incidental, a small flourish the book can lose without noticing. I invent when the joke carries weight, when a character is defined by wit or a scene turns on a laugh. And I reserve footnotes for the rare case where the original words matter more than any effect they produce, as in a pun on a historical figure's name that readers will meet again. What I have stopped doing is pretending that any of these choices is neutral. Each is a decision about what the book is for, and a translator who will not make that decision has simply let it be made by default.

passages.title: The Mast Year
passages.text:
In some autumns the ground beneath a stand of oaks is nearly bare. In others, acorns lie so thick that walking on them feels like walking on marbles. Ecologists call these sudden, synchronized bumper crops "mast years," and for most of the twentieth century they treated them largely as a matter of weather: a warm spring and a wet summer produced a large crop, and a late frost or a drought produced a small one.

The weather explanation has an obvious appeal, and it is not wrong so much as incomplete. Weather does affect seed production. But if weather were the whole story, the size of a crop should track the quality of the growing season fairly closely, and it does not. Researchers who compared decades of seed counts with climate records found mast years following ordinary summers and poor crops following excellent ones. More puzzling still, trees of the same species hundreds of kilometers apart, growing under different local conditions, often mast in the same year. Whatever coordinates them, it seems to be more than the weather each tree happens to experience.

One alternative begins not with the trees but with the animals that eat their seeds. A squirrel or a weevil that depends on acorns can multiply only as fast as its food supply allows. If oaks produced a steady, moderate crop every year, seed eaters would settle at a population large enough to consume most of it. By producing almost nothing for several years and then a flood of seeds all at once, the trees starve their predators down and then overwhelm them: in a mast year there are simply too few mouths to eat everything, and many seeds survive to sprout. This idea, known as predator satiation, predicts that masting should be most pronounced in species whose seeds are eaten by specialists, animals that depend heavily on that one food, a pattern that several studies have reported.

A second explanation concerns pollination. Oaks, like many masting trees, are pollinated by wind, an inefficient method in which most pollen never reaches a flower. When many trees flower heavily in the same year, the air is thick with pollen and a larger share of flowers are fertilized. A tree that flowered heavily on its own, out of step with its neighbors, would waste much of the effort.

Neither explanation tells us how trees spread across a region manage to act together. Here weather may return, though in a different role. A tree that has spent several years storing resources may need only a cue, such as an unusually warm early summer, to commit those resources to flowers. Because a single weather pattern can cover a large region, it can serve as a signal that many trees respond to at once, even if it is not, by itself, the reason they produce so many seeds.

The emerging picture, then, is not a choice between weather and strategy but a division of labor between them. Stored resources determine whether a tree is able to mast; weather often determines when; and the benefits of satiating predators and improving pollination help explain why trees that mast together have prospered. It is an arrangement that no single tree designed, but one that the forest, over many generations, has come to depend on.

passages.title: Others
passages.text:
The sign had been in the window for three weeks before my grandfather admitted that it meant what it said. CLOSING AT THE END OF THE MONTH, it read, in my mother's neat capitals, and every morning he walked past it to unlock the door as though it were a notice for someone else's shop. Customers came in to say they were sorry. He thanked them, took their watches, and wrote out repair tickets with dates two and three weeks away, some of them later than the last day of the month.

My mother had asked me to spend my Saturdays there, helping him decide what would be sold and what would be thrown out. I was fifteen and had my own ideas about how Saturdays should be spent, but I went. The shop was narrow and smelled of oil and brass. Along the back wall stood a cabinet of shallow drawers, each one labeled in his small, slanting hand: mainsprings, crowns, crystals, and one drawer, near the bottom, labeled simply "Others."

"What goes in Others?" I asked on the first Saturday.
"Things that don't fit," he said, and went back to his bench.

We did not sort much that day, or the next. He would hand me a box of parts and tell me to separate the good from the bad, and when I held up a gear and asked which it was, he would take it from me, turn it under the lamp, and begin explaining how it had been cut, by whom, and in what year, until the afternoon was gone and the box was still full. I began to suspect that the sorting was not really the point, though I could not have said what the point was.

In the third week a woman came in with a pocket watch that had belonged to her father. My grandfather opened the case, held it to his ear, and told her it needed only a cleaning. He did the work while she waited, and when she tried to pay, he waved the money away. After she left, he stood at the window for a long time with his back to me, and I pretended to be busy with the box of gears.

On the last Saturday of the month, the shop was quieter than I had ever heard it. The repair tickets had been called in, the watches returned, and the cabinet stood half empty. My grandfather sat at his bench with nothing on it. I opened the drawer labeled "Others" at last. Inside were not parts but tickets, dozens of them, yellowed, for watches that had never been collected. Each had a name and a date, some forty years old, and on each, in the same slanting hand, he had marked the repair as finished.
"Why did you keep these?" I asked.
He looked at the drawer for a while before he answered. "Somebody might come back," he said.

I did not tell my mother about the drawer. When we carried the cabinet out to her car that evening, I made sure the bottom drawer stayed shut, and when she asked whether there was anything in it worth keeping, I said I would go through it myself.

passages.title: The Length of a Wait
passages.text:
Anyone who has waited in line knows that ten minutes can feel like five or like thirty. Operations researchers, who study how to make systems run efficiently, spent much of the twentieth century trying to shorten actual waits: adding servers, smoothing the flow of arrivals, predicting busy periods. The mathematics they developed, known as queueing theory, is still used to decide how many agents a call center needs or how many booths a toll plaza should open. Their work was valuable, but it rested on an assumption that turned out to be only half true: that what people mind about waiting is the time itself.

In the 1980s a business scholar named David Maister proposed that the experience of waiting depends at least as much on how a wait feels as on how long it lasts. Unoccupied time, he argued, feels longer than occupied time. Uncertain waits feel longer than waits of known length, and unexplained waits feel longer than explained ones. People waiting alone notice the time more than people waiting in groups, and a wait that seems unfair, with someone who arrived later being served first, feels longer than an equal wait that seems fair.

Some of the most cited applications of these ideas cost almost nothing. When passengers at one airport complained about long waits for their luggage, the airport moved arriving flights to gates farther from the baggage claim. Passengers now spent most of the interval walking instead of standing, and complaints dropped, although the total time from plane to bag stayed about the same. Mirrors in elevator lobbies, which give waiting people something to look at, are often explained in the same way. So are restaurants that hand waiting diners a menu before a table is free: a wait that feels as though service has already begun seems to pass more quickly than one that does not.

Not everyone is comfortable with this approach. Critics point out that a company can use the psychology of waiting to avoid fixing the underlying problem: a theme park that entertains people in a ninety-minute line has made the wait more bearable without making it any shorter. In their view, distraction manages customers' perceptions instead of respecting their time.

Defenders reply that the two goals are not in competition. Shortening a wait often requires expensive changes, such as hiring staff or building new facilities, that take years to complete; making a wait feel shorter can be done tomorrow. A hospital that posts estimated waiting times in its emergency room, they note, has not reduced those times, but it has removed one of the main sources of distress for patients who must wait regardless.

Perhaps the most intriguing finding is how little the clock seems to matter in memory. Studies of people leaving lines suggest that their satisfaction depends heavily on how the wait ended and on whether it moved steadily, rather than on its total length. A line that advances a little at a time can be remembered more kindly than a shorter one that stalls and then lurches forward. If waiting is partly a story we tell ourselves afterward, then the people who design lines are, in a sense, also its authors.

passages.title: Camouflage Without Color
passages.text:
Octopuses are among the most skilled camouflage artists in the ocean. In less than a second, an octopus can change the color, pattern, and even the texture of its skin to match a patch of coral, a sandy bottom, or a rock covered in algae. Some species can even raise small bumps on their skin, called papillae, to imitate the rough surface of a sponge or a clump of seaweed. The speed is remarkable. What puzzles biologists is something else: by the standard tests of vision, octopuses appear to be colorblind.

Color vision usually depends on having several kinds of light-sensitive cells in the eye, each tuned to a different range of wavelengths; the brain compares their signals to tell colors apart. Octopus eyes contain only one kind. In experiments that ask animals to distinguish between colors of equal brightness, octopuses perform no better than chance. How, then, does an animal that cannot tell red from green manage to turn itself the right shade of reddish brown?

One proposal looks at the skin rather than the eyes. Researchers have found that octopus skin contains some of the same light-sensitive proteins that are found in eyes, which suggests that the skin itself might respond to light directly. In one study, small patches of skin removed from an octopus changed color when light was shone on them, which lends the idea some support. Skin that could sense its surroundings would not need to wait for instructions from the brain. But the proteins found so far appear to be of a single type, like those in the eye, so even if the skin senses light, it is not clear that it could sense color.

A second, more unusual proposal concerns the shape of the octopus's pupil. Octopus pupils are often U-shaped or dumbbell-shaped rather than round. A lens focuses different wavelengths of light at slightly different distances, an effect that makes inexpensive cameras produce colored fringes around objects. In most eyes, a small, round pupil limits this blurring. An unusually shaped pupil does the opposite: it exaggerates it. Two researchers have argued that an octopus, by shifting its focus slightly, could use these differences in blur to infer the color of an object, recovering through optics what its retina cannot detect.

Neither proposal has been confirmed, and the two are not mutually exclusive. Some biologists also point out that an octopus may not need to match colors exactly. Many of the animals that hunt octopuses see color poorly or not at all, so matching the brightness and texture of a background may be enough to stay hidden from the predators that matter most. Others note that the octopus may simply be matching the patterns of light and dark that it can see, with colors that happen to follow along.

What makes the question compelling is that it overturns an easy assumption. We tend to think of camouflage as a copy of what the animal sees. The octopus suggests that a creature can match a world it does not perceive in the way we do, and that the explanation may lie in places, such as skin or the geometry of a pupil, where we would not have thought to look.

passages.title: Keep It Sharp
passages.text:
For my first three months at the Brass Lantern, Chef Albescu said exactly four words to me that were not instructions. They were "Your knives are dull," and she said them on my first morning, in front of the entire kitchen, after watching me struggle through a crate of onions.

I sharpened the knives that night and every night after. I learned to dice an onion in the time it took the dishwasher to fill a sink. I learned that a sauce should coat the back of a spoon and hold a clean line when you drew a finger through it, and that Albescu could tell from across the room whether it would. She never said whether mine did. She would taste, set the spoon down, and move on, and I would spend the rest of the shift trying to read her silence.

Some nights I resented her for it. I would walk home past the bakery on Ninth Street, already dark, and rehearse speeches I would never give: that I had been cooking since I was twelve, that my grandmother had taught me to braise, that no one could be expected to improve without being told what was wrong. By morning the speeches seemed foolish, and I would be back at my station before anyone else, sharpening.

The other cooks had a theory about her. Albescu, they said, had trained in a kitchen in Lyon where praise was considered a kind of laziness, a way of telling a cook to stop improving. Whether that was true, no one knew. She never talked about Lyon, or about anything else that had happened before she bought the restaurant.

In my fourth month, a critic from the city paper came in unannounced. We knew who he was only because the host recognized him and came back to the kitchen white-faced. Two of the line cooks stopped working altogether, and someone dropped a pan. Albescu didn't look up. She finished plating the dish in front of her and then, without a word, slid the critic's ticket down the line to my station. It was the braised lamb, my dish, the one I had made every night for six weeks.

I don't remember cooking it. I remember the plate leaving the kitchen and the hum of the dining room and Albescu's back, which did not move. The review ran on Sunday, and I read it standing up in the tiny kitchen of my apartment. It praised the lamb in a single sentence and spent three paragraphs on the dessert, which I had not made.

On Monday I came in early, as I always did, and found a new knife at my station, a heavy carbon-steel blade wrapped in a clean dish towel. There was no note. When Albescu came in an hour later, she glanced at the knife, then at me. "Keep it sharp," she said, and went to check the walk-in cooler. I used that knife for eleven years, and I have it still.

passages.title: The Price of a Gift
passages.text:
Between 1883 and 1919, the industrialist Andrew Carnegie paid for the construction of more than 1,600 public library buildings in the United States. Many still stand, recognizable by their wide front steps, tall windows, and the word LIBRARY carved above the door. In some small towns the Carnegie library was the first public building made of stone, and for decades it was also the place where clubs met, lectures were held, and newcomers learned to read English. It is tempting to see them simply as gifts, the generosity of a wealthy man spread across the map. But Carnegie's arrangement with the towns that received them was more demanding, and more interesting, than a gift.

Carnegie would pay for a building only if a town supplied the land and promised to spend, every year, an amount equal to a tenth of his grant on books, staff, and upkeep. A town that accepted $10,000 for a building was committing itself to $1,000 a year, indefinitely. Carnegie believed that people valued what they paid for, and that a library supported by local taxes would be treated as a public responsibility rather than as a rich man's charity.

Not every town agreed, and the reasons for refusing varied as much as the towns themselves. Some refused because they could not afford the yearly cost. Others refused on principle. Labor organizers in several cities, remembering a bitter strike at one of Carnegie's steel mills, argued that money earned by cutting workers' wages should not be accepted as a favor. A few towns that had accepted the money later failed to keep their promise, and their libraries closed or were absorbed by other institutions.

The buildings themselves changed how libraries worked. In many older libraries, books were kept in closed stacks; a patron asked a clerk for a title, and the clerk retrieved it, often after a wait. Readers could see only the titles listed in a printed catalog, and many had no way of knowing what else the collection held. Many Carnegie libraries were designed instead with open shelves that readers could browse on their own, arranged around a central desk from which a single librarian could see the whole room. The design saved money on staff, but it also changed the experience of reading: a visitor who came for one book might leave with another, found by chance on a nearby shelf.

Historians still disagree about how to judge the program, and the disagreement has lasted for more than a century. To some, it was a model of partnership between private wealth and public institutions; to others, it was a way for a man with a damaged reputation to purchase gratitude. Both views may be partly right. What is harder to dispute is that the requirement Carnegie attached to his money did as much to shape American libraries as the money itself. By making towns pay to keep the doors open, he made the library a line in the local budget, and lines in a budget are hard to erase.

passages.title: Paths Nobody Planned
passages.text:
Almost every park or campus has one: a strip of bare dirt cutting diagonally across a lawn, worn down by thousands of shoes. Planners call it a desire path. It appears wherever the route a designer laid out is longer, or less direct, than the route people want to take. A sidewalk that turns two neat right angles around a lawn will, sooner or later, acquire a desire path along the lawn's diagonal.

The obvious explanation is that people are saving time, but the savings are often tiny. Observers have noticed walkers cutting a corner that spares them only a few steps, and doing so even when they are in no hurry at all. A desire path, it seems, is less about minutes than about a feeling: the satisfaction of walking straight toward the place one means to go. The path records not a calculation but an impulse, repeated by enough people that the grass gives up.

Planners have responded in roughly three ways. The first is resistance: a fence, a hedge, or a sign asking people to keep off the grass. Resistance rarely works for long; walkers step over low fences, and hedges develop gaps. The second is surrender, in which the path is simply paved. The third is patience. A story often told about a university campus describes builders who planted grass between the new buildings, waited a year, and then paved the paths the students had worn. The story may be improved in the retelling, but its appeal is easy to understand. It imagines a design process in which the people who use a place are allowed to help draw it.

Still, not every desire path deserves to be paved. Some cross ground too fragile to bear constant traffic, such as a stream bank or a bed of young trees. Others are made by a small number of people whose shortcut costs everyone else something, as when a path through a community garden tramples the plants. A desire path is evidence of what people want; it is not, by itself, a verdict on what they should get. The planner's task is to weigh that evidence, not simply to obey it.

In recent years, some planners and advocates have begun to treat these traces as data. After a snowfall, the tracks of cars and feet show which parts of a wide intersection are never used, and photographs of the untouched snow have been used to argue for wider sidewalks and shorter crossings. Researchers have also studied satellite images of worn grass to see where official paths fail. Read this way, the strip of bare dirt is a kind of vote, cast slowly, one step at a time, by people who were never asked.

passages.title: Water That Rises at Night
passages.text:
On dry summer nights in some forests and scrublands, instruments buried a few inches underground record something that seems impossible. The soil near the surface, parched by the day's heat, slowly grows wetter. No rain has fallen, no dew has formed, and no one has watered anything. By the next afternoon the moisture is gone again, and the following night it returns.

The water is coming from below, carried by the plants themselves. During the day, a tree draws water up through its roots and releases it through tiny pores in its leaves. At night those pores close, and the upward pull weakens. But a deep-rooted tree may have some roots in moist soil far underground and others in the dry soil near the surface. With the pull from the leaves gone, water moves through the root system from where the soil is wet toward where it is dry, and some of it leaks out of the shallow roots into the surrounding earth. Scientists call this hydraulic lift. It requires no effort from the tree; the water simply follows the difference in moisture, much as heat flows from a warm object to a cool one.

Researchers first noticed the nightly pattern while measuring soil moisture around desert shrubs, and for years it was treated as a curiosity. Later studies went further. Water from deep soil often carries a slightly different chemical signature than water from shallow soil, and by measuring that signature in nearby plants, researchers found that some shallow-rooted neighbors of deep-rooted trees were drinking water that had come up through the trees' roots.

It is tempting to describe this as generosity, a tree sharing its water with the plants around it. The evidence does not require that interpretation. Hydraulic lift may benefit the tree first: moist surface soil keeps its shallow roots alive through dry spells, and many of the nutrients a tree needs are concentrated near the surface, where they can be absorbed only when the soil is damp. The neighbors that drink the lifted water may simply be taking advantage of a process that exists for the tree's own sake, and some of those neighbors are its competitors.

Whatever its purpose, hydraulic lift has drawn the attention of agricultural researchers, who wonder whether planting deep-rooted crops beside shallow-rooted ones might help both survive droughts. The idea is promising but unproven. The amounts of water moved are often small, they vary widely from one species and one soil to another, and no one yet knows how much they matter in a field rather than a forest. The wet soil at midnight is a real phenomenon. How far it can be put to use is a question still waiting for its own measurements.

passages.title: The Bottom Drawer
passages.text:
Theo arrived at the hardware store on the last Saturday before the sale. The shelves were half empty, and the light through the front window fell on rows of bare pegboard. The bell over the door still rang when he came in, though no customer had come through it all morning. His grandmother, Ruth, was moving down an aisle with a roll of masking tape and a marker, writing prices on the tape and pressing it onto bins of screws and hinges. "Everything goes," she said when she saw him, "except what nobody wants."

She gave him the counter. For forty years his grandfather had stood behind it, and its drawers held what Theo expected: rubber bands, pencil stubs, a stapler, receipt books gone soft at the corners. In the bottom drawer, under a tangle of string, he found a cigar box. Inside were slips of paper in his grandfather's square handwriting. "Owe 2 hinges, R. Malloy." "Paint, 1 gal., Delgado, pay Friday." "Chain saw blade, Pruitt, after harvest." Some were dated, the oldest more than thirty years back. There were forty-one of them, and not one had been crossed out.

Theo added them up on the back of a receipt. Eight hundred twelve dollars and forty cents. He had always thought of his grandfather as a careful man, the kind who sorted every bolt by size and could tell you, without looking, which drawer held the quarter-inch washers. When Theo was small, his grandfather had let him count nails into paper sacks, and had checked every count twice. He carried the box to the back of the store, half expecting his grandmother to be angry, or at least embarrassed.

Ruth read three slips, then a fourth, and laughed. "He knew," she said. "He always knew." Malloy's barn had burned the year of the hinges. The Delgados had six children and a truck that broke down every winter. "Your grandfather thought writing it down was nearly the same as being paid," she said. "It meant he'd noticed."

Theo asked whether they should try to collect now, with the store closing and the bills still coming. Ruth closed the lid and put the box into her purse, not on the pile of things to be sold. "Some of these people will be at the sale," she said. "I'd like them to find the prices fair." Theo looked down the aisle at the strips of masking tape. Every price on them was lower than he would have guessed.

passages.title: The Wet Match
passages.text:
Translators of poetry have argued for centuries, and the argument tends to divide them into two camps. The first camp holds that a translator's duty is to the words: render each phrase as closely as the new language allows, and let readers do the work of meeting a foreign poem on its own terms. The second camp holds that a translator's duty is to the effect: produce a poem that reads as naturally in English as the original did in its own language, so that the reader never stumbles over the fact of translation. Each camp accuses the other of betrayal. To the first, the second is rewriting; to the second, the first is producing cribs that no one would mistake for poems.

Consider a simple case. Suppose a poem's speaker says, word for word, "my heart is a wet match." In the poem's language, the phrase is a common idiom for discouragement, about as ordinary as "feeling blue" is in English. A translator in the first camp keeps the wet match. A translator in the second writes something like "I feel low."

Both choices lose something, and it is worth being precise about what. The literal version gives English readers an image that is vivid and strange, a heart that will not light, when the poem's original readers would have heard only a familiar expression. It adds a freshness the original did not have. The natural version is faithful to that familiarity, but it removes an image that, although dead to native speakers, is still present in the words and may be waiting to be brought back to life. Neither version is simply faithful. Each is faithful to one thing at the expense of another.

The way out, I think, is to stop asking which camp is right and to ask instead what the phrase is doing in this particular poem. If the poem is about the flatness of ordinary speech, the dullness of the idiom is the point, and "I feel low" serves it better. If, however, the poem returns a few lines later to fire, to sparks or smoke or a stove that will not catch, then the poet has noticed the image buried in the idiom and is using it, and the translator who drops the match has dropped the poem's thread. The choice cannot be made phrase by phrase; it depends on a reading of the whole.

This is why the old argument never ends. Each camp has mistaken a method for a principle, as if one could decide in advance, for every poem, whether words or effects come first. But a translation is not a neutral transfer of content from one language to another. It is an argument about what a poem is, and like any argument, it can be made well or badly, and it can be judged only by returning to the evidence.

passages.title: The Price of a Mug
passages.text:
In a classic experiment, economists handed coffee mugs to half the students in a classroom and nothing to the other half. The students with mugs were asked the lowest price at which they would sell one; the students without mugs were asked the highest price they would pay. Standard economic theory predicted that the two prices would be about the same, since the mugs were identical and had been distributed at random. Instead, the sellers asked for roughly twice what the buyers were willing to pay. Simply owning the mug, it seemed, had made it more valuable to its owner.

The pattern already had a name, the endowment effect, coined by one of the economists a decade earlier, and the mug studies became its best-known demonstration. The researchers also offered an explanation for it. People, they argued, feel losses more sharply than equivalent gains. Giving up a mug registers as a loss, while acquiring one registers only as a gain, so an owner demands more to part with the mug than a non-owner will pay to get it. The idea was appealing because it seemed to explain a wide range of behavior, from homeowners who refuse reasonable offers to investors who hold falling stocks too long.

Later studies complicated the picture. When researchers observed experienced traders at sports-card shows, people who bought and sold cards regularly, the gap between selling and buying prices was much smaller, and among the most active traders it nearly disappeared. Other experiments found that the effect shrank when participants were told that the object was intended for trade, or when the procedure was explained more carefully. Some researchers concluded that the original gap reflected confusion about the task as much as any deep feature of human nature.

None of this means that the endowment effect is an illusion. The gap has appeared in many settings, with many kinds of objects, and ordinary experience suggests that people do become attached to what they own. But the later findings show that the effect is not a fixed law. It is strongest for objects people intend to use rather than sell, and weakest for those who are used to thinking of goods as things to be exchanged.

The debate over the mugs is, in this sense, a debate about context. A person deciding whether to sell a grandmother's ring and a dealer deciding whether to sell the same ring are not facing the same choice, even if the ring and the price are identical. Economists who once hoped to find a single rule for how people value things have learned to ask a prior question: valued by whom, and for what?

passages.title: The Year Without a Summer
passages.text:
In April 1815, Mount Tambora, a volcano on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa, erupted with a force that dwarfed anything in recorded history. The explosion killed thousands of people on the island and in the surrounding seas, and it hurled ash and gas high into the atmosphere. Then, for a time, nothing unusual seemed to happen elsewhere in the world. The strangest consequences arrived more than a year later and half a planet away.

The eruption had injected enormous amounts of sulfur gas into the stratosphere, well above the level where rain could wash it out. There the gas formed a thin haze of tiny droplets that spread around the globe and reflected part of the incoming sunlight back into space. The cooling it caused was modest when averaged over the whole Northern Hemisphere, less than one degree Celsius. But averages can hide a great deal.

In New England, snow fell in June 1816, and hard frosts returned in July and August, killing corn and other crops just as they began to ripen. In parts of Europe, cold, relentless rain rotted the harvest in the fields. Grain prices soared, and in some regions food riots broke out. Farmers who had never thought about the upper atmosphere found their year ruined by it. Few people in Europe or North America had even heard of the eruption, and no one yet understood how a volcano could change the weather an ocean away; many blamed sunspots, or simply bad luck.

The year 1816 came to be called the Year Without a Summer, and it shows something that a single average figure cannot. A small drop in mean temperature matters less than when the cold arrives. A few unseasonable frosts in the middle of the growing season can destroy a crop that would have survived a winter several degrees colder than usual.

The cold summer also left a cultural trace. Kept indoors by storms at a villa near Lake Geneva, a group of young English writers held a contest to see who could write the most frightening story, and Mary Shelley began the novel that became Frankenstein. It is tempting to say that the volcano produced the novel, and the story is often told that way. It would be more accurate to say that the weather supplied the occasion; the ideas were already Shelley's own.

passages.title: Second Chair
passages.text:
Nadia found out from the list taped to the band-room door, the way everyone at Westbrook High found out everything. First violin, first chair: Lucy Han. Second chair: Nadia Osei. She read it twice, as though the names might trade places if she gave them time, then went to her locker and stood in front of it without opening it.

She and Lucy had shared a music stand for two years. Lucy was the one who counted under her breath, who forgot her rosin, who once played an entire rehearsal with her shoe untied because she had not noticed. Nadia was the one who noticed things. She had assumed—she could see now that she had assumed—that noticing was the same as leading.

The spring concert was three weeks away. Second chair turns the pages. It is a small job, and everyone in the section knows exactly how small. At the first rehearsal Nadia turned the pages a beat late, then a beat early, and once so hard that the page tore along the binding. Lucy taped it back together without a word.

"You can just say it," Nadia told her afterward, in the parking lot.
"Say what?"
"That I'm being a baby."
Lucy shifted her case to her other hand. "I was going to say you turn pages like you're mad at them." She waited, and when Nadia did not laugh, she added, "Mr. Ferrante said it was close. He said the audition came down to the slow movement."
"That's supposed to help?"
"No," Lucy said. "It's just true."

That night Nadia played the slow movement alone in her room, recorded it on her phone, and listened back with her eyes closed. She had always thought of that movement as the easy part: long notes, nothing fast. On the recording the long notes sagged in the middle, like a rope held by people who had stopped paying attention. She played it again, and again. By eleven o'clock the notes held their shape, mostly, and she understood, without enjoying the understanding, what Mr. Ferrante had heard.

At the concert she turned every page exactly on time. Halfway through the slow movement, Lucy's note slipped flat, a small sour sag that probably no one in the audience could have named. Nadia heard it at once. Without looking up, she eased her own note down to meet it, so that for two bars the stand sounded like one instrument slightly out of tune instead of two instruments arguing. Lucy glanced at her, then back at the music.

Afterward Lucy found her by the coat racks. "You covered for me," she said.
"I noticed," Nadia said. It was not quite an answer, but Lucy seemed to take it as one, and for the first time in three weeks Nadia found that she did not mind being the one who noticed.

passages.title: The Tick and the Tempo
passages.text:
Before the early nineteenth century, a composer who wanted to tell performers how fast to play a piece had only words to work with. Italian terms such as allegro (literally "cheerful," and by extension "fast") and adagio ("at ease," and so "slow") described a general character but no exact speed, and the same word could mean different things in different cities, or to different players in the same orchestra.

The metronome promised to end that uncertainty. Patented by Johann Maelzel in 1815, the device used a weighted pendulum to tick at a steady, adjustable rate, so that a composer could specify, for example, eighty beats per minute. Ludwig van Beethoven was among its earliest champions. In 1817 he published metronome markings for his first eight symphonies, and in a letter that year he remarked that he had long thought of giving up the traditional Italian terms altogether.

The numbers did not settle the matter. Many of Beethoven's markings are startlingly fast; the one at the opening of his Hammerklavier Sonata strikes many pianists as nearly unplayable. Scholars have proposed explanations ranging from a faulty metronome to the composer's deafness to errors in copying. The most revealing explanation may be the simplest, however: a tempo that sounds right in a composer's head, with no instrument to resist the fingers and no hall to swallow the sound, may not sound right anywhere else.

Performers have always adjusted tempo to circumstances. A large, echoing church blurs fast passages that would ring clearly in a small room, so organists in such spaces often slow down. A piano with a heavy action, a singer who needs to breathe, an audience of restless children: each pulls the music toward a different speed. A number on a page cannot anticipate any of these, while a word such as adagio at least invites the performer to judge.

None of this means that metronome markings are useless. They record something real: the tempo a composer imagined, at one moment, for one ideal performance. Treated as evidence of that imagining, they are valuable. Treated as a law, they become what the old Italian words never were: a promise the music cannot always keep.

passages.title: Ending Library Fines (paired passages)
passages.text:
SOCIAL SCIENCE: Passage A is from an essay by a librarian; Passage B is from an essay by a city budget analyst. Both are original texts written for this practice set.

Passage A

For most of the twentieth century, the overdue fine seemed as natural a part of the public library as the card catalog. A few cents a day, the reasoning went, would remind borrowers that a book belonged to everyone. Over the past decade, however, many library systems in the United States have stopped charging fines, and the results have persuaded a number of librarians that the old reasoning was backward.

The first surprise was who had been paying. When library systems examined their records, they often found that blocked accounts (cards suspended because of unpaid fines) were concentrated in the poorest neighborhoods. A child who owed eight dollars could not check out another book until the debt was paid, and many such children simply stopped coming. The fine had not taught responsibility; it had taught some families that the library was not for them.

The second surprise was what happened to the books. Many systems that ended fines reported that most borrowers continued to return items on time, and several saw long-overdue materials come back as patrons who had stayed away for years returned. Without the embarrassment of an unpayable bill, bringing back a late book became an ordinary errand rather than a confession.

Nor were fines ever a large part of library budgets. In most systems they brought in less than one percent of revenue, and collecting them took staff time at the desk that could have been spent helping readers. Measured against the library's mission, fines were expensive.

Passage B

Advocates of ending library fines have assembled an appealing story, and parts of it are true. Fines do fall hardest on families with the least money, and a suspended card can keep a child away from the library at exactly the age when reading habits form. Any library that blocks children's accounts over a few dollars should rethink that policy.

But the evidence that fine-free policies cause no harm is thinner than the story suggests. Most of the reports come from the libraries themselves, typically comparing a single year before the change with a single year after it. Circulation, staffing, and the local economy all shift from year to year, and a library that has just made a well-publicized change has every reason to emphasize good news. Few systems have tracked what happens to the small share of borrowers who keep popular items for months, and those are precisely the borrowers a fine was meant to influence. When a library owns only three copies of a new bestseller, one patron who keeps a copy for an extra six weeks makes dozens of others wait longer.

Nor is the budget question as simple as it sounds. Fines may amount to less than one percent of a large system's revenue, but in a small rural library the same few thousand dollars may be a meaningful share of the money available for new books. A policy that works in a city of a million people may not transfer to a town of four thousand.

None of this is an argument for keeping fines exactly as they were. It is an argument for measuring carefully before declaring victory, and for designing policies, such as forgiving children's fines while keeping modest charges for adults, that address the real harms without assuming that removing fines costs nothing.

passages.title: The Web Beneath the Forest
passages.text:
Beneath almost any forest floor runs a web of fungal threads finer than a human hair. Many of these fungi are mycorrhizal: they wrap around or grow into the roots of trees and trade water and mineral nutrients, which their threads gather from the soil, for sugars that the trees make by photosynthesis. The partnership is ancient and, for most land plants, essential. Tree seedlings grown in sterilized soil, without such fungi, often grow poorly.

Because a single fungus can connect to the roots of several trees at once, researchers in the 1990s began to ask whether the network might do more than serve each tree individually. Could it carry resources from one tree to another? Early experiments using carbon labeled with rare isotopes found that small amounts of carbon taken up by one tree later turned up in a neighbor. A journal cover in 1997 called the system a "wood wide web," and the phrase stuck.

In the decades since, the idea has grown in the retelling. Popular books and documentaries have described large "mother trees" that recognize their own offspring and nourish them through the network, and forests in which trees warn one another of insect attacks. The image is appealing: a forest not as a crowd of competitors but as a cooperative community.

A review published in 2023 examined the field studies behind these claims and found the evidence far thinner than the popular accounts suggested. In many experiments, the tracer carbon could have moved between trees through the soil, or through roots that had grown together, rather than through fungal threads. The amounts transferred were usually small, and few studies showed that they made a measurable difference to the receiving tree's growth or survival. Whether mature trees preferentially help their own seedlings had been tested in only a handful of cases, with mixed results.

None of this means that the networks do not exist or that they are unimportant. The fungi's role in supplying individual trees with water and nutrients is well established. What remains uncertain is the more dramatic claim: that the network serves as a channel through which trees share resources with, or send signals to, one another. Keeping those two claims apart, the reviewers argued, matters for forest management as well as for science, since policies built on an exaggerated picture might, for instance, protect particular "mother trees" at the expense of approaches better supported by evidence.

passages.title: What the Horn Heard
passages.text:
When people listen to the earliest recordings of music, made in the decades around 1900, they often assume they are hearing how the musicians of that era sounded. The assumption is understandable. A recording seems to be a kind of window: the performer played, the machine listened, and the result was preserved. But the machines of that period did not listen the way a person in a concert hall did, and the musicians who made records knew it. What survives is less a window than a negotiation between players and a device with strong preferences of its own.

Before about 1925, records were made acoustically. There was no microphone and no electrical amplifier. Musicians played or sang into the wide mouth of a large horn, which funneled the sound onto a thin diaphragm. The diaphragm vibrated, and a stylus attached to it cut a wavering groove into a slowly turning disc of soft wax. Everything depended on the energy of the sound itself. A loud, focused tone pushed the diaphragm hard and cut a clear groove; a soft or scattered one barely moved it.

The horn's preferences shaped the music in ways that a listener today can easily miss. Very low notes registered poorly, so the deep pulse of a string bass often vanished from the groove. Recording directors commonly replaced it with a tuba, whose blunter tone carried better. Violins, whose sound spreads in many directions, were sometimes swapped for an odd hybrid instrument that sent the strings' vibration through a metal horn of its own, aimed straight at the recording horn. Pianos were pushed close and raised on blocks. Singers with gentle voices were told to project as though addressing the back row of a theater, and to step back from the horn on their loudest notes so that they would not overload the groove.

Time was limited as well. A ten-inch disc turning at roughly seventy-eight revolutions per minute held about three minutes of music on a side. A popular song could be trimmed to fit, but a longer work could not simply be played as written. Symphonies were divided into segments, and the performers had to stop, wait for a fresh wax blank, and begin again, sometimes at a tempo a little quicker than they would have chosen in a concert, so that a movement would fit on as few sides as possible.

None of this means that early records are worthless as evidence. They preserve real details of phrasing, ornament, and pronunciation that no written score could capture, and historians of performance study them closely. But they must be read the way one reads any document produced under unusual conditions: with attention to what the conditions encouraged and what they made impossible. A forceful delivery on a disc from 1910 may tell us less about the singer's taste than about the horn the singer was standing in front of.

When electrical recording arrived, with microphones and amplifiers, the negotiation changed its terms. A microphone could catch a quiet voice from a short distance, and a new, intimate style of popular singing, soft and conversational, became possible almost at once. It is tempting to say that the technology simply freed performers to sound like themselves. Yet microphones had preferences too. They rewarded a different kind of singer, and some voices that had thrived in front of the horn sounded harsh or thin up close. Each new device, it seems, did not remove the go-between standing between performer and listener. It replaced one go-between with another, and musicians, as they always had, learned to play to it.

passages.title: Beyond the Tragedy
passages.text:
In 1968 the ecologist Garrett Hardin published an essay with a memorable title, "The Tragedy of the Commons." Imagine, he wrote, a pasture open to every herder in a village. Each herder gains the full benefit of adding one more animal to the pasture but bears only a small share of the damage that the extra grazing does. Reasoning this way, every herder adds animals, and the pasture is ruined. Hardin himself called for "mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon," but his essay was widely read as showing that shared resources would be destroyed unless they were either divided into private property or placed under the control of a government.

The argument was elegant, and it spread quickly. It seemed to explain overfished seas, polluted rivers, and exhausted groundwater. For years many economists treated the tragedy less as a hypothesis to be tested than as a law to be applied.

The political scientist Elinor Ostrom was not satisfied. Rather than reasoning about an imagined pasture, she went looking for real ones. With her colleagues, she gathered hundreds of case studies of fisheries, forests, irrigation systems, and grazing lands that communities had shared for long periods. In a Swiss mountain village, farmers had grazed cattle on common summer pastures for centuries under rules that limited how many animals each family could send up the mountain. In parts of Spain, farmers had shared water from irrigation canals for generations, taking turns according to schedules that everyone could see and that neighbors enforced on one another. Elected water judges heard complaints at regular public meetings, and a farmer caught taking water out of turn paid a fine set by people who knew the canal as well as the farmer did. Similar arrangements turned up in fishing villages, in forests held by villages in Japan, and in shared grazing lands elsewhere.

Ostrom did not claim that every commons succeeds. Many of her cases ended in collapse, just as Hardin predicted. Her point was that collapse is not inevitable. What distinguished the lasting cases, she argued, was not private ownership or outside control but a set of arrangements the users had worked out themselves. The boundaries of the resource and the list of people entitled to use it were clear. The people bound by the rules had a voice in changing them. Users monitored one another, and penalties for breaking the rules were graduated: a first offense might bring a small fine or a public warning, while repeated offenses brought heavier ones. Disputes could be settled quickly and cheaply, often by the users themselves.

Some of her findings ran against common sense. Rules imposed by distant authorities, however well designed, often worked worse than rougher rules that users had made, partly because outsiders could not watch every field and canal, and partly because people who had no say in a rule had less reason to respect it. In several cases, a government that took over a well-run commons with good intentions destroyed the very cooperation it meant to protect.

In 2009 Ostrom became the first woman to receive the Nobel Prize in economics. Her work did not prove Hardin wrong so much as show that he had described one possible ending as if it were the only one. The herders in his story never speak to one another. Ostrom's herders do, and that difference turns out to matter a great deal.
