passages.title: The Island in the City
passages.text:
On a still summer evening, a thermometer in the center of a large city may read several degrees higher than one in the farmland a few miles away. The difference is not a quirk of a single instrument. Measured across many cities and many years, the pattern is consistent enough to have a name, the urban heat island, and it is usually strongest not in the afternoon, when the sun is high, but after dark. In a large city on a calm, clear night, the gap between downtown and the surrounding countryside can be considerably larger than it is at midday, and it tends to shrink when clouds or a strong wind move in.

That timing is a clue to the cause. Asphalt, brick, and concrete absorb much of the sunlight that strikes them and store the energy as heat. A field of grass or a stand of trees absorbs sunlight too, but plants also release water vapor through their leaves, and turning liquid water into vapor uses energy that would otherwise warm the air. A city has replaced much of that cooling vegetation with materials that soak up heat all day and give it back slowly through the night. Tall buildings add to the effect by trapping some of the heat that the streets radiate upward, and engines, air conditioners, and furnaces add heat of their own.

The consequences are not evenly shared. Within a single city, temperatures can differ sharply from one neighborhood to the next, and the hottest blocks are often those with the fewest trees and the most pavement. Because heat that lingers into the night denies the body a chance to recover, these blocks can carry real risks to health during a heat wave, especially for older residents and for people without air conditioning.

One response has been to make surfaces reflect more sunlight. A roof coated in a pale, reflective material can stay far cooler on a sunny afternoon than a dark one, and some cities now require or encourage such roofs on new buildings. The idea is simple, but its effects depend on circumstances. In a place with hot summers and mild winters, a reflective roof saves energy that would have gone to cooling. In a place with long, cold winters, the same roof also reflects sunlight that would have helped warm the building, and part of the summer savings may be lost.

Trees offer a different kind of help. A street tree shades the pavement beneath it, so less sunlight is stored in the first place, and it cools the air through its leaves. Unlike a coating, though, a tree takes years to grow, needs water and room for its roots, and can be lost to drought or disease. Planners who want quick results may favor coatings; planners who think in decades often favor trees. Many cities now try to do both.

Researchers continue to argue about how much each measure can accomplish, and the answer clearly varies from city to city. What is no longer in dispute is the basic picture: a city's temperature is partly a product of the choices made in building it, which means that it can also be changed by the choices made in rebuilding it.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Proof
passages.text:
My aunt Lena opened the bakery at four every morning, and that summer I opened it with her. I had asked for the job because I wanted money for a used guitar, and she had agreed because, as she told my mother on the phone, it would be good for me to see what four in the morning looked like. I did not yet know that she meant this as a kindness.

The first week, she let me do almost nothing. I swept flour from the corners, carried trays, and watched her hands. She worked the dough without hurrying, folding it over itself, pressing it down with the heel of her palm, turning it a quarter turn, and folding again. When I asked how she knew when it was ready, she said, "It tells you," and kept folding. I took this for the kind of thing adults say when they do not want to explain.

In the second week she gave me a bowl of my own. I folded and pressed and turned exactly as I had seen her do, and my dough stayed sticky and slack. I worked faster. It got worse. Lena glanced over once, said nothing, and went back to her ovens. By six the first customers were lined up outside, and my bowl sat on the back counter under a damp towel like something I hoped nobody would ask about.

I remember being furious, though not at her. I was furious at the dough, which seemed to have decided against me, and at myself for having believed that watching was the same as knowing. My father, who builds cabinets, once told me that the first hundred drawers a carpenter makes are practice for the next hundred. I had always heard this as a joke about patience. That morning it sounded more like a warning.

On the third Monday I came in early, before Lena, and let myself in with the key she had given me without comment the week before. I mixed a batch and, instead of copying her hands, paid attention to my own. I noticed when the dough fought me and when it gave, how it went from tacky to smooth against my palm, how it began, after a while, to push back. I did not hurry. When Lena arrived she hung up her coat, tied on her apron, and stood beside me for what felt like a long time.

"Again," she said. I folded it again. "There," she said, and walked off to light the ovens.

That was all. She did not tell me it was good, and I understood, standing there with flour to my elbows, that she was not going to. What she had given me instead was the key, the early mornings, and a bowl of my own to ruin. I had spent two weeks waiting for her to explain something that could not be explained, only noticed. The loaves from my batch went into the case at seven, unmarked among hers, and I watched a woman in a green coat buy one without looking twice.

I bought the guitar in August. I still play it, badly, most evenings. But when people ask what I learned that summer, I do not tell them about bread. I tell them that some things wait to be noticed, and that the people who know them best are often the ones who say the least about them.

passages.title: The Rhyme Problem
passages.text:
Every translator of poetry eventually faces the same choice, and most of us make it badly at least once. The poem in front of you rhymes. The language you are translating into does not share its sounds. You can keep the rhyme and bend the meaning to fit it, or keep the meaning and let the rhyme go. For years I believed that the second choice was the honest one.

My reasoning seemed sound. A rhyme is an accident of a particular language: that "heart" rhymes with "part" in English says nothing about hearts. When a translator forces English rhymes onto, say, an Italian poem, the English words are chosen for their endings rather than their sense, and the poem fills with padding—adjectives that are there only because they chime, lines turned around until they sound like nothing anyone has ever said aloud. I had read enough rhymed translations of that kind to distrust the whole enterprise. So for my first book I translated a collection of short rhymed lyrics into plain, unrhymed lines, and I was proud of how closely each line followed the original.

The book was reviewed kindly and read by almost no one. That in itself did not trouble me; translated poetry is rarely read widely. What troubled me was a letter from a reader who had grown up hearing these poems sung by her grandmother. She wrote that my versions were accurate and that she did not recognize them. "You have told me what the poems say," she wrote. "You have not told me what they are like."

I resisted her point for a long time, because accepting it seemed to mean accepting the padding I disliked. But the more I reread the originals, the more I saw that their rhymes were not decoration laid over the meaning. In many of the poems, the rhyme was where the meaning happened: a word at the end of one line would be answered, two lines later, by a word that sounded like it and meant something close to its opposite, so that the ear heard agreement while the mind heard argument. My accurate versions had kept both words and lost the collision between them.

This did not convert me to rhyme at any cost. Some of the strictly rhymed translations I had distrusted really are as bad as I thought. What changed was my sense of what a translator owes the original. I had treated a poem as a set of statements that happened to come in a pleasing shape. I now think of the shape as one of the statements. A translation can fail by distorting the sense, but it can also fail by keeping the sense and discarding what the sense was doing.

In practice this has meant compromise, and compromise in translation is never comfortable. In my second book, I used rhyme where the poems seemed to depend on it and let it go where they did not. Sometimes I used near-rhymes—"stone" and "gone," "field" and "held"—which English readers hear as an echo rather than a chime. Sometimes I moved a rhyme from the end of a line to the middle, so that the collision still happened, if a little earlier. Purists on both sides have objected. Those who value accuracy say I have taken liberties; those who value form say I have not taken enough.

They are both right, and I have stopped expecting to satisfy either. A translation is a set of losses chosen on purpose. The translator's job is not to avoid loss—that is impossible—but to decide which losses the poem can survive. I did not know how to make that decision when I began. I learned it, in part, from a woman who had never translated anything, and who knew the poems better than I did because she had heard them before she could read.

passages.title: Choosing by Default (paired passages)
passages.text:
SOCIAL SCIENCE: Passage A is from an essay by an economist; Passage B is from an essay by a policy writer. Both are original texts written for this practice set.

Passage A

In the late 1990s, a large American company changed one rule in its benefits paperwork. New employees had previously been required to sign up if they wanted to join the company's retirement savings plan; now they were enrolled automatically unless they filled out a form to opt out. Nothing else about the plan changed. The company's matching contributions, the investment choices, and the employees' freedom to leave the plan were all exactly as before.

The effect was striking. Among workers hired under the old rule, fewer than half had joined the plan within their first year or so. Among workers hired under the new rule, participation was close to ninety percent. Economists who studied the change found that the difference was largest among the employees who were least likely to save on their own: younger workers and those with lower incomes.

Findings like this one have made the default a favorite tool of policymakers. A default does not forbid anything or cost anyone money; it simply decides what happens when a person does nothing. Because doing nothing is what most people do most of the time, the choice of a default is never neutral. Someone has to choose it, and choosing it well can accomplish what years of reminders and lectures about saving could not.

To its supporters, that is the appeal of the approach: it respects people's freedom while acknowledging that freedom is exercised by busy, distracted human beings.

Passage B

No one disputes that automatic enrollment gets people into retirement plans. What the early studies also revealed, though less loudly, is that it tends to keep people wherever it puts them. Most automatically enrolled workers stayed at the plan's default contribution rate, which was often low, and left their money in the default investment, which was often a cautious fund that grew slowly. Some workers who would have joined on their own and chosen to save more ended up saving less. The default pulled them in and then held them in place.

This is not a flaw in the idea so much as the idea itself, seen from the other side. A default works because people tend to stay with whatever requires no action. That same tendency means that a poorly chosen default is hard to escape, and that its effects can last for decades, quietly, in millions of accounts.

Some designers have tried to put that tendency to better use. In one well-known program, employees agreed in advance to have their contribution rate rise automatically each time they received a raise. Because the increases came out of future pay rather than the pay employees already had, few people objected, and few later bothered to stop them; within a few years, participants' average savings rate had more than tripled. The lesson is not that defaults are good or bad but that the default is the policy. Whoever sets it is deciding for everyone who never gets around to deciding.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: What the Stripes Are For
passages.text:
Few animal patterns are as familiar as a zebra's stripes, and few have provoked as many explanations. For more than a century, biologists have proposed reasons that a horselike animal grazing on open grassland might benefit from bold black and white bands. The stripes might hide zebras from predators, confuse a lion in mid-chase, help the animals stay cool, or allow zebras to recognize one another. Each idea has had its champions. Until recently, few had been tested in ways that could tell them apart.

The camouflage idea faced an obvious objection: to a human observer, a zebra on a plain is anything but hidden. Defenders replied that lions and hyenas do not see the way people do. A study published in 2016 took that reply seriously. Its authors used what is known about the sharpness of lions', hyenas', and zebras' vision to estimate the distances at which stripes could be made out at all. In daylight, they concluded, a lion could resolve the stripes only from within about fifty meters, close enough that it would probably already have heard or smelled its prey. Farther away, the stripes would blur into a uniform gray that offered no special concealment. At dusk, when lions often hunt, the distances shrank further.

Another idea, long treated as a curiosity, concerned insects. In Africa, horseflies and other biting flies carry diseases that can be fatal to horses and their relatives, and a zebra's short coat offers little protection against them. A 2014 analysis compared the ranges of living horse species with a range of environmental factors and found that striping was most closely associated not with predators or heat but with the regions where biting flies are most active.

Correlation, though, could not show that the stripes did anything. So in 2019 a team watched horseflies approach zebras and ordinary horses kept at the same farm in Britain. The flies circled both kinds of animals about equally often. But they landed on the zebras far less often; many seemed to fly in too fast, bump against the zebra, and bounce off, as though they had failed to slow down for a landing. The researchers then dressed horses in coats of different patterns. Flies landed much less often on horses wearing striped coats than on the same horses wearing plain black or plain white coats, yet the horses' uncovered heads were landed on about equally often whatever coat the animal wore.

None of this proves that flies are the only reason zebras are striped. A trait can serve more than one purpose, and some researchers think the stripes may also matter for heat or for social life. But the fly hypothesis has something its rivals have so far lacked: experiments in which the pattern was the only thing that changed, and the animals' experience changed with it. Exactly how stripes throw off a landing fly remains uncertain. One possibility is that bold, repeating bands disrupt the way a fly judges its speed as it closes in on a surface.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Shock Absorber
passages.text:
By the time I was twelve I had a second job that no one paid me for. At the bank, at the pharmacy, on the phone with the gas company, I stood beside my father and turned his sentences into English and the clerks' sentences back into the language we spoke at home. I was good at it. I was fast, I knew which words the clerks wanted to hear, and I had learned that a request delivered politely in English got further than the same request delivered the way my father said it, which was the way a man asks for something he believes he has already paid for.

So I adjusted. It seemed harmless. When my father told the man at the gas company that the bill was a theft, I told the man there seemed to be a mistake. When the pharmacist said, with a tight smile, that she had already explained the dosage twice, I told my father she was happy to explain it again. Everyone stayed calm. Things got done. I thought of myself less as a translator than as a kind of shock absorber, taking the jolts out of every conversation before they reached the other side.

The parent-teacher conference for my brother, Tomas, was in March. He was nine, bright, and in trouble for talking in class, and his teacher, Ms. Pruitt, had asked to meet with "Tomas's father and an interpreter." The interpreter was me. Tomas sat in the hall outside, swinging his feet.

Ms. Pruitt was kind and direct. Tomas interrupted, she said. He finished other children's sentences for them, and when he was corrected, he argued. "He's very smart," she added, "but he treats every conversation as if it belongs to him." I opened my mouth to translate and heard myself begin, "She says Tomas is very smart and talks a lot," and stopped.

It was not the sentence I had been given. It was the sentence I would have wanted to hear. And I realized, sitting in that small chair with my knees near my chin, that I did not know what my father would have done with the real one, because for years I had never let him have it.

My father was looking at me. So was Ms. Pruitt. I started again, and this time I gave him everything: the interrupting, the arguing, the conversations that belonged to Tomas. It came out slower than my usual translations, with pauses where I would normally have smoothed. My father listened without moving. When I finished, he was quiet for a long moment, and I braced for the sharpness I had spent years catching before it landed.

Instead he laughed, a short, surprised laugh, and said something I did not translate right away. Then I did. "He says Tomas gets it from him," I told Ms. Pruitt. "He says he will talk to him, and he says thank you for telling him straight."

On the walk home, Tomas ran ahead, kicking at slush. My father walked beside me and, after a block, said in our language that I had been quiet in there. I said I had been trying to get it right. He nodded as if that were obvious, as if it were what he had assumed I had been doing all along, and I did not have the heart, or maybe the nerve, to tell him otherwise.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The Day of Two Noons
passages.text:
In the middle of the nineteenth century, it was noon in an American town at roughly the moment the sun stood highest over it. Because the sun appears to move westward across the sky by one degree of longitude about every four minutes, noon in Boston came several minutes before noon in New York, and noon in Chicago came well after both. For most of history, the difference had hardly mattered. A farmer had no need to know what time it was a hundred miles away, and a traveler on horseback could simply adjust a watch along the road.

The railroads changed that. A train that left one city on its local time and arrived in another on a different local time produced schedules that were hard to read and, on single-track lines where trains running in opposite directions had to meet and pass at sidings, dangerous to get wrong. Each railroad solved the problem for itself by running on the time of a chosen city, often the one where it had its headquarters, so that by the early 1880s the nation's railroads were using dozens of different times. A traveler changing trains at a large station might find several clocks on the wall, each correct for some line and none correct for the street outside.

In 1883, after years of proposals, the railroads' own association agreed on a simpler system. The country would be divided into four broad zones, each keeping the mean time of a single meridian, so that clocks in neighboring zones would differ by exactly one hour. On Sunday, November 18, telegraph signals coordinated the change, and railroad clocks across the country were reset. In towns east of their zone's central meridian, where local noon had already passed, clocks were turned back several minutes, and noon arrived a second time; newspapers called it the Day of Two Noons.

What is striking is who made the change. No act of Congress required it; the federal government did not make standard time law until 1918. The railroads simply announced a schedule, and because so much of daily life now ran on train times, much of the public followed. Many cities adjusted their own clocks within weeks. Others resisted, some for years, and objectors complained that the railroads had no right to decide what time it was. They were, in a sense, correct: the railroads had no legal authority at all. They had something more effective, which was a network that everyone else needed to use.

The episode is often told as a story about technology, and in part it is. But the deeper change was in what people understood time to be. For a town that kept local time, noon was a fact about the sky, which anyone could check by watching a shadow. Under standard time, noon became an agreement, correct only because enough people had decided to keep it. The sun did not move, and no one was asked to stop watching it. What moved was the authority to say what time it was, from the sky to the timetable.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The Space Between Words
passages.text:
Imagine opening a book and finding every line printed like this: THEREADERHADTOFINDTHEWORDSHIMSELF. By the later centuries of the Roman Empire, readers of Latin faced something close to that. Earlier Latin had often marked word breaks with small dots, but many manuscripts of this period ran their letters together without spaces, a style scholars call continuous script. To a modern eye, a page written this way looks less like a text than like a puzzle.

It was not, for its first readers, as hard as it looks. Ancient readers very often read aloud, to themselves or to listeners, and a voice sounding out syllables could hear where one word ended and the next began even when the eye could not see it. A text in continuous script was in some ways closer to a musical score than to a modern page: it recorded sounds to be performed, and the performer supplied the breaks.

The spaces arrived from an unexpected direction. In the seventh and eighth centuries, scribes in Ireland and Britain, copying Latin texts in monasteries, began separating words with small gaps. For these scribes, Latin was not a native tongue but a learned one, and the boundaries that a Roman ear might have caught at once were not obvious to them. Spacing was a way of making a foreign language easier to read accurately. Some scribes added other aids as well, such as a larger letter at the start of a sentence, so that the page itself began to show readers how to divide it. Over the following centuries, the practice spread across Europe.

Some historians have argued that this small change had large consequences. With words already separated on the page, they suggest, a reader no longer needed to sound out a line to make sense of it; the eye could take in whole words at a glance. On this view, word spacing helped turn silent reading from an unusual skill into an ordinary habit, and with it came a more private, faster kind of reading.

Other scholars think this story exaggerates the change. They point out that ancient writers mention people reading silently without treating it as remarkable. The most famous evidence on the other side comes from Augustine, who described his surprise at seeing the bishop Ambrose read with his eyes moving and his voice silent. The scene is often cited as proof that silent reading was strange in the fourth century. Skeptics reply that Augustine goes on to guess at Ambrose's reasons, perhaps to rest his voice or to avoid being drawn into discussions by listeners, which, they argue, suggests that what surprised him was a public figure's choice, not an impossible feat.

Both sides may be partly right. Spaces did not invent silent reading, which some ancient readers clearly practiced. But a habit that is possible is not the same as a habit that is easy, and a page that does some of the reader's work can change who reads, and how, without anyone deciding that it should. The history of reading, in other words, is partly a history of what pages ask of the people who read them.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The Frog That Freezes
passages.text:
In the forests of North America, a small brown frog spends the winter in a state that looks, by every ordinary sign, like death. Buried under a few inches of leaf litter, the wood frog freezes. Its heart stops beating, its lungs stop moving, and much of the water in its body turns to ice. In spring, it thaws, its heart starts again, and within a day or so it is hopping toward a pond to breed. The frog is not the only animal that survives being frozen, but it is among the best studied.

Freezing kills most animals not because cold itself is harmful but because of what ice does to cells. When water inside a cell freezes, the growing crystals can tear the cell's membrane apart, and the damage cannot be undone when the ice melts. Ice that forms between cells, by contrast, does relatively little harm. The wood frog survives by controlling where the ice forms. Ice builds up in the spaces between its cells and in its body cavity, while the water inside the cells mostly stays liquid. As ice forms outside them, the cells lose water and shrink, and the fluid left inside becomes more concentrated and harder to freeze.

That shrinking would be dangerous on its own, since a cell that loses too much water can be damaged as well. Here the frog's second defense comes in. Within minutes after ice first touches its skin, the frog's liver begins converting a stored carbohydrate called glycogen into the sugar glucose and releasing it into the blood. Over the next several hours, glucose levels rise to many times their normal level, high enough to be deadly to a human. The sugar moves into the cells, where it holds on to water and limits how far the cells shrink. The frog also builds up a waste product called urea, which appears to help in a similar way.

Not all wood frogs can survive the same degree of cold. Frogs from populations in the southern part of the range survive only a few degrees below freezing. Frogs studied in Alaska, by contrast, have survived much lower temperatures in some studies. Researchers found that the Alaskan frogs entered winter with far larger stores of glycogen in their livers, and that they accumulated more urea during the fall. In the far north, where temperatures can stay well below freezing for months, that difference may decide which frogs live to breed in spring.

Biologists are interested in the wood frog for more than its own sake. Human organs donated for transplant can be kept outside the body for only a matter of hours, partly because they cannot be safely frozen. If tissue could be cooled below freezing without damage, organs might be stored for days or weeks instead. A frog that freezes and thaws every year without harm has been treated as a natural model for how living tissue might one day be preserved, though no one yet knows how far the frog's methods can be copied.

passages.title: Heavyweight
passages.text:
For eleven Septembers, the heaviest pumpkin at the Corley County Fair had come from one of two backyards on Mill Road, and the two backyards shared a fence. Ruth Okafor had won six of those years and Dale Pruitt five, and neither of them could tell you the other's numbers without also telling you, unprompted, what had gone wrong for the other that year: the hailstorm, the split stem, the summer Dale's hose timer failed while he was at his daughter's wedding.

Ruth was seventy-three and did not consider herself competitive. She considered herself thorough. She kept a notebook for each plant—soil temperature at dawn, inches of growth, gallons of water—and in the evenings she sat on her back step with the notebook open and pretended not to listen to Dale talking to his pumpkin on the other side of the fence. He talked to it the way some people talk to horses, low and steady, and he swore it made a difference. Ruth had told her sister on the phone that this was unscientific, which was true, and that it was ridiculous, which she was less sure of.

This year both plants had done well. Ruth's was the largest she had ever grown, and from the way Dale had started whispering to his, she guessed his was too.

The storm came the night before the weigh-off. Ruth woke at two to rain hitting the windows sideways and went out in her slicker with a flashlight to check the tarps over her own plant. They were holding. Then she swung the light toward the fence and saw that the plastic sheeting over Dale's hoop house had torn loose and was snapping in the wind like a sail, and that water was pooling around the base of his pumpkin. His windows were dark. His truck was gone; she remembered then that he had driven to the city to pick up his grandson.

She stood there long enough for the rain to find its way down the back of her collar. A pumpkin left sitting in water overnight could soften on the bottom, and a soft spot could get it disqualified. She thought of the notebooks, of the six ribbons in the hall closet, and of the satisfaction—she would not pretend it wasn't there—of the one year she had beaten him by more than a hundred pounds. Then she went to the garage for the stepladder and a box of clamps.

It took her forty minutes. She dug a shallow trench with a trowel to lead the water away, and she clamped the sheeting back onto the frame, and when she finished she was soaked through and her hands were shaking, only partly from the cold. She did not leave a note.

At the weigh-off the next afternoon, Dale's pumpkin came in three pounds heavier than hers. The crowd cheered, someone handed Dale the ribbon, and Ruth clapped with everyone else and found, to her surprise, that she meant it, or at least most of it.

That evening she was on her back step with the notebook when she heard him on the other side of the fence. He was not talking to a pumpkin. "Somebody dug a trench in my hoop house last night," he said. "Clamped the plastic down, too. Nice work. Not the way I'd have done the clamps."

"I'm sure I wouldn't know," Ruth said.

There was a long pause. "Next year," Dale said, "I'm going to beat you by a hundred."

Ruth turned to a clean page and wrote the date at the top. "You can try," she said.

passages.title: Thirty-Eight Witnesses
passages.text:
In March 1964, a young woman named Kitty Genovese was attacked and killed near her apartment building in Queens, New York. Two weeks later, the New York Times reported that thirty-eight of her neighbors had seen or heard the attack and that none of them had called the police until it was over. The story became a national symbol of the indifference of city life, and it inspired a generation of research on why people fail to help strangers in trouble.

Among the first researchers were the psychologists John Darley and Bibb Latané. In a series of experiments in the late 1960s, they staged emergencies—a participant might overhear what sounded like another student having a seizure, for example, or sit in a room that slowly filled with smoke—and measured how quickly people responded. Their central finding was striking: people who believed they were alone usually helped, and helped quickly, while people who believed others were present were less likely to help at all. Darley and Latané proposed two explanations. When many people witness an emergency, each may feel less personally responsible, assuming that someone else will act. And each may look to the others for cues; if no one else seems alarmed, the situation may not seem like an emergency. The pattern came to be called the bystander effect.

The bystander effect has been reproduced in many laboratory studies, and it became one of the best-known findings in psychology. But the story that launched it turned out to be less accurate than it first appeared. Later investigations, including reporting by the Times itself, concluded that the number of witnesses had been exaggerated, that few if any of them saw the whole attack, and that at least one neighbor had called the police and another had gone outside to help.

More recently, researchers have asked whether the laboratory finding holds in real emergencies at all. In a study published in 2019, a team led by the psychologist Richard Philpot examined security-camera footage of more than two hundred public conflicts—arguments and fights—recorded in cities in the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and South Africa. In about nine of every ten conflicts, at least one bystander stepped in, whether by gesturing to calm someone down, pulling an aggressor away, or comforting a victim. And the more bystanders were present, the more likely it was that someone intervened.

These findings do not necessarily contradict the laboratory research. The bystander effect concerns the likelihood that any particular individual will help, and a person in a crowd may indeed be less likely to act than a person alone. But a victim needs only one helper. A crowd can contain many people who hold back and still, as a group, be more likely than a single witness to produce someone who steps forward. If so, the lesson of the bystander research may be less about human indifference than about how responsibility gets divided—and how, often enough, it does not disappear.

passages.title: Second Thoughts in Paint
passages.text:
When conservators at the Old Masters Picture Gallery in Dresden began cleaning Johannes Vermeer's Girl Reading a Letter at an Open Window in 2017, they expected mainly to remove centuries of yellowed varnish. They already knew, from X-ray images made decades earlier, that a large painting of Cupid, the god of love, lay hidden beneath a stretch of plain wall behind the young woman, and scholars had long assumed that Vermeer himself painted over it, having changed his mind about what the room should contain. But when the conservators analyzed the layers of paint, they found that the covering had been added well after Vermeer's death. Someone else had hidden the Cupid. After much debate, the museum removed the later paint, and in 2021 the picture went back on display with Cupid restored.

The Dresden case is unusual, but the kind of hidden layer that started the story is not. Painters have always changed their minds, and traces of those changes often survive beneath the finished surface. Art historians call such traces pentimenti, from an Italian word meaning "repentances." A few become visible to the naked eye as the upper layers of oil paint grow more transparent with age: in Pablo Picasso's The Old Guitarist, painted in the early 1900s, the faint outline of a woman's head can be seen near the guitarist's neck. Most, however, are found with tools that see below the surface. X-rays pick up dense pigments such as lead white, and infrared cameras can reveal sketches drawn on the canvas before any paint was applied.

For historians, pentimenti offer something that finished paintings rarely do: a record of decisions. A shifted arm, a hand painted in two positions, a window that was once a door—each shows that the composition we see was not the only one the artist considered. Studying such changes, scholars can sometimes tell an original from a copy, since a copyist who already knows the final image has little reason to try out alternatives. They can also watch an artist working through a problem, rejecting one solution and choosing another.

Yet pentimenti also raise an uncomfortable question about what, exactly, a painting is. If a painting is whatever its artist finally intended, then the Dresden conservators were right to remove a covering added by someone else. But the plain wall had been part of the painting for most of its existence. Generations of viewers had known the work only in that form, and some critics argued that its empty background had become part of the picture's quiet appeal. Removing it, they said, meant trading a painting people had admired for centuries for one that only Vermeer and his first viewers had seen.

No rule settles such disputes. Conservators must weigh the artist's intention against the history of the object itself, and reasonable experts disagree about how to do so. What pentimenti make clear is that a painting is less a single fixed image than a surface that holds many moments at once: the artist's first ideas, second thoughts, and final choices, and sometimes the choices of people who came later.

passages.title: Seconds Ahead of the Shaking
passages.text:
In an earthquake, the ground begins to shake only after waves of energy have traveled outward from the fault where rock suddenly slipped. Those waves do not all travel at the same speed. The first to arrive, called P waves, move through rock at roughly six kilometers per second and usually cause only mild shaking. The slower S waves, at about three and a half kilometers per second, and the surface waves that follow them do most of the damage.

Earthquake early warning systems take advantage of this gap. A network of sensors detects the first P waves near the source, computers estimate the quake's location and size within a few seconds, and an alert is sent—by radio, by cell phone, or directly to machinery—to places farther away. Because electronic signals travel almost instantly compared with waves moving through rock, the alert can outrun the damaging shaking.

How much warning a place receives depends on its distance from the source. A city 100 kilometers away might receive fifteen or twenty seconds of notice; a town 30 kilometers away might get only a few. Closest to the source lies what seismologists call the blind zone, where the damaging waves arrive before any alert can be issued.

A few seconds may not sound like much, but the uses are concrete. Trains can begin braking, surgeons can lift their instruments away from patients, elevators can stop at the nearest floor and open their doors, and students can take cover under their desks. Mexico City has operated a public warning system since the early 1990s. The city lies roughly 300 kilometers from the coastal faults that produce many of its strongest earthquakes, which gives it unusually long warnings. Japan's nationwide system sends alerts through television, radio, and phones.

Early warning has limits. A system must estimate an earthquake's size from only the first few seconds of data, and the largest earthquakes can keep growing for a minute or more after they begin, so early estimates may be too low. False alarms are another risk: alerts that turn out to be unnecessary can teach people to ignore later ones. Engineers are working on faster detection and better estimates, but no system can eliminate the blind zone. The gain from early warning is measured not in minutes but in seconds—and in what people manage to do with them.

passages.title: What Fine Looks Like
passages.text:
For three summers, Mara Lindqvist had watched the water at the Elm Street pool from a white chair six feet above the deck, and in all that time she had never pulled anyone out. She had blown her whistle at boys running on the wet concrete, reminded a hundred children to walk, and once fished a set of car keys out of the deep end. But the rescues she practiced every June in training—the reaching assists, the rear approaches, the long tows to the wall—remained exercises, performed on teenagers pretending to struggle.

Her younger brother teased her about it. "Professional sitter," he called her, and at dinner he would ask, with exaggerated concern, whether anyone had been saved from boredom that day. Mara laughed along, but privately she had begun to wonder what the job was for. Every forty-five minutes she rotated to a new chair and scanned her section of water the way she had been taught: left to right, near to far, every face, every ten seconds. Nothing ever happened in it.

The last Saturday of August was hot and crowded. Mara was in the chair by the shallow end when she noticed a small boy in orange trunks near the rope that marked the drop-off. He was not splashing or calling out. His head was tilted back, his mouth at the surface of the water, and his arms pressed down at his sides as if he were trying to climb a ladder no one else could see. A woman two yards away was laughing with a friend and had not turned around.

Afterward, Mara could not remember deciding anything. She remembered the whistle—three short blasts—and the slap of the water, and the weight of the boy against her arm, lighter than any of the teenagers she had practiced on. She remembered setting him on the deck and the sound of his coughing, which was the best sound she had ever heard. He was fine. His mother, who had been sitting by the fence, reached them before the other guards did.

That evening her brother asked, as usual, whether she had saved anyone. Mara said, "One," and went on eating, and for once he had nothing to add.

She thought later that the moment itself had lasted less than a minute. What had made it possible were the thousands of minutes before it: the ten-second scans of water where nothing happened, the training she had sometimes found pointless, the habit of looking at every face even when every face was fine. The boy had not looked like someone drowning. He had looked, she realized, almost exactly like someone who was fine. She had seen the difference only because she had spent three summers learning what fine looked like.

passages.title: Language Nests
passages.text:
Of the roughly 7,000 languages spoken today, linguists estimate that about 40 percent are endangered, meaning that fewer and fewer children are learning them. When the last speakers of a language die, a way of naming the world can disappear with them, along with songs, stories, and knowledge of local plants and places.

For a long time, many observers assumed that this process could not be reversed. Once parents stopped speaking a language to their children, the thinking went, the language was on a one-way path to silence. Several communities have since challenged that assumption.

The best-known example is Hebrew. For many centuries it was used mainly in prayer, scholarship, and writing rather than in everyday conversation. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, families and schools in what is now Israel began using it as a language of the home and the classroom, and today it has millions of native speakers. Other communities, facing far greater odds, have tried to follow a similar path.

In New Zealand, the Māori language declined sharply during the twentieth century, as many Māori families moved to cities and children were discouraged from speaking it in school. By the 1970s, surveys found that relatively few Māori children could speak it. In 1982, Māori communities began opening kōhanga reo, or "language nests": preschools in which elders spoke only Māori with young children throughout the day. Within a decade, hundreds of nests had opened, and many graduates went on to Māori-language primary schools. A similar approach was adopted in Hawaiʻi, where by the early 1980s fewer than fifty children were thought to speak Hawaiian as a first language.

These programs share a central idea: a language survives only if children use it, and children learn a language most fully when they hear it early and often. Adult classes, dictionaries, and recordings all matter, but they cannot by themselves make a language part of daily life. Researchers who study revitalization often point to the home as the decisive setting. A language that children hear at school but never at the dinner table may become something they know about rather than something they speak.

That is why revitalization is so difficult. Many parents in endangered-language communities never learned the language themselves; they must learn it as adults before they can pass it on, often while working and raising families. Even so, the results so far suggest that the outcome is not fixed. Languages that once seemed to be fading have gained new young speakers, not because of laws or scholarship alone, but because families decided to speak them.

passages.title: Letters by Hand
passages.text:
The summer I turned sixteen, my mother arranged for me to work in my aunt Rosalind's shop, which she described to her friends as "a sign business" in the tone people use for a relative who has taken up the accordion. I expected to sweep floors. Instead, on the first morning, Rosalind handed me a brush with a chisel-shaped tip, a jar of black enamel, and a sheet of glass, and told me to paint the letter O until I hated it.

I did hate it, by noon. My O's sagged on one side or bulged on the other, and the paint pooled at the bottom of each stroke like water collecting in a footprint. Rosalind looked at each one without comment and then scraped the glass clean with a razor. When I asked how many more she wanted, she said, "That depends on the O."

Most of her customers, I learned, were not looking for anything she offered. A print shop across the highway could cut vinyl letters for a storefront in an afternoon, in any of four hundred typefaces, for less than she charged for a day of work. People came to Rosalind when a window had an unusual curve, or when an owner wanted the gold leaf that the print shop could not imitate, or, more often, when someone's grandfather had once had a sign painted and the family wanted the new one to look the way the old one had. She kept a box of photographs of those old signs, many of them by painters who had died before I was born, and she studied them the way other people read letters.

By the third week, my O's had stopped sagging. I was promoted to the rest of the alphabet and then, in August, to a real job: the name of a hardware store, to be painted on its front window in letters a foot high. I worked from Rosalind's chalk outline and did not breathe through the first R. When I finished, I stepped back to the curb and saw what I had not seen up close. The second R leaned a few degrees farther than the first, and the S was a hair too wide at the bottom.

I offered to scrape it off. Rosalind stood beside me for a long time, long enough that the owner came out to see what we were looking at. "Leave it," she said finally. "A machine would have made both R's the same. That's how people would know a machine made them." The owner, who had been frowning at the S, seemed to decide that he had been admiring it all along.

I have since come to doubt that she believed this entirely; she scraped her own mistakes off without a second look. But I think she understood something about the people who came to her shop that I did not yet understand. They were not paying for letters. They were paying to have someone stand on the sidewalk and look, for a long time, at the front of the place they had built. On the bus home that evening, I noticed the signs along the route for the first time—which ones had been cut and which had been painted—and I found that I could tell.

passages.title: Steering by Starlight
passages.text:
A dung beetle that has shaped a ball of dung faces an immediate problem: other beetles at the same pile would rather steal a finished ball than make their own. The safest strategy is to leave quickly, and the fastest way to leave a crowded spot is to travel in a straight line. A beetle that wanders in circles may end up back where it started, among the thieves.

Rolling a ball in a straight line is harder than it sounds. The beetle pushes the ball backward with its hind legs while walking on its front legs, head down, facing away from where it is going. Before setting off, many beetles climb on top of the ball and turn in place, a movement researchers sometimes call a "dance." Studies suggest that the beetle is using this moment to fix its bearings on something in the sky.

By day, that something is often the sun. But some species roll their balls at night, and in the early 2000s researchers working in South Africa showed that these beetles could use the pattern of polarized light around the moon to hold a course. That finding raised a further question. On moonless nights, the beetles still traveled in fairly straight lines. What were they steering by?

To find out, a research team led by Marie Dacke brought beetles into a planetarium, where the night sky could be controlled. When the dome showed a full starry sky, the beetles rolled almost as straight as they did outdoors. When it showed only a diffuse band of light corresponding to the Milky Way, with no individual stars, they still kept a steady course. When the dome was dark, they wandered. In another test, outdoors, the researchers fitted some beetles with small cardboard visors that blocked their view of the sky. Those beetles also wandered, while beetles fitted with transparent visors did not.

The results suggested that the beetles were steering not by particular stars but by the glow of the Milky Way as a whole. This made sense, the researchers argued, because a beetle's compound eyes are probably not sharp enough to pick out most individual stars, while the bright band of the galaxy is visible to them. The beetle does not need to know where it is going, only to keep going the same way.

The study drew wide attention, in part because it was the first to show an animal orienting by the Milky Way. But the researchers were careful about what it did not show. The beetles were not navigating to a destination, as migrating birds do; they were simply holding a straight line. And the experiments did not rule out the possibility that, under some skies, the beetles also use other cues, such as the brightest stars or the moon when it is up.

passages.title: Golden Joinery
passages.text:
Most methods of repairing a broken bowl aim at disappearance. A good glue line is a thin one; a skilled restorer fills chips and matches the glaze so that a visitor to a museum cannot tell where the object was damaged. The Japanese practice known as kintsugi, or "golden joinery," takes the opposite approach. The pieces are rejoined with lacquer, and the seams are then dusted or painted with powdered gold, so that the repair becomes the most conspicuous feature of the object.

A story often told about kintsugi's origin places it in the fifteenth century. According to the story, a Japanese military ruler sent a cracked tea bowl to China to be mended, and it came back held together with crude metal staples. Disappointed, Japanese craftsmen set out to find a repair that would be beautiful in its own right. Historians treat the story with caution; no document from the period records it, and lacquer had been used to mend ceramics in Japan long before. But the story persists, perhaps because it captures something true about the practice: kintsugi is a judgment about what a repair should look like, not merely a technique for making one.

The traditional method is slow. The lacquer, made from the sap of a tree, hardens only in warm, humid conditions, and each layer must cure for days before the next is applied. A single bowl may take weeks to restore. In recent years, kits sold online have promised "kintsugi in an afternoon," using quick-setting epoxy and gold-colored powder. Some practitioners object that these kits imitate the appearance of kintsugi while abandoning the patience that once made it meaningful. Others reply that the gold seam, not the lacquer, is what most people value, and that a cheaper method has simply brought the idea to more households.

Writers who admire kintsugi often describe it as a philosophy of embracing imperfection, and some go further, presenting it as a lesson for mending damaged relationships or recovering from personal loss. These comparisons are appealing, but they can obscure what the craft actually involves. A kintsugi repair does not pretend that the break never happened; neither does it celebrate breakage for its own sake. No restorer smashes a bowl in order to mend it. The practice values the object's whole history, including the accident, and asks the mender to make that history visible with care.

Perhaps that is why kintsugi bowls are rarely displayed as curiosities. In a tea room, a mended bowl is still used for tea. Its golden seams are not a sign that the bowl has been retired, but a record that someone thought it was worth keeping.

passages.title: Too Many Jams?
passages.text:
In a study published in 2000, psychologists Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper set up a tasting booth for jams in an upscale grocery store. On some days the booth offered 24 flavors; on others, it offered 6. The larger display attracted more shoppers to stop, but the smaller one produced far more sales: roughly 30 percent of the shoppers who stopped at the 6-flavor booth bought a jar, compared with about 3 percent at the 24-flavor booth.

The finding seemed to overturn a common assumption. Economists had long reasoned that more options can only help a shopper, who is free to ignore the ones she does not want. The jam study suggested instead that a large assortment could discourage people from choosing at all, an effect that came to be called "choice overload." The idea spread quickly into business books and advice columns, and some companies reduced the number of products they offered.

Later researchers were less certain. When a team of psychologists gathered the results of fifty experiments that had tested the effect, they found that the average effect across all of them was close to zero. Some studies found that larger assortments reduced choosing; others found that they increased it; many found no difference at all.

This did not mean that the original study was wrong. Rather, it suggested that choice overload depends on circumstances. Researchers have since proposed several conditions under which large assortments are most likely to discourage choosing: when shoppers have no clear preference before they start, when the options are hard to compare, and when shoppers must decide quickly. A person who already knows she wants strawberry jam, for example, is unlikely to be troubled by a shelf of thirty flavors.

The history of choice overload illustrates a pattern that is common in the study of human behavior. A striking result is reported, widely repeated, and then tested again under many conditions. What emerges is usually less dramatic than the original claim and more useful: not a simple rule that fewer options are better, but a description of when, and for whom, they might be.

passages.title: What the Viewer Keeps
passages.text:
People who learn that I write subtitles for a living usually ask me the same question: isn't it frustrating to throw so much away? They imagine that a good translation keeps every word, and that a subtitle, which must fit in two short lines and vanish after a few seconds, is simply a translation with pieces missing. During my first year in the job, I imagined the same thing.

The first film I worked on was a comedy about a family running a failing restaurant. In one scene the grandmother delivers a long, furious speech to a supplier, piling insult upon insult in a regional dialect that even many native speakers would struggle to follow. I translated every insult. The result filled four lines, stayed on screen for less than five seconds, and was, as my supervisor pointed out, unreadable. "The audience doesn't need to know what she said," she told me. "They need to know that she won."

That remark changed how I thought about the work. A viewer watching a film with subtitles is doing two things at once: reading and watching. Every word I add pulls the viewer's eyes away from the actors' faces, where much of the meaning lives. A shrug, a pause, a glance at another character—these say things that no subtitle could, and a viewer who is busy reading misses them. The question I learned to ask was not "What did the character say?" but "What does the viewer need in order to follow what is happening on screen?"

Sometimes the answer is surprisingly little. When a character greets a neighbor with a long, formal blessing, a subtitle reading "Good morning" may be enough, because the warmth is in the actor's voice. At other times the answer is more than the dialogue contains. A joke that depends on a pun in the original language must often be replaced with a different joke altogether, one that does the same work in the scene even though it says something else. I once spent most of an afternoon on a single line—a play on the similar sounds of the words for "wedding" and "tax"—before settling on a joke about in-laws that made the test audience laugh at the same moment the original audience had.

None of this means that subtitles are a lesser kind of translation. I have come to think that they are a more honest one. A printed translation of a novel can create the illusion that nothing has been lost, because its reader never sees the original. A film's audience, however, hears the actors' real voices beneath every line I write. If the grandmother shouts for ten seconds and my subtitle says only "You thief!", anyone watching knows that I have made a choice. The subtitle does not pretend to be the original; it stands beside it, and the viewer can feel the difference.

I still lose things, of course. But I no longer think of my job as deciding what to throw away. I think of it as deciding what the viewer should keep.

passages.title: The Fairy Circles
passages.text:
Across a long strip of the Namib Desert in southwestern Africa, the grassland is dotted with bare, circular patches of sand, typically several meters across, each ringed by a band of grass taller than the grass around it. There are millions of them. Seen from the air, they are spaced with surprising regularity, almost like the cells of a honeycomb. People in the region call them fairy circles.

Over the years, explanations have ranged from poisonous plants to gases seeping up from underground. Two have survived serious testing. According to the first, the circles are the work of sand termites, which feed on the roots of grasses. By killing the plants in a ring around their colony, the termites create a bare patch from which no roots draw water. Rain then soaks into the bare sand and is stored below the surface, where it supports both the termites and the taller grass at the circle's edge. Supporters of this view point out that when they dug into circles, they found sand termites in nearly all of them.

According to the second explanation, no animal is needed at all. Where water is scarce, grasses compete for it, and a plant growing close to others is drained by its neighbors. Mathematical models show that, when rainfall is low enough, this competition alone can produce bare patches in a regular pattern: each patch acts as a reservoir that feeds the ring of grass around it, while the thirsty ring keeps new grass from taking hold inside. On this view, termites are common in the circles because the circles, with their stored water, are good places for termites to live, not because termites made them.

Each side has evidence the other must answer. The regular spacing of the circles is hard to explain if every circle is the work of a separate colony, since the colonies would have to space themselves almost perfectly—though some insects do keep their distance from neighboring colonies by fighting them. Similar circles were later reported in Western Australia, where researchers did not find termites consistently associated with them. Supporters of the termite explanation reply that the Australian circles may form differently, and that a pattern found in two places need not have one cause in both.

Many researchers now suspect that both processes may be at work. Termites might start circles that competition for water then shapes and spaces, or competition might create a pattern that termites take advantage of. Settling the question will require experiments, such as removing termites from some circles and watching whether grass grows back. Such experiments are slow, because individual circles can persist for decades. Whatever the outcome, the fairy circles are a reminder that the regularity of a pattern, however striking, cannot by itself reveal what produced it.

passages.title: The Unguarded Queen
passages.text:
Every Sunday since I was eight, my grandfather and I had played chess at the card table by his window. He never let me win. When I was nine and cried after losing my queen, he handed me a tissue and said, "A piece you leave unguarded is a piece you have given away," and then he took my rook. I hated him a little that afternoon. By the time I was twelve, I could repeat the sentence along with him.

The spring I turned fifteen, I began to win. The first time, I thought it was luck. The second time, I thought I had finally learned something. By the fifth time, I had started telling my friends at school that I could beat my grandfather, a man who had once played in tournaments, and I liked the way they looked at me when I said it.

Then, in early May, he moved his bishop to a square where my knight could take it for nothing. I stared at the board. It was exactly the kind of move he had spent seven years teaching me never to make. I took the bishop, and he nodded as if I had done something sensible, and twenty minutes later I won again.

That night I lay awake replaying the game. There were only two explanations I could think of, and I did not like either of them. Either he was letting me win, which meant that every victory I had bragged about was a gift, or he was no longer seeing the board the way he used to, which meant something I did not want to name.

The next Sunday I decided to find out. Halfway through the game, I left my queen where his knight could take it—a mistake so plain that the nine-year-old version of me would have seen it. I kept my eyes on the board and waited.

He looked at the queen for a long time. His hand moved toward the knight, stopped, and settled on a pawn instead, which he pushed forward one square. Then he looked up at me, and I could not tell whether his expression was kind or confused, or whether there was any difference.

I could have asked him. The question was right there, as plain as the unguarded queen. Instead I moved my queen to safety, and we played on, and I lost, and I was more grateful for that loss than for any of my wins. When we finished, I set the pieces back on their starting squares the way he had taught me, white on the right, and asked whether he wanted to play again next week.

passages.title: Making Room for Cars
passages.text:
Passage A

For most of the last century, American cities have required builders to provide a minimum number of parking spaces with every new apartment building, store, and office. The rules were meant to keep cars off crowded streets. Their effects have reached much further. A parking space in a garage can cost tens of thousands of dollars to build, and that cost is folded into rents and prices whether or not a tenant owns a car. On small or oddly shaped lots, the required spaces can make a project impossible, so the housing is never built at all.

Minimum parking rules also shape how people travel. When every destination promises free parking, driving becomes the easy default, and buses and bike lanes struggle to attract riders. Several cities have recently eliminated their minimums, leaving it to builders to decide how much parking their customers actually want. Builders have not stopped providing parking; they have simply provided less of it in places where residents can walk or take transit. That, rather than any single number written into a code, is how parking ought to be decided.

Passage B

Critics of parking minimums make a strong case, and in dense neighborhoods with frequent trains and buses, I find it persuasive. But most Americans do not live in such places. In a suburb where the nearest bus comes once an hour, a household without parking at home is not a household without a car; it is a household that parks on the street. When a new building is approved without spaces, the cars of its residents do not disappear. They spill onto nearby blocks, where longtime residents, many of whom bought their homes counting on curbside parking, suddenly cannot find a space.

None of this means that the old rules should stay as they are. Many codes demand far more spaces than buildings ever fill. A better approach would be to lower minimums where transit is strong and to tie any remaining requirements to how often buses actually run. Eliminating minimums everywhere at once trades one uniform rule for another, and uniform rules are exactly what got cities into trouble in the first place.

passages.title: Off the Script
passages.text:
When I started playing the saxophone at fourteen, I believed that improvising meant playing whatever came into my head. My teacher, a retired bandleader named Mr. Okafor, let me believe this for exactly one lesson. He put on a recording, told me to play along with "anything you like," and listened while I honked and squealed for three minutes. Then he lifted the needle. "That was free," he said. "It was not improvised."

I did not understand the distinction until much later. Jazz musicians who improvise are not starting from nothing. They are working within a set of chords that repeat beneath the melody, and every note they choose either fits those chords, leans against them, or clashes with them for a moment before resolving. A listener may hear a solo as spontaneous, and it is, but it is spontaneous in the way a conversation is spontaneous: the speakers have not rehearsed their words, yet they share a language whose rules they rarely break by accident.

Mr. Okafor's method for teaching that language was old-fashioned. He had me transcribe solos—listen to a recording of a great saxophonist, slow it down, and write out every note by ear. It took me most of a month to transcribe a single two-minute solo. I complained that I wanted to find my own voice, not copy someone else's. He answered that a voice is built from what it has absorbed, and that nobody ever learned to speak by inventing words.

He was right, though not entirely. After two years of transcribing, I could play convincing imitations of half a dozen musicians, and for a while that was all I could do. My solos were collages of borrowed phrases, stitched together competently and saying nothing in particular. The breakthrough, when it came, was not a matter of learning more. It came on a night when I forgot a phrase I had memorized halfway through playing it and had to find my own way back to the chord. What I played was clumsy. It was also, for the first time, mine.

I teach now, and I still assign transcriptions. But I also tell my students about that night, because I think the lesson runs both ways. Without the language, there is nothing to say. Without the occasional mistake that forces you off the script, there is no one saying it.

passages.title: Written in Light
passages.text:
On a summer evening in a meadow, the flashes of fireflies can look random, a scattering of sparks with no pattern at all. To the fireflies themselves, they are anything but. In many species, the flashes are a conversation between potential mates, and each species has its own dialect.

In a typical exchange, a male flies over the grass flashing a pattern specific to his species: a single long flash, perhaps, or a quick double pulse repeated every few seconds. A female of the same species, perched on a leaf below, answers after a precise delay. The timing of her reply matters as much as the flash itself. A male who sees a flash at the wrong interval is likely to keep flying, because the reply does not come from a female of his kind. When the timing is right, he lands and approaches, and the two may exchange flashes several more times before they meet.

Because the code is so specific, it can be exploited. Females of one group of fireflies, known as Photuris, are able to imitate the replies of females from other species. A male of another species who sees the right response at the right delay flies down expecting a mate and instead finds a predator. The Photuris female eats him. She gains more than a meal: the males she catches carry defensive chemicals that make fireflies distasteful to spiders and birds, and Photuris females, which cannot make these chemicals themselves, take them in from their prey.

Researchers have found that some Photuris females adjust their imitation to whatever species of male is flying nearby, switching from one reply pattern to another during a single evening. This flexibility has led some biologists to describe the females as aggressive mimics. Others prefer more cautious language, noting that the switching may be less a matter of deliberate choice than of a simple rule: answer whatever flash pattern appears overhead.

For the males being imitated, the risk creates a kind of arms race. A male who approaches every reply quickly may find mates sooner, but he is also more likely to be eaten. In some populations, males of preyed-upon species approach answering females more slowly and flash more times before landing, as if testing the reply. The meadow's apparent randomness, in other words, conceals not only courtship but also deception, appetite, and caution, all written in light.

passages.title: Bulbs
passages.text:
Mr. Halvorsen had sold his house in August, and he was moving to his daughter's apartment across the state on the first of November. So I did not understand why, on a gray afternoon in late October, he asked me to help him plant two hundred tulip bulbs along the front walk.

"They won't come up until April," I said, kneeling beside him with the trowel. I was fourteen and believed that pointing out the obvious was a kind of help.

"That's right," he said, and handed me another bulb. He showed me how deep to set each one—three times its own height—and which end to point toward the sky. His hands, which had built half the fences on our street, shook a little now, so he let me dig while he sorted the bulbs by color in his lap: red ones near the steps, yellow ones by the mailbox, a few white ones scattered where, he said, they would surprise people.

We worked until the light went thin. I kept waiting for him to explain, and he kept not explaining. Once he stopped and looked at the house for a long time, and I looked at the dirt, because that seemed like the polite thing to do.

The family who bought the house moved in the week after he left. They had a little boy who rode a red tricycle up and down the walk all winter, over the place where the bulbs were sleeping. I watched from my window and said nothing to anyone.

In April the tulips came up exactly as he had arranged them, red by the steps and yellow by the mailbox. The white ones appeared in odd places, one beside the drain spout, two under the maple, and the boy's mother stood in the yard one morning with her coffee, turning slowly, as if someone had left her a message she was still working out how to read.

I wrote to Mr. Halvorsen that week. I told him about the colors and the white ones under the maple. I did not ask him why he had planted them. By then I thought I knew, and I suspected that if I wrote the reason down, it would come out smaller than it was.

passages.title: The Missing Step
passages.text:
Almost every cook knows the sting: a few strokes of the knife through an onion, and the eyes begin to water. For about three decades, chemists believed they understood why. An intact onion, they knew, stores sulfur-containing compounds in one part of each cell and an enzyme called alliinase in another. Cutting ruptures the cells, the two meet, and a chain of reactions begins. The explanation seemed complete: alliinase broke down the sulfur compounds, and the products drifted up and irritated the eyes.

The trouble was that alliinase does much the same work in garlic, and garlic does not make people cry. In 2002, a team of researchers in Japan reported that the explanation was missing a step. Alliinase, they found, produces an unstable intermediate compound. In garlic, the corresponding compound mostly reacts with itself, forming the compounds behind garlic's sharp smell. In onion, a second enzyme seizes most of it first and converts it into a volatile compound that is the real irritant. The researchers named the newly identified enzyme lachrymatory-factor synthase, after the Latin word for tears.

The discovery mattered for more than chemistry trivia. Because the irritant and many of the compounds that give onion its flavor come from the same starting material, cooks and growers had long assumed that a tearless onion would also be a bland one. The new finding suggested otherwise. If only the second enzyme could be switched off, the intermediate compound might follow the garlic-like path instead, and the onion might keep, or even gain, flavor while losing its sting.

Researchers in New Zealand and Japan later tested the idea by using genetic techniques to suppress the enzyme in onion plants. The resulting onions released far less of the irritant, and chemical analysis found higher levels of other sulfur compounds associated with flavor. Those onions were never sold, however; genetically modified onions faced regulatory and consumer hurdles. A Japanese company took a slower route, breeding onions over many years, without genetic engineering, that produce little of the irritant. Its tearless onion reached stores in Japan in the 2010s.

Familiar kitchen advice, meanwhile, makes sense in light of the chemistry. Chilling an onion before cutting slows the enzymes and the evaporation of the irritant. A sharp knife crushes fewer cells than a dull one, so it releases less of the starting material. Cutting beside an open window or a fan simply carries the irritant away before it reaches the eyes. None of these tricks stops the reaction; each only reduces how much of the irritant forms or how much of it arrives.

For the onion, of course, the reaction was never aimed at cooks. The two-step chemistry appears to be a defense: an animal that bites into the bulb breaks its cells and is met with a burst of irritants. That the same defense works on a person holding a knife is, from the onion's point of view, an accident.

passages.title: The Single Eye
passages.text:
Sometime around 1415, the Florentine architect Filippo Brunelleschi stood in the doorway of the unfinished cathedral and painted a small panel of the octagonal Baptistery across the square. What he did next is better remembered than the painting, which has not survived. He drilled a hole through the panel at the point toward which the building's receding lines converged, and he invited viewers to look through the hole from the back, at a mirror held in front of the painted side. Seen this way, from a single fixed position, the reflected image was said to be hard to tell apart from the building itself.

The demonstration is usually told as the moment when painters discovered how vision works. Within two decades the humanist Leon Battista Alberti had set down a method in his treatise On Painting, describing the picture as a window through which the viewer looks at the scene, and the rules of linear perspective spread through the workshops of Italy and then of Europe. In the familiar telling, earlier painters had simply been wrong about space, and the Renaissance corrected them.

That telling is not false, but it is incomplete. In a 1927 essay, the art historian Erwin Panofsky called perspective a "symbolic form," by which he meant that it expresses a particular way of conceiving the world rather than a neutral record of it. The system rests on assumptions that no actual viewer meets: a single eye rather than two, an eye that does not move, and a visual field that is flat rather than curved. Brunelleschi's peephole is revealing precisely because it enforces those assumptions. The illusion succeeds only when the viewer is made to see as the system requires.

None of this makes perspective arbitrary. Its geometry is exact: given the position of an eye and a flat picture plane, the place where each point of a scene should appear can be calculated. What is conventional is the decision to treat that single, motionless eye as the standard of truth. Medieval painters who enlarged a saint or showed the inside and outside of a building at once were not failing to see; they were answering a different question, about importance or about what a viewer needed to know, rather than about how a scene would look from one spot.

The distinction matters because conventions, once learned, become invisible. A modern viewer who finds a fourteenth-century altarpiece "flat" or "naive" is judging it by rules that were themselves invented, however well they were founded. To see Brunelleschi's mirror clearly is to see both achievements at once: a precise solution to a problem of projection, and a quiet redefinition of what a picture is for.
