passages.title: Paying for the Road (paired passages)
passages.text:
Passage A

A road is a valuable piece of land that most cities give away. At rush hour, each driver who enters a crowded street slows everyone behind, yet no driver pays for that delay. Economists have argued for decades that charging drivers for the congestion they cause would ration road space the way prices ration everything else, and two cities have put the idea to the test.

London introduced a daily charge for driving into its center in 2003. Stockholm began a trial of its own charge in 2006, and in both cities traffic in the charged zone fell sharply almost at once. Stockholm's experience is especially telling. Before the trial, most residents opposed the charge. After seven months of shorter commutes, a majority of voters in the city voted in a referendum to keep it, and it became permanent in 2007. People who had predicted gridlock at the zone's edges found instead that many drivers had simply combined trips, skipped optional ones, or switched to buses and trains.

The lesson is not that a price solves every transportation problem. It is that drivers respond to prices more than they say they will, and that the benefits of a charge are easier to see once people have lived with it.

Passage B

No one seriously disputes that a congestion charge can cut traffic. Supporters of such charges like to describe them as neutral: everyone pays the same fee, and everyone benefits from faster traffic. But a fee that is the same for everyone is not the same burden for everyone. A daily charge that a lawyer barely notices can be a real cost for a home health aide who must drive between clients' houses on a schedule set by someone else.

This does not mean that charges are a mistake. It means that their fairness depends on what a city does with the money and on what alternatives it offers. A charge whose revenue improves bus service in the neighborhoods where lower-income workers live is a different policy from one whose revenue disappears into a general budget, even if the two look identical at the toll gantry.

Nor should early public support be taken as proof that a charge treats everyone well. The residents who vote in a referendum are not always the ones who bear the heaviest costs, and a policy can grow popular because it benefits the majority while asking a minority to absorb most of its burden.

passages.title: The Back Page
passages.text:
The week the music shop closed, my uncle Arno asked me to help him count everything. Not to sell it, he said. The new owners of the building would take the display cases, and a dealer from the city would take the stock. He only wanted to know what had been there.

So for five days I stood on the rolling ladder and read numbers down to him: forty-two packs of violin strings, eleven boxes of clarinet reeds, one accordion left from a polka craze nobody remembered. He wrote each number in the old green ledger he had kept behind the counter for decades, in handwriting so small and even it looked printed. When I asked why it mattered, since nobody was going to read the ledger, he said, "I'll read it," and went on writing.

On the fourth afternoon a man came in carrying a dented trumpet wrapped in a bath towel. He was only a few years younger than Arno, and he set the trumpet on the counter as if it might break. He had borrowed it, he said, in 1987, to play in his high school's spring concert, and had meant to bring it back the following Monday. He had heard the store was closing. He thought he had better hurry.

Arno unwrapped the trumpet and turned it over. I expected him to laugh, or to tell the man to keep it; it was a cheap student model, and its valves were stuck. Instead he opened the ledger to the back page, found a line I had not seen him write, and drew a neat stroke through it. Then he thanked the man, and the man left, and Arno went back to the numbers as if nothing had happened.

I climbed down from the ladder and looked at the back page. It was a list, in the same tiny hand, of things that had gone out the door and not come back: a cello, two flutes, a music stand, a trumpet. Each line had a name beside it and a date. Some were thirty years old. Only the trumpet had been crossed out.

"You kept track of all of these?" I asked.

"Somebody had to," he said. He did not look up. "People always mean to bring things back."

On the last day we locked the door at noon. Arno put the ledger under his arm, and he did not offer to let me carry it.

passages.title: Hanging by a Thread
passages.text:
A gecko can run straight up a pane of glass and hang from a ceiling by a single toe, and for most of the twentieth century no one could fully explain how. The obvious guesses failed one by one. Suction seemed unlikely once experiments showed that geckos still clung in a vacuum. Glue was ruled out because gecko feet have no glands that secrete anything sticky. Tiny hooks catching on rough spots could not explain how the animals held on to polished glass.

The answer turned out to lie in structure rather than substance. The underside of each toe is lined with ridges covered in hundreds of thousands of microscopic hairs called setae, and the tip of each seta splits into hundreds of even finer branches. These branches are so small that they can come extremely close to the surface beneath them, close enough for weak attractive forces between molecules, known as van der Waals forces, to act. Any single contact is feeble, but billions of them together produce a grip strong enough to hold many times the animal's weight.

Not everyone accepted this explanation at once. Some researchers suspected that thin films of water, which coat most surfaces in ordinary air, were doing the work through capillary attraction. To decide between the ideas, investigators measured how well setae stuck to surfaces that attract water and to surfaces that repel it. If water films were essential, the setae should have gripped the water-attracting surfaces far more strongly. Instead, the grip was similar on both, a result that pointed to van der Waals forces as the main source of adhesion, though later studies found that humidity can strengthen the grip somewhat.

An equally puzzling question was how a gecko lets go. A grip strong enough to support the animal would seem to make every step a struggle, yet geckos run quickly. The solution lies in angle. When a gecko curls its toes upward, the setae peel away from the surface a few at a time, the way tape comes off more easily when pulled from one edge than when pulled straight out. The adhesion is strong in one direction and almost absent in another.

Engineers have spent years trying to copy these feet. Synthetic materials with forests of tiny fibers can now hold heavy objects on smooth walls and release them cleanly, though none yet matches the gecko's ability to stay clean and keep working after thousands of steps across dusty ground.

passages.title: The Number in the Room
passages.text:
In a well-known experiment from the 1970s, the psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman spun a wheel marked from 0 to 100 in front of their participants. The wheel was rigged to stop at either 10 or 65. Participants were first asked whether the percentage of African countries in the United Nations was higher or lower than the number on the wheel, and then asked to estimate the actual percentage. Those who had seen 10 gave a median estimate of 25 percent; those who had seen 65 gave a median of 45 percent. A number that everyone could see was random had pulled their judgments toward it.

Psychologists call this effect anchoring. When people must estimate an uncertain quantity, they often begin from whatever number is at hand and adjust away from it, but not far enough. The anchor need not be relevant, and it need not be believed. It needs only to be noticed.

One might expect expertise to protect against so crude an influence. In a later study, however, experienced real estate agents toured a house and were given a packet of information that included a listing price, which the researchers varied from one group to another. The agents' own appraisals of the house rose and fell with the listing price they had been shown. When asked what had influenced their judgments, few mentioned the listing price at all.

That last detail may be the most important. Anchoring is difficult to resist not because people are careless but because it does its work before deliberate reasoning begins. A person who tries to correct for an anchor starts the correction from the anchor itself, and the correction tends to stop too soon. Simply warning people about the effect has often done little to reduce it.

Researchers have had more success with strategies that change the starting point rather than the effort. Asking people to consider reasons why the anchor might be wrong, or to generate their own estimate before seeing any number, can weaken its pull. Such findings suggest that the remedy for anchoring lies less in trying harder than in arranging, ahead of time, which numbers a decision begins from.

passages.title: A Lie from Beginning to End
passages.text:
By the 1840s, the cathedral of Notre-Dame in Paris was in poor condition. Revolutionaries had pulled down and beheaded the statues of its gallery of kings half a century earlier, its medieval spire had been taken down as unsafe in the 1780s, and decades of neglect had left its stone crumbling. Eugène Viollet-le-Duc, the architect best remembered for saving it, did far more than patch. He replaced lost sculptures with new ones of his own design, and he raised a tall new spire that the cathedral's medieval builders had never seen.

He was not embarrassed by these additions. "To restore a building," he later wrote, "is not to preserve it, to repair it, or to rebuild it; it is to reinstate it in a condition of completeness that could never have existed at any given time." The restorer, in his view, should understand a style so thoroughly that he could build what its original architects would have built had they possessed the means, or the time.

John Ruskin had already rejected this approach. In The Seven Lamps of Architecture (1849), he called restoration "the most total destruction which a building can suffer" and "a lie from beginning to end." For Ruskin, the value of an old building lay partly in the marks that centuries had left on it, such as the weathered carving and the worn step, and these could not be reproduced. A copy of a thirteenth-century capital carved in 1850 was a nineteenth-century capital, however exact. Better, he argued, to prop a building up with iron and timber, to tend it carefully, and, when it could no longer stand, to let it fall.

Ruskin's view found an institution in 1877, when William Morris founded the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings. Its members, nicknamed "Anti-Scrape" for their opposition to scraping the weathered surfaces of old buildings clean, urged owners to "put Protection in the place of Restoration." Their principles, to repair rather than replace and to let new work look new, shaped preservation practice for the next century.

In April 2019, fire destroyed Notre-Dame's roof and brought down Viollet-le-Duc's spire. The debate that followed would have been familiar to both men. Some proposed a bold modern spire; others insisted on rebuilding exactly what had fallen. France chose the second course, and in 2024 the cathedral reopened beneath a faithful copy of the nineteenth-century spire. There is an irony here that neither Ruskin nor Viollet-le-Duc could have foreseen: the restorer's invention, once a liberty taken with a medieval building, had itself become a piece of history worth preserving.

Perhaps that is the lesson. Ruskin was right that a copy cannot carry the years that made the original. But a building is not only a record of its first builders. It also records what each later generation believed the building should be, including, sometimes, a restorer's liberties.

passages.title: The Lift
passages.text:
The typewriter arrived in a cardboard box that still smelled of my great-aunt Vesna's apartment: lemon oil and radiator dust. My mother had wanted to give it away. I had asked for it before I knew why, and now that it sat on my desk, heavy and green and faintly ridiculous beside my laptop, I was not sure I could explain myself.

The machine worked, mostly. The e stuck. Every time I struck it, the type bar rose, kissed the paper, and hung there a beat too long, so that the next letter landed on top of it unless I waited. Typing a sentence was like walking beside someone who kept stopping to look in shop windows.

Mr. Pellerin's repair shop was a single room above a dry cleaner. He lifted the cover, peered inside, and pressed the e with one thick finger. "Sixty years of oil and dust," he said. "I can clean it. Or I can replace the whole linkage, new spring and new bar, and it will never stick again." He named two prices. The second was three times the first.

I chose the second without much thought. Fixing a thing properly seemed like the respectful choice. Mr. Pellerin nodded, but before I left he rolled a sheet of paper into the machine and typed a line, slowly, letting each e come home. He tore the sheet out and handed it to me. "For comparison," he said. "Afterward."

That night I found Vesna's letters at the bottom of the box: forty years of carbon copies, one for every letter she had sent. I had never read them. I read them now, and halfway through the first one I stopped, because I recognized the e's. Each one sat a hair higher than its neighbors, a small lift in every word, as if the page were breathing. I laid Mr. Pellerin's line beside hers. The same lift. The machine had been doing this for longer than I had been alive.

I called the shop in the morning. Mr. Pellerin did not sound surprised. "Cleaning only, then," he said. "It will still stick a little. You'll learn the rhythm." I said I would. What I did not say, because I did not yet have the words for it, was that I had not really been asking him to fix a machine. I had been asking him to help me keep someone, and I had nearly paid him to erase her.

passages.title: The Spitting Hunter
passages.text:
Along the mangrove coasts of Southeast Asia and northern Australia, the archerfish hunts by spitting. When it spots an insect on a leaf above the water, it presses its tongue against a groove in the roof of its mouth, snaps its gill covers shut, and fires a jet of water that can knock the insect into the water, where the fish quickly snatches it.

This is harder than it sounds. Light bends as it passes from air into water, so an insect seen from below is not where it appears to be. Yet archerfish routinely hit targets while looking up at a slant, correcting for the bending. Young archerfish miss often, and their accuracy improves with practice, which suggests that the correction is at least partly learned.

Researchers who filmed the jets at high speed found another refinement. The fish does not release its water at a steady speed. It pushes the rear of the jet out faster than the front, so that the back catches up with the front and the water gathers into a single large drop just before it reaches the target. By adjusting this timing to the distance of its prey, the fish delivers much of its force at the moment of impact.

Archerfish can also improve by watching. In one experiment, fish that observed a skilled shooter hitting moving targets later hit such targets more often than fish that had not watched, even though the observers had not practiced on moving targets themselves.

Perhaps the most surprising finding came in 2016, when a team of researchers trained archerfish to spit at one particular human face shown on a screen. Offered that face among many unfamiliar ones, the fish chose correctly far more often than chance would predict, even though fish lack the part of the brain that primates use to recognize faces.

Findings like these are a reminder that sophisticated skill does not require a large brain. With a mouth, a pair of eyes, and a modest nervous system, the archerfish solves problems that scientists once associated only with far more complex animals.

passages.title: The Feeling of Knowing
passages.text:
In the 1880s, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus became his own experimental subject. He memorized long lists of nonsense syllables, such as "dax" and "bok," chosen so that no meaning or association could help him, and then tested himself after intervals ranging from minutes to a month. Most of what he learned slipped away within the first day, and the loss then slowed. He also found that lists he relearned on several separate days stayed with him far longer than lists he crammed in a single sitting.

A century later, researchers began asking a related question: what kind of studying best slows forgetting? In one well-known experiment, students read a short passage and then either read it again or tried to write down as much of it as they could remember, with no feedback. Five minutes later, the students who had reread the passage remembered slightly more. A week later, the pattern had reversed: the students who had practiced recalling the passage remembered far more than those who had reread it.

The most striking result, however, concerned the students' own predictions. Asked how well they expected to remember the passage, the rereaders were more confident than the students who had practiced recall. Rereading had made the material feel familiar, and the students mistook that familiarity for learning.

Psychologists now describe this mistake as an illusion of fluency. Material that has just been reread is processed easily, and that ease feels like mastery. Trying to recall material, by contrast, is effortful and often frustrating; a student who struggles to remember a passage may conclude that the method is not working, even as the struggle is strengthening the memory.

None of this means that rereading is useless or that every struggle is productive. Effort that leads nowhere, such as attempting a test on material one has never seen, does little good. But the research suggests that the comfort many students seek in their study habits may be a poor guide to what those habits accomplish. The methods that feel least effective in the moment are sometimes the ones that last.

passages.title: Four Minutes of Listening
passages.text:
On an August evening in 1952, in a concert hall near Woodstock, New York, the pianist David Tudor sat down at a piano, closed the lid over the keys, and started a stopwatch. For the next four minutes and thirty-three seconds, divided into three movements that he marked by opening and closing the lid, he played nothing. The piece was John Cage's 4′33″, and many in the audience left convinced that they had been the victims of a joke.

Cage insisted that they had not been. The piece, he argued, was not silent at all. During the first movement, listeners could hear the wind outside; during the second, raindrops on the roof; during the third, the audience itself, talking and walking out. The performer's silence was meant to frame these sounds, which were always present but which concertgoers had been trained to ignore.

Cage had come to this view partly through an experience not long before. He visited an anechoic chamber at Harvard University, a room built to absorb sound so completely that nothing echoes. Expecting perfect silence, he instead heard two sounds, one high and one low. An engineer told him that these were his own nervous system and his own blood in circulation. Cage concluded that true silence does not exist for a living listener; there is only sound we attend to and sound we do not.

Critics have never fully agreed about what to make of the result. For some, 4′33″ is a philosophical statement more than a musical work, an idea that loses its force once it has been understood. For others, it is a genuine composition that changes with every performance, since no two rooms and no two audiences sound the same.

Both views, perhaps, miss the piece's quietest achievement. Whatever 4′33″ is, it is difficult to hear it once without listening differently afterward. A listener who has sat through it may find, walking out of the hall, that the traffic and voices of the street have become something worth noticing. That change in attention, more than any argument about whether the piece counts as music, may be what Cage was after.

passages.title: The Door That Swung Both Ways
passages.text:
In the 1960s, the Soviet climate scientist Mikhail Budyko built a simple mathematical model of Earth's climate and found something unsettling. Ice reflects more sunlight than ocean or bare land does, so as ice sheets spread, the planet absorbs less heat, cools further, and grows still more ice. In Budyko's model, if the ice ever spread far enough toward the equator, this feedback would run away and the entire planet would freeze. Budyko did not believe this had ever happened. Once frozen, he reasoned, a white Earth would reflect so much sunlight that it could never thaw, and since Earth was plainly not frozen now, the runaway must never have begun.

Geologists, meanwhile, had a puzzle of their own. In rocks roughly 700 million years old, they kept finding deposits left by glaciers, jumbled mixtures of boulders and fine clay of the kind that ice sheets drop as they melt. Measurements of the rocks' ancient magnetism indicated that some of these deposits had formed near the equator. Some researchers suspected that the magnetic measurements were wrong; others proposed that Earth's axis had once been tilted so steeply that the tropics were colder than the poles. Neither explanation won many converts.

In 1992, the geologist Joseph Kirschvink offered a bolder answer in a short paper: perhaps Budyko's runaway had happened after all. Kirschvink called the idea "snowball Earth," and he also proposed a way out of Budyko's trap. On a frozen planet, volcanoes would keep releasing carbon dioxide into the air. Normally, rain and the weathering of rock gradually remove that gas, but with the continents buried in ice and the oceans sealed beneath it, there would be almost nothing to take it out. Over millions of years, carbon dioxide would build up until the greenhouse effect grew strong enough to melt the ice. Once melting began, the same feedback that had frozen the planet would run in reverse, darkening the surface and speeding the thaw.

Later in the 1990s, the geologist Paul Hoffman and his colleagues found evidence that seemed to fit this scenario remarkably well. In Namibia, directly on top of the glacial deposits, lay thick layers of carbonate rock, the kind that typically forms in warm, shallow seas. An abrupt shift from glacial debris to warm-water sediment was just what one would expect if a carbon-dioxide-rich atmosphere had rapidly melted a frozen world.

Not everyone was persuaded. The strongest objection came from life itself. Photosynthetic organisms, including algae, existed before the glaciations and survived them. If the oceans had been covered by thick ice for millions of years, critics asked, how could anything that depends on sunlight have survived? Some researchers have proposed a "slushball" Earth instead, in which a band of open or thinly frozen water remained near the equator. Defenders of the original idea reply that life could have held on in cracks in the ice, around hot springs, or beneath thin, clear ice near volcanic islands.

The debate continues, but it has already changed the questions scientists ask. Budyko treated a frozen Earth as a one-way door, and he used that assumption to rule out the possibility altogether. Kirschvink's insight was that the door might swing both ways. Whether or not the oceans froze completely, it now seems that Earth's climate can lurch between extremes once thought impossible, and that the planet's own processes, given enough time, may be capable of pulling it back.

passages.title: The Beats
passages.text:
The summer I turned sixteen, my mother arranged for me to work for her sister, Ines, who tuned pianos for a living. I had imagined spending those months at the community pool with my friends, and I let everyone know it. On the first morning, Ines handed me a canvas bag full of tools I could not name and said only, "Carry this. Don't drop the forks."

The forks, I learned, were tuning forks, and Ines owned a dozen of them, though she rarely used more than one. Our first stop was a church basement where an upright piano had been pushed against a damp wall for what looked like decades. Ines lifted the lid, played a single chord, and winced as if someone had stepped on her foot. To me it sounded like a piano. "Listen to the beats," she said, striking two keys together. I heard nothing but two notes. She did not explain further. She simply went to work, turning pins with a lever and stopping every few seconds to listen with her head tilted, as though the instrument were whispering.

For the first two weeks, I was mostly bored. I carried the bag, handed her mutes and felt strips when she held out her hand, and watched the clock on whatever wall was nearest. Ines did not seem to mind my silence; she was not much of a talker herself. At lunch she ate the same sandwich every day, cheese and pickles, and read paperback mysteries with the covers torn off. When I asked why she tore them off, she said she didn't like being told what to expect.

It was in the third week, in the living room of an elderly man named Mr. Okafor, that something shifted. His piano was old but well cared for, and while Ines worked, he sat in an armchair and told me that his late wife had played it every evening. "I don't play," he said. "But I like to know it's ready." Ines tuned for nearly two hours, longer than she had spent on any instrument that summer, though to my ears the piano had sounded fine when we arrived. When she finished, she played a slow piece I didn't recognize, and Mr. Okafor closed his eyes.

On the drive home, I asked her why she had taken so long on a piano no one played. She was quiet for a while. "He listens," she said finally. "That's someone playing it."

The next morning she handed me a fork and pointed at the A above middle C on an old practice piano in her garage. "Strike them both," she said. I did, and for the first time I heard it: a faint wavering, a slow pulse inside the sound, like two people walking almost but not quite in step. I turned the pin a fraction, and the pulse slowed. I turned it again, and it vanished. I looked up, expecting her to say something. She was already reading her mystery, but she had stopped turning the pages.

choices.D: reluctance to keep reading the letters.

questions.stem: According to the narrator, what indicated that the aunt had returned to the letters again and again?

choices.A: The letters came from one woman over thirty years.
choices.B: The box was hidden behind a stack of blankets.
choices.C: The envelopes were soft at the edges from handling.
choices.D: The box held about two hundred separate letters.

questions.stem: The narrator's statement that "A list can be honest about every item on it and still be a disguise" (paragraph 5) most directly suggests that the ledger:

choices.A: hid what mattered most to the aunt by omitting it while recording everything else accurately.
choices.B: contained deliberate errors that were meant to mislead the lawyer about the estate's value.
choices.C: was written in a private code that only members of the aunt's family could ever understand.
choices.D: turned out to be far less accurate than the narrator had believed during the first week.

questions.stem: The narrator's final actions of making tea in the copper kettle and writing nothing down most likely signal:

choices.A: the narrator's decision to sell off the house's contents now that the inventory is done.
choices.B: the narrator's wish to imitate the aunt's household routines as closely as possible.
choices.C: a break from the narrator's own habit of recording, prompted by what the box revealed.
choices.D: the narrator's relief at having finally finished checking every room against the ledger.

questions.stem: The main purpose of the passage is to:

choices.A: argue that sham ruins deserve the same careful preservation as genuine old buildings.
choices.B: describe the building techniques used to make new structures look centuries old.
choices.C: reinterpret a practice that can seem dishonest by explaining what it was meant to do.
choices.D: criticize the modern preservation movement for valuing authenticity too highly.

questions.stem: According to the passage, builders of sham ruins were sometimes instructed to:

choices.A: leave stones scattered around the base of the structure.
choices.B: reuse stones taken from genuine medieval buildings nearby.
choices.C: place each ruin where it could be seen from the main road.
choices.D: copy the exact design of a particular medieval chapel.

questions.stem: The comparison to a souvenir in paragraph 2 primarily serves to:

choices.A: show that eighteenth-century visitors bought souvenirs when they toured ruins.
choices.B: illustrate a modern objection that the author then goes on to challenge.
choices.C: reveal that the author considers sham ruins to be essentially worthless.
choices.D: explain why landowners chose to build ruins near their own grand houses.

questions.stem: The author mentions that "guidebooks said so" (paragraph 3) mainly as evidence that:

choices.A: guidebooks were the main source of historical knowledge for visitors.
choices.B: visitors of the period preferred new ruins to genuinely old ones.
choices.C: owners were privately embarrassed by the ruins they had built.
choices.D: the builders were not trying to fool visitors about the ruins' age.

questions.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 3, the word "occasion" most nearly means:

choices.A: celebration.
choices.B: opportunity.
choices.C: excuse.
choices.D: anniversary.

questions.stem: Based on paragraph 4, the author would most likely say that a sham ruin succeeded if it:

choices.A: convinced visitors that it had truly been built in the Middle Ages.
choices.B: taught visitors accurate facts about the history of their region.
choices.C: led visitors to reflect on time and the impermanence of their world.
choices.D: matched the architectural style of the main house on the estate.

questions.stem: In the last paragraph, the author's attitude toward the modern preservation movement is best described as:

choices.A: approving of what it has saved, while noting that the wish for a feeling of age persists.
choices.B: dismissive, because it values original materials more than the moods buildings create.
choices.C: nostalgic for the period before the movement existed, when ruins were built freely.
choices.D: neutral, since the author describes the movement without evaluating it in any way.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the structure of the passage's argument?

choices.A: It traces the history of ruins in England from the Middle Ages to modern times.
choices.B: It compares two rival theories of why ruins were built and then endorses one of them.
choices.C: It describes a practice, states an objection, rebuts it, and links the practice to the present.
choices.D: It argues that modern preservation is misguided and proposes a better alternative.

questions.stem: The passage mainly focuses on:

choices.A: the routes European robins follow between breeding and wintering grounds.
choices.B: efforts to explain how migrating birds sense Earth's magnetic field.
choices.C: evidence that young birds learn to navigate by following older birds.
choices.D: the ways birds use the positions of the sun and stars to find north.

questions.stem: According to the passage, young birds raised in isolation:

choices.A: still orient in roughly the right direction when the season arrives.
choices.B: fail to migrate until they have watched older birds do so.
choices.C: orient correctly only after learning the night sky as adults.
choices.D: can sense magnetic fields only when kept in complete darkness.

questions.stem: The statement that magnetic fields "pass through living tissue almost without effect" (paragraph 2) primarily serves to:

choices.A: show that no animal is able to detect magnetic fields under any conditions.
choices.B: suggest that birds rely mainly on the sun and stars rather than on magnetism.
choices.C: introduce the magnetite proposal as the proven answer to the problem.
choices.D: explain why a sense that detects magnetic fields would need a special mechanism.

questions.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 3, the word "dominates" most nearly means:

choices.A: controls by force.
choices.B: is the leading view in.
choices.C: towers physically over.
choices.D: defeats in a contest.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the cryptochrome hypothesis described in paragraph 4?

choices.A: Robins lacking cryptochrome in their eyes lose magnetic orientation but keep their sun compass.
choices.B: Robins orient more accurately on cloudy nights than on clear nights with visible stars.
choices.C: The iron-rich cells in robins' beaks turn out to be nerve cells connected to the brain.
choices.D: Strong magnets placed beside a robin's cage have no effect on the direction it faces.

questions.stem: The author notes that the radio-frequency noise was "far too weak to move a compass needle" (paragraph 4) most likely to:

choices.A: suggest that the birds' sense works differently from an ordinary magnetic compass.
choices.B: show that the robins in the experiments were not actually affected by the noise.
choices.C: argue that laboratory experiments on birds are too imprecise to be trusted.
choices.D: prove that robins navigate by the stars rather than by the magnetic field.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the cryptochrome hypothesis is best described as:

choices.A: fully convinced, since experiments have proved that robins see magnetic fields.
choices.B: dismissive, since the chemistry it requires is too small to measure at all.
choices.C: interested but cautious, since it has not been confirmed in a living bird.
choices.D: indifferent, since the author regards the compass sense as unimportant.

questions.stem: Based on the passage as a whole, which conclusion about bird navigation is best supported?

choices.A: Birds likely combine several senses, with magnetism giving direction but not position.
choices.B: Birds navigate entirely by magnetism, and the sun and stars play no real role.
choices.C: Birds learn every part of their routes from older birds during their first year.
choices.D: Scientists have now fully explained how birds know where they are during migration.

questions.stem: The examples of reclaimed barn wood and a housing development named for a farm (paragraph 5) mainly serve to:

choices.A: illustrate the preservation movement's insistence on using original materials.
choices.B: show that a modern version of the sham ruin's appeal still exists today.
choices.C: criticize modern builders for deliberately deceiving their customers.
choices.D: explain the reasons that eighteenth-century landowners built ruins.

questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.A: explaining why most consumers choose the cheaper of two subscription plans.
choices.B: arguing that businesses should stop adding decoy options to their product lineups.
choices.C: showing that a simple model of choice accurately predicts how people decide.
choices.D: describing a pattern in decision-making and weighing how far it holds outside the laboratory.

questions.stem: In the opening example, adding the print-only plan most likely made the print-and-online plan more attractive because the new plan:

choices.A: gave people an easy comparison that print-and-online clearly won.
choices.B: lowered the effective price of the print-and-online plan for readers.
choices.C: gave readers new information about how valuable a print edition is.
choices.D: made the online-only plan seem more expensive than it really was.

questions.stem: The parenthetical remark in paragraph 2 primarily serves to:

choices.A: suggest that print subscriptions are more valuable than online ones.
choices.B: explain why almost no one chooses the online-only subscription plan.
choices.C: clarify why the decoy is clearly worse than one of the other options.
choices.D: show that the print-and-online plan is the cheapest of the options.

questions.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 3, the word "troubling" most nearly means:

choices.A: distressing.
choices.B: problematic.
choices.C: annoying.
choices.D: dangerous.

questions.stem: According to the passage, decoys often have little influence when:

choices.A: choices involve many features or people already have firm preferences.
choices.B: the decoy is priced far below every other option offered.
choices.C: people make their choices in a controlled laboratory setting.
choices.D: only two options are available rather than three or more.

questions.stem: The author's view of how much the decoy effect matters in everyday shopping is best described as:

choices.A: open, since the research has not settled how well decoys work in stores.
choices.B: confident that decoys are the main force shaping most shoppers' choices.
choices.C: skeptical that the effect has ever been observed in any setting at all.
choices.D: sure that businesses are wasting money when they include decoy options.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers in paragraph 4 who think the effect's everyday importance has been overstated?

choices.A: Laboratory volunteers given simple price tables reliably chose the option a decoy favored.
choices.B: A restaurant that added a decoy dish saw orders of the dish it favored rise sharply.
choices.C: Most shoppers say in surveys that they compare products carefully before buying.
choices.D: Shoppers comparing real appliances with many listed features ignored added decoys.

questions.stem: How does paragraph 5 relate to paragraph 4?

choices.A: It notes that businesses use decoys despite the doubts that paragraph 4 raises.
choices.B: It provides experimental evidence that resolves the doubts raised in paragraph 4.
choices.C: It repeats paragraph 4's claim that the decoy effect appears only in laboratories.
choices.D: It argues that the researchers in paragraph 4 misunderstood the decoy effect.

questions.stem: Based on paragraph 3, the later findings about the iron-rich cells weakened the magnetite proposal mainly because they suggested that:

choices.A: pigeons do not actually migrate and so cannot reveal how robins navigate.
choices.B: magnetite cannot exist inside the body of any living animal at all.
choices.C: the cells thought to detect magnetism may serve an unrelated function.
choices.D: a bird's upper beak is too small to contain crystals of magnetite.

questions.stem: The passage is mainly about:

choices.A: the narrator's struggle to master the technical skills of lettering and drawing.
choices.B: a lasting conflict between the narrator and a demanding teacher that was never resolved.
choices.C: how the narrator came to grasp a teacher's lesson that mapping means choosing what to omit.
choices.D: the history of how the narrator's parish was surveyed and mapped over many years.

questions.stem: The examples of the ford and the ruined wall in paragraph 3 mainly serve to:

choices.A: show that small features on a map are always less important than large ones.
choices.B: describe features that Brandt specifically asked the narrator to record on surveys.
choices.C: contrast the maps the narrator made with the maps Brandt himself had made.
choices.D: show how unexamined choices could lead a mapmaker to include or omit the wrong features.

questions.stem: When Brandt complains that the narrator "had drawn the sea instead of the shore" (paragraph 4), he most likely means that the narrator:

choices.A: used an ink for the water that was much too dark for the rest of the map.
choices.B: gave attention to the wrong feature instead of the edge the map needed to show.
choices.C: placed the coastline several miles from where it actually lay.
choices.D: worked so slowly on the coastline that the map was finished late.

questions.stem: According to the passage, during the narrator's first month in the workshop Brandt:

choices.A: had the narrator survey and take notes rather than draw.
choices.B: taught the narrator to draw rivers, roads, and farmhouses.
choices.C: made the narrator redraw a coastline four separate times.
choices.D: asked the narrator to count the livestock in every field.

questions.stem: The narrator's description of Brandt in paragraph 4 suggests that Brandt was:

choices.A: harsh in every respect and unwilling to hear any explanation.
choices.B: patient about lettering but rigid about the narrator's choices.
choices.C: exacting about technique yet genuinely open to the narrator's reasons.
choices.D: more concerned with coastlines than with any other feature.

questions.subskill: Relationship of the conclusion to the passage
questions.stem: Which choice best describes how the final paragraph relates to the rest of the passage?

choices.A: It shows that Brandt's question still shapes the narrator's work and remains hard to answer.
choices.B: It reveals that the narrator eventually stopped making maps and chose another trade.
choices.C: It explains why the narrator came to reject Brandt's way of teaching apprentices.
choices.D: It introduces a new lesson that contradicts what Brandt had taught the narrator.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, Brandt would most likely judge a map to be poor if it:

choices.A: included details chosen without thought for what a reader would need.
choices.B: left out features that the mapmaker had deliberately judged unimportant.
choices.C: showed fewer features than the land it represented actually contained.
choices.D: had lettering that was neat but simple and without decoration.

questions.stem: According to the simple model of choice described in paragraph 3, adding the print-only plan should have:

choices.A: increased the share of people choosing the print-and-online plan.
choices.B: left people's preferences between the other two plans unchanged.
choices.C: caused many people to switch to the new print-only plan instead.
choices.D: made people judge each plan by comparing it with the other plans.

questions.stem: In paragraph 2, the author suggests that a translation that renders a funeral pun word for word, leaving readers puzzled, has:

choices.A: been more faithful to the author than a version that substitutes a new joke.
choices.B: been dishonest, because it alters the words the author actually wrote.
choices.C: made the funeral scene more shocking than the author originally intended.
choices.D: kept the author's words while losing what the sentence was mainly meant to do.

questions.stem: The statement "Both sides are right, which is why the argument never ends" (paragraph 3) most strongly suggests that the author believes:

choices.A: inventing a joke can be justified, but how acceptable it is depends on how often it is done.
choices.B: the critics of substitution are, in the end, more persuasive than its defenders.
choices.C: translators could avoid the whole debate simply by using footnotes instead.
choices.D: the defenders of substitution have misunderstood what the original author intended.

questions.stem: The fourth paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: argue that footnotes should never appear in translated novels.
choices.B: describe the author's own rules for deciding how to handle untranslatable jokes.
choices.C: weigh the third option, noting when it is useful and what it costs a reader.
choices.D: explain why readers tend to prefer literal translations.

questions.subskill: Meaning of a phrase in context
questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 3, the phrase "before its author disappears" most nearly refers to the point at which:

choices.A: the original author's name is no longer printed on the translation.
choices.B: readers can no longer tell which jokes appeared in the original version and which did not.
choices.C: the original author stops writing new jokes in later novels.
choices.D: the translated book reflects the translator's choices more than the original writer's.

questions.stem: Based on the final paragraph, the author would most likely invent a new joke when translating which of the following?

choices.A: A comic novel's scene that turns on a pun by its hero, who is known for quick wordplay
choices.B: A history book's pun on a king's name, which later chapters refer to again
choices.C: A long novel's single passing pun in a description of the weather
choices.D: A study edition of a play for students who want to know the exact wording of each line

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward translators who treat their choices as neutral is best described as:

choices.A: admiring, because staying neutral protects the original author's words.
choices.B: critical, because such translators let important decisions be made without thought.
choices.C: indifferent, because the choice of method rarely affects a book's purpose.
choices.D: sympathetic, because the author still finds that position mostly convincing.

questions.subskill: Connecting the opening to the conclusion
questions.stem: In light of the final paragraph, the description of the three choices as "none of them good" (paragraph 1) is best understood to mean that:

choices.A: translators should decline to translate books that depend heavily on jokes.
choices.B: the author has since discovered a fourth option that keeps the words, the joke and the experience.
choices.C: each choice gives something up, so the right one depends on what matters most in a given case.
choices.D: the literal option is usually the least harmful, as most readers suspect.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 4, a joke explained in a footnote fails in a novel meant to be read mainly because the reader:

choices.A: understands the joke but no longer experiences it as funny.
choices.B: cannot find out what the original sentence actually said.
choices.C: usually skips footnotes and so misses the joke entirely.
choices.D: is distracted by the translator's long and inaccurate notes.

questions.stem: When Brandt says, "You were right. But you did not know you were deciding" (paragraph 2), he most likely means that the narrator:

choices.A: made a sound omission without realizing that it was a choice.
choices.B: should have counted the sheep after all, since every detail matters.
choices.C: had recorded so many details that the notebook was nearly useless.
choices.D: had been careless in measuring the width of the road and the stream.

questions.stem: The author mentions that trees "hundreds of kilometers apart" often mast in the same year (paragraph 2) mainly to:

choices.A: suggest that something beyond each tree's local weather coordinates masting.
choices.B: show that weather has no effect on how many seeds a tree produces.
choices.C: support the idea that predator satiation is the full explanation for masting.
choices.D: illustrate how far seed-eating animals travel in search of acorns.

questions.stem: Based on paragraph 3, masting would be expected to be LEAST pronounced in a tree species whose seeds are eaten mainly by:

choices.A: weevils that feed almost entirely on that species' seeds.
choices.B: squirrels whose numbers rise and fall with the size of the crop.
choices.C: animals that also eat many other kinds of food.
choices.D: a beetle that lays its eggs only inside those seeds.

questions.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 3, the word "pronounced" most nearly means:

choices.A: spoken.
choices.B: marked.
choices.C: declared.
choices.D: predicted.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 4, a tree that flowered heavily in a year when its neighbors did not would most likely:

choices.A: waste much of its effort, since little of the pollen in the air would reach its flowers.
choices.B: attract more seed predators than its neighbors, since its crop would stand out.
choices.C: produce more seeds than usual, since it would face less competition for pollen.
choices.D: be pollinated by insects instead of by wind, since the air would contain little pollen.

questions.stem: Paragraphs 3 and 4 differ from paragraph 5 in that paragraphs 3 and 4 mainly explain:

choices.A: how trees coordinate the timing of masting, while paragraph 5 explains why masting benefits them.
choices.B: the history of research on masting, while paragraph 5 presents the author's own field observations.
choices.C: masting in oaks only, while paragraph 5 extends the explanation to every kind of tree.
choices.D: why masting benefits trees, while paragraph 5 explains how trees coordinate its timing.

questions.stem: The last sentence of the passage mainly serves to:

choices.A: suggest that individual trees plan their seed crops several years in advance.
choices.B: warn that forests will decline sharply if mast years ever stop occurring.
choices.C: stress that masting is a shared pattern that developed over time without any plan.
choices.D: introduce a new hypothesis that researchers will need to test in the future.

questions.stem: The passage indicates that for most of the twentieth century, ecologists believed that mast years:

choices.A: resulted mainly from good or poor growing conditions.
choices.B: were triggered by rising numbers of seed-eating animals.
choices.C: occurred when distant trees signaled to one another.
choices.D: depended chiefly on how efficiently pollen spread.

questions.stem: Taken together, the repair tickets the grandfather writes in the first paragraph and his answer "Somebody might come back" in the sixth paragraph suggest that he:

choices.A: still expects the shop to be rescued before the end of the month.
choices.B: is careless about dates and the details of his customers' orders.
choices.C: struggles to accept that the shop and its work are coming to an end.
choices.D: wants customers to pay in advance for repairs he will not finish.

questions.stem: The narrator's statement "I began to suspect that the sorting was not really the point" (paragraph 4) most nearly means that the narrator sensed:

choices.A: the Saturdays mattered to the grandfather for some reason other than clearing the shop.
choices.B: the grandfather secretly hoped to train the narrator to take over the shop as a watchmaker someday.
choices.C: the narrator's mother had invented the whole task mainly to keep the narrator busy on weekends.
choices.D: the grandfather could no longer tell good parts from worn ones.

questions.stem: The description of the drawer labeled "Others" in paragraphs 2 and 3 mainly serves to:

choices.A: show how carefully the grandfather organized the parts he used for repairs.
choices.B: set up a small mystery that the narrator resolves near the end of the passage.
choices.C: hint that the narrator will someday inherit and reopen the shop.
choices.D: explain why the shop was no longer able to stay in business.

questions.stem: The narrator's actions in the final paragraph most strongly suggest that the narrator:

choices.A: plans to sell the old tickets to collectors as valuable antiques.
choices.B: fears the mother will be angry that the drawer was not emptied.
choices.C: intends to track down the owners named on the tickets and return their watches to them.
choices.D: wants to keep the grandfather's private attachment from being treated as clutter.

questions.stem: According to the passage, who wrote the sign in the shop window?

choices.A: The narrator's grandfather
choices.B: The narrator
choices.C: The narrator's mother
choices.D: A longtime customer

questions.subskill: Meaning of a phrase in context
questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 6, the phrase "called in" most nearly means:

choices.A: claimed by their owners.
choices.B: telephoned ahead.
choices.C: summoned for questioning.
choices.D: canceled by the shop.

questions.stem: The grandfather's habit of explaining how each gear "had been cut, by whom, and in what year" (paragraph 4) suggests that he:

choices.A: dislikes being interrupted while he is working at his bench.
choices.B: values the history and craft behind the parts he has handled.
choices.C: considers the narrator too young to be trusted with the parts.
choices.D: is preparing to write a history of watchmaking in the region.

questions.stem: The passage is narrated from the point of view of:

choices.A: the grandfather, looking back on the end of his career.
choices.B: the narrator's mother, describing her father's shop.
choices.C: an outside observer who knows every character's thoughts.
choices.D: a grandchild recalling a time when the narrator was fifteen.

questions.subskill: Connecting an example to an earlier idea
questions.stem: Posting estimated waiting times in an emergency room (paragraph 5) most directly addresses which feature of waiting described in paragraph 2?

choices.A: Waiting alone rather than with other people
choices.B: Not knowing how long the wait will last
choices.C: Seeing someone who arrived later served first
choices.D: Having nothing to occupy one's attention

questions.stem: Based on paragraph 6, which of the following lines would most likely be remembered more favorably?

choices.A: A 15-minute line that does not move for 10 minutes and then empties quickly
choices.B: A 12-minute line that moves steadily at first and then stops for the last 8 minutes
choices.C: A 25-minute line that alternates between long stops and sudden bursts of movement
choices.D: A 20-minute line that advances a few steps every minute until the end

questions.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 6, the word "lurches" most nearly means:

choices.A: stops completely.
choices.B: tilts to one side.
choices.C: moves suddenly and unevenly.
choices.D: moves forward at a slow, steady pace.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the author's attitude toward Maister's ideas about waiting?

choices.A: The author treats them as insightful and influential while acknowledging a debate about how they are used.
choices.B: The author doubts them and suggests that only the actual length of a wait matters to people.
choices.C: The author argues that they make it unnecessary for any business to shorten its customers' waits.
choices.D: The author reports them without expressing any view about their importance or their usefulness.

questions.stem: In the final sentence, the author's claim that the people who design lines are "also its authors" most nearly means that they:

choices.A: write the rules that customers must follow while they are waiting in line.
choices.B: shape the experience people later recall, not just the time people spend.
choices.C: ask customers to write about their experiences after leaving a line.
choices.D: alone decide how long every wait will last for each customer in line.

questions.subskill: Connecting a proposal to an earlier constraint
questions.stem: In light of paragraph 2, the pupil proposal described in paragraph 4 is notable mainly because it suggests that the octopus could:

choices.A: gain information about color without having more than one kind of light-sensitive cell.
choices.B: have more kinds of light-sensitive cells than the standard tests of vision revealed.
choices.C: see colors more accurately than animals whose pupils are small and round.
choices.D: use its skin to focus light in the same way that the lens of an eye does.

questions.stem: The reference to inexpensive cameras that produce "colored fringes around objects" (paragraph 4) mainly serves to:

choices.A: argue that an octopus's eyes are less sophisticated than modern camera lenses.
choices.B: explain why round pupils are so rare among the animals that live in the ocean.
choices.C: suggest that photographers first noticed octopuses using blur to judge color.
choices.D: illustrate a familiar effect that the pupil proposal says the octopus could make use of.

questions.stem: Which new finding would most strengthen the skin proposal as an explanation of how octopuses match colors?

choices.A: Octopus skin responds to changes in light more quickly than octopus eyes respond to the same changes.
choices.B: Octopus skin contains several types of light-sensitive proteins, each tuned to a different range of wavelengths.
choices.C: Octopus pupils change shape whenever an octopus moves close to a brightly colored patch of coral.
choices.D: Octopuses can match the texture of nearby rocks even when they are kept in complete darkness.

questions.subskill: Inferring the significance of a point
questions.stem: The point in paragraph 5 that many of the animals that hunt octopuses "see color poorly or not at all" mainly suggests that:

choices.A: octopuses are not nearly as skilled at camouflage as the first paragraph claims they are.
choices.B: the predators of octopuses rely mainly on their sense of smell rather than their sight.
choices.C: the puzzle may matter less for survival, since such predators cannot see color mismatches.
choices.D: the pupil proposal has been shown to be wrong by recent studies of predators.

questions.stem: According to the passage, when octopuses are asked to distinguish between colors of equal brightness, they:

choices.A: succeed only when the colors are red and green.
choices.B: succeed more often than most other animals do.
choices.C: perform well only after many training sessions.
choices.D: perform no better than they would by guessing.

questions.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 4, the word "exaggerates" most nearly means:

choices.A: increases.
choices.B: misrepresents.
choices.C: conceals.
choices.D: praises.

questions.stem: The main purpose of the passage is to:

choices.A: argue that the pupil proposal has been proven to explain how octopuses match colors.
choices.B: present a puzzle about octopus camouflage and consider possible explanations for it.
choices.C: describe the methods octopuses use to hunt prey on the ocean floor.
choices.D: compare octopus vision with human vision across a wide range of tasks.

questions.stem: The author most likely calls the operations researchers' assumption "only half true" (paragraph 1) because:

choices.A: operations researchers seldom managed to make the waits they studied any shorter.
choices.B: people care more about the fairness of a wait than about any other feature of it.
choices.C: the length of a wait matters, but so do features such as uncertainty and fairness.
choices.D: most people greatly overestimate how long they have actually spent waiting.

questions.subskill: Applying one group's view to an example
questions.stem: The critics described in paragraph 4 would most likely regard the airport's change described in paragraph 3 as:

choices.A: a way of improving how the wait felt without dealing with how long it actually took.
choices.B: an unfair practice, because it made passengers' total waiting time noticeably longer.

choices.D: A speaker who adjusts gestures and pacing to suit a television camera rather than the people in the room

questions.subskill: Central claim of a research narrative
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Shared resources are usually ruined in the end unless they are divided up into private property.
choices.B: Governments often manage shared resources more fairly than the people who actually use them.
choices.C: Village herders in Switzerland have shared their summer pastures for many centuries.
choices.D: Field studies showed that the users of a shared resource can sometimes avoid the ruin one theory predicted.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Hardin's essay was widely read as showing that shared resources would be destroyed unless they were:

choices.A: split into private holdings or put under government control.
choices.B: managed by rules the users had made for themselves.
choices.C: protected by a law limiting each village to a fixed number of herders.
choices.D: shared only among herders who had grazed the land for many years.

questions.stem: The main purpose of paragraph 2 is to:

choices.A: present evidence that Hardin's idea correctly explained overfishing.
choices.B: show how widely Hardin's idea was accepted before anyone tested it closely.
choices.C: introduce the research methods that Ostrom later used.
choices.D: criticize economists for ignoring problems such as polluted rivers.

questions.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 4, the word graduated most nearly means:

choices.A: having finished a course of study.
choices.B: marked with measuring lines.
choices.C: increasing in steps.
choices.D: applied the same way to everyone.

questions.subskill: Inference about why outside rules failed
questions.stem: Based on paragraph 5, rules imposed by distant authorities often worked worse than rules made by users partly because the distant authorities:

choices.A: could not observe how the resource was actually being used day to day.
choices.B: designed rules that were more lenient than the users' own rules.
choices.C: lacked the money needed to enforce penalties on users.
choices.D: intended to take control of the resource away from the users.

questions.subskill: Function of examples within an argument
questions.stem: The examples of the Swiss pastures and the Spanish irrigation canals in paragraph 3 mainly serve to:

choices.A: prove that every shared resource can be managed well by its users.
choices.B: show that European farmers were more cooperative than farmers elsewhere.
choices.C: illustrate Hardin's argument that shared pastures are soon overgrazed.
choices.D: give real cases in which a shared resource lasted under rules its users enforced.

questions.subskill: Author's view of an earlier argument
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the author's view of Hardin's argument, as expressed in the last paragraph?

choices.A: It identified a real danger but overlooked that users can sometimes prevent it.
choices.B: It was mistaken about every one of the shared resources that Ostrom later studied.
choices.C: It was correct, and Ostrom's research merely added further supporting examples to it.
choices.D: It was too abstract to say anything useful about real pastures or fisheries.

questions.stem: The author's statement that "The herders in his story never speak to one another" (last paragraph) most strongly suggests that Hardin's model left out:

choices.A: the damage that extra animals do to a shared pasture.
choices.B: the ability of users to agree on and enforce shared rules.
choices.C: the role of governments in dividing land among herders.
choices.D: the benefit each herder gains from adding one more animal.

questions.subskill: Applying the findings to a new case
questions.stem: Based on the passage, which of the following arrangements for a shared community well would Ostrom most likely expect to last?

choices.A: A distant agency sets detailed rules and sends an inspector to the well once each year.
choices.B: Each household may draw as much water as it likes, and no one ever checks how much is taken.
choices.C: Neighbors set and revise the rules, take turns checking the well, and raise fines for repeat offenses.
choices.D: A single household buys the well and sells water to neighbors at whatever price it chooses.

questions.subskill: Inference across paragraphs about which performers benefited
questions.stem: Based on paragraphs 3 and 6, which singer would most likely have found it easier to record after microphones arrived than before?

choices.A: A singer whose gentle voice barely moved the diaphragm of a recording horn
choices.B: A singer whose forceful voice could fill a large theater without strain
choices.C: A singer who preferred songs that ran longer than three minutes
choices.D: A singer who had learned to step back from the horn on loud notes

questions.stem: Which of the following findings, if true, would most directly support the explanation for the urban heat island given in paragraph 2?

choices.A: At midnight, a dark-paved block is warmer than a nearby pale-paved block with the same trees.
choices.B: At noon, the center of a city is a few degrees warmer than the farmland a few miles away.
choices.C: At midnight, a large park in a city is about as warm as a nearby parking lot.
choices.D: In winter, a city's furnaces add far more heat to the outdoor air than its cars do.

questions.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 3, the word carry most nearly means:

choices.A: transport.
choices.B: pose.
choices.C: support.
choices.D: win.

questions.subskill: Applying the passage to a new case
questions.stem: Based on the passage, which of the following places would most likely be the warmest at midnight during a summer heat wave?

choices.A: A block of apartments in the city center surrounded by parking lots and almost no trees
choices.B: A downtown block of tall office buildings with wide sidewalks lined by large shade trees
choices.C: A suburban street of houses with dark roofs set among tall, closely spaced shade trees
choices.D: A neighborhood at the edge of the city next to open farmland, with lawns and gardens

questions.subskill: Applying a qualified claim to choose a setting
questions.stem: Based on paragraph 4, a reflective roof would most likely produce the greatest net energy savings over a year in which of the following places?

choices.A: A desert city where summers are long and very hot and frosts are rare
choices.B: A northern city with brief, warm summers and months of snow
choices.C: A city with very hot summers and long winters with heavy snow
choices.D: A coastal city that stays cool and overcast for most of the year

questions.subskill: Linking a cause to a stated consequence
questions.stem: The author's statement that heat lingering into the night "denies the body a chance to recover" (paragraph 3) helps explain why:

choices.A: older residents are less likely than other residents to own air conditioners.
choices.B: temperatures can differ sharply from one neighborhood to the next.
choices.C: reflective roofs work better in some climates than they do in others.
choices.D: the heat island's timing makes it especially harmful to health.

questions.stem: Based on paragraph 5, planners who think in decades most likely favor trees because they believe that:

choices.A: trees cost much less to plant than the coatings that are applied to roofs.
choices.B: over many years, a tree's slow start matters less than its two benefits.
choices.C: coatings cannot be applied to buildings that have already been built.
choices.D: trees, unlike roof coatings, can never be lost to drought or disease.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes how the passage is organized?

choices.A: It presents a theory, tests it against new measurements, and finally rejects it.
choices.B: It describes a pattern, explains its causes and effects, and weighs two responses.
choices.C: It compares two particular cities and recommends the policies of one of them.
choices.D: It traces an idea's history from its first discovery up to the present day.

questions.stem: The main purpose of the passage is to:

choices.A: argue that cities should require reflective roofs on all new buildings.
choices.B: explain why cities run warmer than their surroundings and weigh ways to reduce the gap.
choices.C: describe how one city measured its neighborhoods' temperatures on summer nights.
choices.D: warn that heat waves have become more frequent and dangerous in recent decades.

questions.stem: In paragraph 5, the sentence "Many cities now try to do both" mainly serves to suggest that:

choices.A: cities have found that coatings work better than trees in most places.
choices.B: planners have stopped disagreeing about how to cool their cities.
choices.C: the strengths of coatings and trees can make up for each other's weaknesses.
choices.D: trees are planted mainly to hide the reflective coatings on nearby roofs.

questions.stem: In Passage A, the author most likely includes the statement "Nothing else about the plan changed" in order to:

choices.A: rule out other explanations for the rise in participation that followed.
choices.B: suggest that the company's retirement plan was unusually generous.
choices.C: emphasize that employees were not told about the change in the rule.
choices.D: show that the company was reluctant to change its other policies.

questions.subskill: Meaning of a claim in context
questions.stem: In Passage A, the statement that "the choice of a default is never neutral" most nearly means that:

choices.A: defaults are usually set to favor employers over their employees.
choices.B: any default shapes what happens to people, whichever option is chosen.
choices.C: the people who set defaults always have something personal to gain.
choices.D: a default leaves people with fewer choices than they had before.

questions.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
questions.stem: As it is used in the last paragraph of Passage A, the word "exercised" most nearly means:

choices.A: trained.
choices.B: strengthened.
choices.C: used.
choices.D: questioned.

questions.stem: In Passage B, the phrase "though less loudly" (paragraph 1) suggests that the finding that enrolled workers tended to stay with the default rate and investment:

choices.A: appeared only in studies done many years after the first ones.
choices.B: received less attention than the finding about participation.
choices.C: was disputed by the same economists who had reported it.
choices.D: was based on far fewer workers than the other finding.

questions.stem: The second paragraph of Passage B mainly serves to:

choices.A: present the drawback as a side effect of what makes defaults effective.
choices.B: concede that the drawback in the first paragraph is too rare to matter much.
choices.C: explain why employers usually choose such low default contribution rates.
choices.D: reject the claim that automatic enrollment actually increases participation.

questions.stem: Passage B suggests that taking the increases out of future raises, rather than out of pay employees already had, made the program easier to accept mainly because employees:

choices.A: would receive somewhat larger raises if they joined the program.
choices.B: could no longer stop the increases once the program began.
choices.C: would not have to save any of their money until they retired.
choices.D: would not see their take-home pay go down when the increases began.

questions.stem: Unlike the rule change described in Passage A, the program described in the last paragraph of Passage B required employees to:

choices.A: fill out a form if they did not want to take part.
choices.B: contribute a share of the pay they already earned.
choices.C: agree beforehand to take part in the program.
choices.D: accept a smaller employer match on their savings.

questions.stem: Passage B's discussion of contribution rates most directly complicates the impression, given in Passage A, that:

choices.A: participation in the plan rose sharply after the rule changed.
choices.B: the rise in participation was largest among younger, lower-income workers.
choices.C: a default respects people's freedom to make a different choice.
choices.D: the jump in participation meant that enrolled workers were saving more.

questions.subskill: Applying one passage to the other
questions.stem: Based on Passage B, which workers in the study described in Passage A were most likely made worse off by automatic enrollment?

choices.A: Workers who were enrolled and later raised their contribution rate on their own
choices.B: Younger workers who would not have joined the plan under the old rule
choices.C: Workers already inclined to save who stopped at the low default
choices.D: Lower-income workers who joined only because enrollment was automatic

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Zebra stripes evolved mainly to hide zebras from lions and hyenas on open plains.
choices.B: Stripes matter more for keeping zebras cool than for protecting them from flies.
choices.C: The camouflage and fly explanations now have roughly equal experimental support.
choices.D: The idea that stripes deter biting flies now has the most support.

questions.stem: The last sentence of the first paragraph ("Until recently, few had been tested in ways that could tell them apart") mainly serves to:

choices.A: set up the passage's focus on evidence that can distinguish among the explanations.
choices.B: suggest that most of the explanations listed have already been disproved.
choices.C: explain why biologists lost interest in zebra stripes for many years.
choices.D: introduce a new explanation that none of the earlier biologists had considered.

questions.stem: In the second paragraph, the statement that the 2016 study "took that reply seriously" most nearly means that the study's authors:

choices.A: agreed that zebras are well hidden from predators.
choices.B: tested the defenders' claim instead of dismissing it.
choices.C: argued that camouflage should be judged by human vision.
choices.D: measured how far away lions can hear and smell prey.

questions.subskill: Purpose of a detail in an argument
questions.stem: The detail that a lion within about fifty meters "would probably already have heard or smelled its prey" (paragraph 2) mainly supports the idea that:

choices.A: lions depend more on smell than on sight in every hunting situation.
choices.B: lions hunt mostly at dusk because their hearing is better at night.
choices.C: stripes would add little concealment even where a lion can see them.
choices.D: zebras can usually detect a lion before the lion detects them.

questions.subskill: What an experiment adds to a correlation
questions.stem: Based on paragraphs 3 and 4, the 2019 study provided which kind of evidence that the 2014 analysis could not?

choices.A: Evidence that changing the pattern changes how flies behave
choices.B: Data on more horse species living in more regions
choices.C: Measurements of how far away predators can make out the stripes
choices.D: Counts of how many biting flies live in each region with zebras

questions.stem: The observation that flies circled zebras and horses "about equally often" (paragraph 4) suggests that the stripes:

choices.A: make zebras harder for flies to locate from a distance.
choices.B: attract more flies to zebras than plain coats attract to horses.
choices.C: have no effect on how flies behave around zebras.
choices.D: do not stop flies from finding zebras but disrupt their landings.

questions.subskill: Purpose of a control in an experiment
questions.stem: The detail that the horses' uncovered heads "were landed on about equally often whatever coat the animal wore" (paragraph 4) is significant mainly because it shows that:

choices.A: the coats' pattern, not the horses themselves, cut the landings.
choices.B: biting flies prefer to land on an animal's head rather than its body.
choices.C: a striped coat protects every part of a horse's body from flies.
choices.D: the horses found the patterned coats uncomfortable to wear.

questions.subskill: Evaluating evidence that would weaken a claim
questions.stem: Which of the following findings, if true, would most directly weaken the fly hypothesis as the passage presents it?

choices.A: Lions turned out to see stripes clearly from much farther than fifty meters.
choices.B: Stripes turned out to help zebras recognize members of their own herd.
choices.C: Flies turned out to circle zebras slightly more often than they circle horses.
choices.D: The most boldly striped zebras turned out to live where biting flies are rare.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states a central idea of the passage?

choices.A: The narrator learns that the father is far more patient with teachers than with clerks.
choices.B: Years of softened translations had kept the narrator's father from responding for himself.
choices.C: The narrator discovers that Tomas's teacher has misjudged Tomas's behavior in class.
choices.D: The narrator decides that the family should stop relying on the narrator to translate.

questions.stem: In paragraph 2, the narrator's description of being "a kind of shock absorber" mainly suggests that the narrator:

choices.A: protected the father from people who were trying to cheat him.
choices.B: absorbed blame for mistakes that other people had made.
choices.C: stopped conversations before they could turn into arguments.
choices.D: softened each side's words so that neither felt their full force.

questions.stem: The narrator's statement that the father made requests "the way a man asks for something he believes he has already paid for" (paragraph 1) suggests that the father's manner was:

choices.A: blunt, as though he were already owed what he asked for.
choices.B: humble, as though he fully expected to be refused.
choices.C: confused, as though he did not quite know what he wanted.
choices.D: dishonest, as though he had not actually paid for it.

questions.stem: The narrator stops in the middle of the first attempt to translate Ms. Pruitt's remarks (paragraph 4) mainly because the narrator:

choices.A: cannot think of a word in the home language for "interrupt."
choices.B: sees that the father already understood the teacher's English.
choices.C: notices that the words soften what the teacher said.
choices.D: is worried that Tomas, waiting in the hall, can hear them.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3, the short sentence "The interpreter was me" mainly serves to:

choices.A: show that the formal role of interpreter fell, as usual, to the narrator.
choices.B: suggest that the narrator resented being asked to interpret again.
choices.C: reveal that the father had hoped to hire a professional interpreter.
choices.D: show that Ms. Pruitt had expected the narrator to come to the meeting.

questions.subskill: How an outcome bears on an expectation
questions.stem: The father's response in paragraph 7 most directly shows that the narrator's long-held expectation about him was:

choices.A: correct, since he reacted sharply before he agreed with the teacher.
choices.B: irrelevant, since Tomas had already told him about the trouble in class.
choices.C: partly correct, since he thanked the teacher but refused to talk to Tomas.
choices.D: mistaken, since he took the teacher's criticism with good humor.

questions.stem: When the father says that "Tomas gets it from him" (paragraph 7), he most likely means that:

choices.A: Tomas learned to interrupt by watching his older sibling translate.
choices.B: he recognizes his own manner of speaking in Tomas's behavior.
choices.C: he is responsible for Tomas's being so smart in class.
choices.D: he had expected Ms. Pruitt to blame his parenting.

questions.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 7, the word "straight" most nearly means:

choices.A: immediately.
