choices.B: neatly.
choices.C: honestly.
choices.D: alone.

questions.stem: On the walk home, when the father says that the narrator "had been quiet in there" (last paragraph), he is most likely referring to the narrator's:

choices.A: slower, more careful translating during the meeting.
choices.B: refusal to answer Ms. Pruitt's questions about Tomas.
choices.C: decision to let Tomas wait outside in the hall.
choices.D: silence while the father laughed at Ms. Pruitt's remarks.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Before 1883, railroad schedules were confusing because each line kept its own time.
choices.B: Railroads made the hour a shared convention rather than a local reading of the sun.
choices.C: The railroads adopted time zones mainly to prevent collisions on single-track lines.
choices.D: Standard time succeeded once the government gave the railroads authority to set it.

questions.stem: Based on the first paragraph, a town located well west of Chicago that kept local time would have reached noon:

choices.A: earlier than Chicago did.
choices.B: at the same moment as Chicago.
choices.C: at the same moment as Boston.
choices.D: later than Chicago did.

questions.stem: The description of a station with "several clocks on the wall" (paragraph 2) mainly illustrates:

choices.A: the confusion that arose when each railroad kept its own time.
choices.B: the high cost of building large railroad stations.
choices.C: the railroads' success in agreeing on a single time.
choices.D: travelers' preference for local time over railroad time.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that mismatched times were especially dangerous on single-track lines because:

choices.A: single-track lines ran through more towns than other lines did.
choices.B: trains on single-track lines traveled faster than other trains did.
choices.C: opposing trains had to meet at set places at set times.
choices.D: single-track lines were owned by several railroads at once.

questions.stem: According to the passage, some towns experienced "two noons" on November 18, 1883, because:

choices.A: their clocks, already past local noon, were set back to noon by the new standard.
choices.B: their clocks were set forward, so noon came earlier than it usually did.
choices.C: they kept local time and standard time on separate clocks all day long.
choices.D: the telegraph signal that set the clocks arrived twice on some lines.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, the author's attitude toward the objectors is best described as:

choices.A: qualified disagreement, because their legal claim was mistaken though their worry was fair.
choices.B: complete agreement, because the change should have waited for Congress to act.
choices.C: indifference, because the objectors had little effect on whether the change happened.
choices.D: qualified agreement, because they were right about the law but missed why the change succeeded.

questions.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 4, the word "striking" most nearly means:

choices.A: forceful.
choices.B: attractive.
choices.C: notable.
choices.D: sudden.

questions.subskill: Applying an idea to a new situation
questions.stem: Which of the following situations best illustrates the change in the meaning of noon described in the last paragraph?

choices.A: A farmer watches a shadow to decide when noon has come.
choices.B: A town's clocks read noon before the sun reaches its highest point.
choices.C: A traveler finds two station clocks that disagree by several minutes.
choices.D: A city passes a law requiring its clocks to match the position of the sun.

questions.subskill: Purpose of a fact in an argument
questions.stem: The fact that "the federal government did not make standard time law until 1918" (paragraph 4) mainly supports the author's point that:

choices.A: standard time spread by practice long before a law required it.
choices.B: the railroads opposed every attempt to make standard time a law.
choices.C: the railroads asked Congress to pass a law right after 1883.
choices.D: the four time zones were redrawn when the law was finally passed.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Medieval scribes added spaces so that monks could read silently in their monasteries.
choices.B: A change in how words appeared on the page may have reshaped how people read.
choices.C: Ancient readers of Latin could not read silently until spaces were added between words.
choices.D: Continuous script was harder for ancient readers than it is for readers today.

questions.stem: The author begins the passage with a line printed without spaces mainly in order to:

choices.A: give modern readers a direct sense of what continuous script was like.
choices.B: show that ancient scribes made frequent errors when copying texts.
choices.C: prove that continuous script was impossible for anyone to read.
choices.D: suggest that modern books should return to continuous script.

questions.subskill: Applying an explanation to a new case
questions.stem: Based on the passage, which of the following readers would most likely have found a page of continuous Latin script hardest to read?

choices.A: A Roman reader reading the page aloud to a group of listeners
choices.B: A Roman reader sounding out the page alone, quietly but aloud
choices.C: A reader who knew Latin only from books, reading the page silently
choices.D: A reader who had heard the same text read aloud many times

questions.stem: The detail that some scribes began a sentence with a larger letter (paragraph 3) mainly supports the idea that the scribes:

choices.A: cared more about making books beautiful than easy to read.
choices.B: borrowed the practice directly from earlier Roman inscriptions.
choices.C: needed to save space on pages that were costly to produce.
choices.D: were starting to use the look of the page to guide readers.

questions.stem: In paragraph 2, the comparison of a text in continuous script to "a musical score" mainly suggests that such a text:

choices.A: left part of the work of reading it to the person performing it.
choices.B: was copied more carefully than other kinds of writing.
choices.C: was meant to be read silently and as quickly as possible.
choices.D: contained marks telling readers how to pronounce each word.

questions.stem: According to the skeptics in paragraph 5, Augustine's account of Ambrose suggests that silent reading at the time was:

choices.A: impossible for anyone who had not received special training.
choices.B: uncommon for someone in Ambrose's position but not unheard of.
choices.C: expected of bishops whenever they read in public.
choices.D: common enough that Augustine saw nothing unusual in it.

questions.stem: The last sentence of the passage mainly serves to:

choices.A: introduce a new piece of evidence about Irish scribes.
choices.B: concede that the skeptics' view is correct after all.
choices.C: widen the point about spacing into a claim about reading.
choices.D: summarize the steps by which spacing spread across Europe.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the skeptics' position described in paragraph 5?

choices.A: Monasteries that adopted word spacing produced more books each year.
choices.B: Modern readers read faster when words are separated by spaces.
choices.C: Irish scribes were the first in Europe to separate words with spaces.
choices.D: Ancient schoolbooks include exercises in reading passages silently.

questions.stem: The fourth paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: explain why Irish scribes chose to add spaces between words.
choices.B: present a claim that the passage then goes on to question.
choices.C: describe the evidence that silent reading was common in ancient times.
choices.D: summarize the author's final view of word spacing.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Wood frogs avoid freezing by burying themselves deep beneath the forest floor.
choices.B: Wood frogs survive freezing by controlling where ice forms and by protecting their cells.
choices.C: Wood frogs have already shown doctors how to freeze human organs safely.
choices.D: Wood frogs from Alaska and from the south use completely different methods.

questions.stem: Based on paragraph 2, a wood frog's cells survive freezing mainly because:

choices.A: the frog's cells contain no water during winter.
choices.B: cold temperatures alone cannot damage animal cells.
choices.C: the frog's body never drops below the freezing point.
choices.D: ice forms around them rather than inside them.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that, compared with a frozen wood frog, a wood frog that has not yet begun to freeze would most likely have:

choices.A: much less glucose in its blood.
choices.B: much less glycogen stored in its liver.
choices.C: a slower heartbeat than a frozen frog has.
choices.D: more ice in the spaces between its cells.

questions.subskill: Applying a mechanism to explain a difference
questions.stem: Based on the passage, the Alaskan frogs' larger stores of glycogen most likely help them survive colder temperatures because:

choices.A: glycogen itself freezes at a lower temperature than water does.
choices.B: larger glycogen stores keep ice from forming outside the cells.
choices.C: the liver can turn more glycogen into glucose when freezing begins.
choices.D: glycogen lets the frog's heart keep beating while it is frozen.

questions.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 2, the word "concentrated" most nearly means:

choices.A: more focused.
choices.B: less diluted.
choices.C: gathered in one place.
choices.D: strengthened by exercise.

questions.stem: The author mentions that the frog's glucose levels would be "deadly to a human" (paragraph 3) mainly to:

choices.A: warn readers about the dangers of high blood sugar.
choices.B: suggest that frogs and humans have identical blood chemistry.
choices.C: emphasize how extreme the frog's rise in blood sugar is.
choices.D: explain why the frog's heart stops when it freezes.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings, if true, would most directly support the passage's claim that glucose protects the frog's cells during freezing?

choices.A: Frogs with more glucose in their blood hopped faster after thawing in spring.
choices.B: Frogs in Alaska stored more urea in the fall than southern frogs did.
choices.C: Frogs began releasing glucose a few minutes after ice touched their skin.
choices.D: Frogs kept from releasing glucose died after freezing that untreated frogs survived.

questions.stem: The last paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: explain why the frog's abilities matter beyond the frog itself.
choices.B: describe how human organs are frozen for transplant today.
choices.C: argue that the frog's methods will soon be copied in hospitals.
choices.D: compare the wood frog with other animals that survive freezing.

questions.stem: The author describes the frozen frog as being in a state that "looks, by every ordinary sign, like death" (paragraph 1) mainly in order to:

choices.A: suggest that many wood frogs do not survive the winter.
choices.B: set up the surprise that the frog revives each spring.
choices.C: argue that scientists once wrongly believed the frogs were dead.
choices.D: explain why the frog is buried under leaf litter in winter.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best describes the passage as a whole?

choices.A: A gardener's long friendship with her neighbor ends after a dispute over a county fair contest.
choices.B: A gardener quietly protects her longtime rival's entry before a contest, and the rivalry continues afterward.
choices.C: Two gardeners compare their methods for growing pumpkins and agree that talking to plants makes little difference.
choices.D: A storm destroys one gardener's pumpkin, and her neighbor wins the county fair contest for the first time.

questions.stem: In paragraph 2, the statement that Ruth "did not consider herself competitive. She considered herself thorough" mainly suggests that Ruth:

choices.A: is not interested in the contest and grows pumpkins only for her own records.
choices.B: believes her neighbor's methods are more thorough than her own.
choices.C: has recently decided to stop competing against her neighbor.
choices.D: describes her careful habits in a way that downplays how much winning matters to her.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Dale's windows were dark on the night of the storm because he:

choices.A: had driven to the city to pick up his grandson.
choices.B: was asleep and did not hear the rain.
choices.C: was at his daughter's wedding.
choices.D: had gone to the fairgrounds to prepare for the weigh-off.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, the description of the plastic sheeting "snapping in the wind like a sail" mainly serves to:

choices.A: suggest that Dale had designed his hoop house to resemble a boat.
choices.B: indicate that the storm was ending and the wind was growing calmer.
choices.C: show how violently the loose sheeting was being whipped around by the storm.
choices.D: explain why Ruth's own tarps had been torn loose by the wind.

questions.stem: The first paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: establish a long, closely matched rivalry in which each gardener keeps track of the other's setbacks.
choices.B: explain the rules that the county fair uses to weigh and judge the pumpkins entered in its contest.
choices.C: introduce the storm that later threatens both gardeners' pumpkins on the night before the weigh-off.
choices.D: suggest that Dale has usually been the more careful and successful of the two gardeners.

questions.stem: In paragraph 2, the narrator's comment that Ruth was "less sure" Dale's habit was ridiculous most strongly suggests that Ruth:

choices.A: has started talking to her own pumpkin in secret when Dale is away.
choices.B: believes that talking to plants is scientifically proven to work.
choices.C: wants her sister to stop asking her so many questions about her neighbor.
choices.D: privately suspects there may be more to Dale's habit than she admits.

questions.stem: The statement that Ruth "meant it, or at least most of it" when she clapped (paragraph 7) suggests that Ruth:

choices.A: regretted having helped Dale protect his pumpkin the night before.
choices.B: was mostly glad for Dale but still felt some disappointment at losing.
choices.C: was pretending to be happy while feeling only anger.
choices.D: did not realize at first that Dale's pumpkin had beaten hers.

questions.stem: Taken together, Dale's remarks in paragraphs 8 and 10 most strongly suggest that he:

choices.A: believes a stranger repaired his hoop house and wants Ruth to help find that person.
choices.B: is angry that someone touched his hoop house without asking.
choices.C: knows Ruth protected his pumpkin and shows his thanks by treating her as a rival again.
choices.D: plans to stop competing because he thinks he won unfairly.

questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 1, the word "unprompted" most nearly means:

choices.A: without being paid.
choices.B: without being asked.
choices.C: without being certain.
choices.D: without being kind.

questions.stem: The final paragraph suggests that Ruth:

choices.A: has decided to stop keeping records of her plants.
choices.B: believes Dale cannot possibly beat her by a hundred pounds.
choices.C: plans to tell Dale that she was the one who fixed his hoop house.
choices.D: accepts Dale's challenge and is already preparing for next year's contest.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: A famous news story from 1964 proved that people living in large cities are less willing to help strangers than people living in small towns.
choices.B: Laboratory studies of the bystander effect have been shown to be false by recent research using security cameras.
choices.C: Research prompted by a famous but flawed news story found that individuals in groups help less, yet groups as a whole often do produce a helper.
choices.D: Psychologists now agree that people are more likely to help in an emergency when they are alone than when others are present.

questions.stem: The main purpose of the first paragraph is to:

choices.A: describe a widely reported event that led researchers to study why people fail to help.
choices.B: argue that the New York Times should not have reported the attack on Kitty Genovese.
choices.C: explain the two causes of the bystander effect proposed by Darley and Latané.
choices.D: present evidence from security cameras that bystanders usually intervene.

questions.stem: According to the passage, one explanation Darley and Latané offered for the bystander effect is that when many people witness an emergency, each person:

choices.A: may be too frightened by the size of the crowd to move toward the victim.
choices.B: may not have a telephone nearby with which to call the police quickly.
choices.C: may believe that the victim is only pretending to be hurt or in danger.
choices.D: may count on another witness to take action instead of doing so personally.

questions.stem: Based on the second explanation Darley and Latané proposed, a participant in the smoke-filled room who sees two other people calmly continuing their work would most likely:

choices.A: leave the room immediately to report the smoke.
choices.B: conclude that the smoke is probably not a sign of danger.
choices.C: ask the two others whether they feel responsible for the smoke.
choices.D: assume that the two others have already reported the smoke.

questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 2, the word "staged" most nearly means:

choices.A: arranged.
choices.B: divided into steps.
choices.C: performed in a theater.
choices.D: delayed.

questions.stem: The third paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: prove that laboratory studies of the bystander effect could not be reproduced.
choices.B: introduce the security-camera study that tested the bystander effect in real life.
choices.C: explain why the bystander effect became well known among psychologists.
choices.D: show that the news story that prompted the research was less accurate than first reported.

questions.stem: According to the passage, in the conflicts that Philpot's team examined, at least one bystander intervened in about:

choices.A: nine of every ten conflicts.
choices.B: one of every ten conflicts.
choices.C: half of the conflicts.
choices.D: every conflict without exception.

questions.stem: Compared with Darley and Latané's experiments, Philpot's study differed mainly in that it:

choices.A: measured how quickly individual participants responded to what sounded like a seizure.
choices.B: examined real conflicts recorded in public rather than emergencies set up by researchers.
choices.C: found that no bystanders ever intervened in conflicts where large groups were present.
choices.D: relied on the reporting of the New York Times to identify and interview the witnesses.

questions.subskill: Applying an argument to new evidence
questions.stem: Which of the following hypothetical findings would be most consistent with the reasoning in the last paragraph?

choices.A: Lone witnesses helped less often than individuals in groups did, and victims with only one witness were also helped less often.
choices.B: Each bystander in groups of ten helped less often than lone witnesses, and victims with ten bystanders were also helped less often.
choices.C: Bystanders in groups helped exactly as often as lone witnesses did, and the size of the group made no difference to how often victims were helped.
choices.D: Each bystander in groups of ten helped less often than lone witnesses did, yet victims with ten bystanders were helped more often than victims with one.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the bystander effect is best described as:

choices.A: accepting that it is a real finding about individuals while questioning what it has been taken to show about people in general.
choices.B: dismissive, because the news story that first inspired the research turned out to be exaggerated and partly false.
choices.C: uncritical, because the effect has been reproduced in many laboratory studies over several decades of research.
choices.D: puzzled, because the laboratory findings and the security-camera findings seem impossible to reconcile with each other.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Vermeer frequently painted over parts of his own finished work, as X-ray studies of many of his paintings in museums have repeatedly shown.
choices.B: Hidden changes beneath paintings reveal how artists worked and raise hard questions about which version of a painting should be preserved.
choices.C: Modern imaging tools have now made it possible to determine exactly what every artist originally intended to paint.
choices.D: Restorers should always return a painting to its earliest known state, as the Dresden museum correctly did in 2021.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what did the conservators' analysis of the paint layers show about the plain wall covering the Cupid?

choices.A: It had been painted by Vermeer shortly before his death.
choices.B: It had been added by Vermeer's students while he was still painting.
choices.C: It had been revealed by X-rays only during the 2017 cleaning.
choices.D: It had been added well after Vermeer died.

questions.stem: The main purpose of the first paragraph is to:

choices.A: present a specific case that introduces both hidden painted layers and the restoration debate discussed later.
choices.B: explain in detail the scientific methods that conservators use to date the separate layers of paint in an old picture.
choices.C: argue that the Dresden museum should have left the painting exactly as visitors had always seen it.
choices.D: compare Vermeer's working methods with those of Pablo Picasso and other painters of later centuries.

questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 5, the word "settles" most nearly means:

choices.A: calms.
choices.B: colonizes.
choices.C: resolves.
choices.D: sinks.

questions.stem: Based on paragraph 3, which of the following might scholars suspect about a painting that shows no pentimenti at all?

choices.A: It could be a copy made by someone who already knew the finished image.
choices.B: It must be an original, since copyists usually make many changes.
choices.C: It was made by an artist who never considered other compositions.
choices.D: It has been damaged by too much cleaning over the years.

questions.stem: According to the passage, infrared cameras can reveal:

choices.A: dense pigments such as lead white in the paint.
choices.B: sketches drawn on the canvas before any paint was applied.
choices.C: the exact date when each layer of paint was added.
choices.D: varnish on the surface that has turned yellow with age.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3, the examples "a shifted arm, a hand painted in two positions, a window that was once a door" mainly serve to:

choices.A: suggest that most artists painted carelessly and had to correct mistakes.
choices.B: describe the specific changes found beneath the Dresden Vermeer.
choices.C: explain how X-rays distinguish one pigment from another.
choices.D: illustrate the kinds of changes that show an artist considered other compositions.

questions.stem: The critics described in paragraph 4 would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

choices.A: A painting should always be returned to the exact state that its artist finally intended for it.
choices.B: Conservators should not use X-rays or other imaging tools to study the hidden layers of old paintings.
choices.C: How a painting has been seen over its long history should count in deciding what form it should take.
choices.D: Vermeer's original Cupid was poorly painted and not worth the effort of uncovering and displaying.

questions.stem: Which example from the passage best supports the author's claim in paragraph 5 that a painting can be "a surface that holds many moments at once"?

choices.A: The Dresden Vermeer described in paragraph 1
choices.B: Picasso's The Old Guitarist, described in paragraph 2
choices.C: The copies that scholars try to identify, described in paragraph 3
choices.D: The examples of changed arms, hands, and windows listed in paragraph 3

questions.stem: According to the passage, some pentimenti become visible to the naked eye because:

choices.A: conservators remove the top layer of paint during cleaning.
choices.B: artists deliberately leave earlier versions showing.
choices.C: X-rays permanently change the color of lead white.
choices.D: the upper layers of oil paint grow more transparent as they age.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Early warning systems use the speed gap between seismic waves to give seconds of useful notice, though they have real limits.
choices.B: Early warning systems can now predict most earthquakes days before they occur, giving whole cities time to evacuate.
choices.C: Mexico City and Japan operate the only earthquake warning systems that have ever worked reliably anywhere in the world.
choices.D: P waves cause more damage than S waves, which is why warning sensors are designed to detect the P waves first.

questions.stem: According to the passage, compared with S waves, P waves:

choices.A: travel more slowly and cause most of the damage.
choices.B: travel at the same speed but arrive later.
choices.C: travel faster and usually cause milder shaking.
choices.D: travel faster and cause most of the damage.

questions.stem: According to the passage, an alert can reach a distant city before the damaging shaking does because:

choices.A: S waves stop traveling once they reach the edge of the blind zone.
choices.B: electronic signals travel almost instantly compared with waves moving through rock.
choices.C: sensors are placed in every city so that each can detect its own shaking.
choices.D: P waves travel faster than electronic signals sent by radio or cell phone.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, which of the following places would most likely receive the longest warning before damaging shaking from an earthquake?

choices.A: A school directly above the point where the fault slipped
choices.B: A train station about 10 kilometers from where the fault slipped
choices.C: A factory about 40 kilometers from where the fault slipped
choices.D: A hospital about 150 kilometers from where the fault slipped

questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 4, the word "concrete" most nearly means:

choices.A: made of cement.
choices.B: difficult to change.
choices.C: specific and practical.
choices.D: hidden from view.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, the examples of trains, surgeons, elevators, and students mainly serve to:

choices.A: show that even a few seconds of warning allow useful protective actions.
choices.B: explain why Mexico City built its warning system in the early 1990s.
choices.C: suggest that warnings are useful only in buildings with modern equipment.
choices.D: demonstrate that the blind zone has been eliminated in large cities.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Mexico City receives unusually long warnings mainly because the city:

choices.A: has installed more earthquake sensors than any other city in the world.
choices.B: lies roughly 300 kilometers from the faults that cause many of its strongest earthquakes.
choices.C: sends its alerts mainly by television and radio instead of by cell phone.
choices.D: has operated a public warning system for longer than any other city has.

questions.stem: Based on paragraph 5, early estimates of the size of the largest earthquakes may be too low because:

choices.A: the sensors located near the source are usually destroyed by the first P waves.
choices.B: large earthquakes produce no P waves at all for the sensors to detect early.
choices.C: false alarms have caused engineers to lower every estimate on purpose.
choices.D: those earthquakes can keep growing well after the first few seconds the system uses.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, a person in the blind zone during an earthquake would most likely:

choices.A: feel the damaging shaking before receiving any alert.
choices.B: receive fifteen or twenty seconds of warning before the shaking.
choices.C: feel no shaking at all, since the waves pass beneath the zone.
choices.D: receive an alert but feel only mild P-wave shaking afterward.

questions.stem: The final sentence of the passage ("The gain from early warning ... do with them") most strongly suggests that the value of an early warning system:

choices.A: is too small to justify the high cost of building and running such systems.
choices.B: depends on whether people and machines are ready to act in the few seconds it provides.
choices.C: will grow to several minutes of notice once engineers improve detection methods.
choices.D: is greatest for the people who live closest to the earthquake's source.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best describes the passage as a whole?

choices.A: A lifeguard's first rescue convinces her that her years of training were mostly unnecessary after all.
choices.B: A lifeguard's rescue convinces her teasing brother that her job is more dangerous than he had thought.
choices.C: A lifeguard who has never made a rescue realizes that her uneventful hours prepared her for a real emergency.
choices.D: A lifeguard's quick thinking earns her praise from the other guards and a promotion to head guard.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, how often did Mara move to a different chair?

choices.A: every forty-five minutes
choices.B: every ten seconds
choices.C: once an hour
choices.D: only at the start of each shift

questions.stem: The second paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: explain the specific rescue techniques that Mara learned in training each June.
choices.B: reveal that Mara's younger brother secretly wanted to become a lifeguard himself.
choices.C: describe the crowd that filled the pool on the hot last Saturday of August.
choices.D: show that the job had come to seem pointless to Mara, setting up later events.

questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 1, the word "fished" most nearly means:

choices.A: caught with a hook.
choices.B: retrieved.
choices.C: searched aimlessly.
choices.D: sold.

questions.stem: Based on paragraphs 3 and 6, the boy's distress was easy to miss mainly because:

choices.A: he was calling for help far too quietly to be heard over the noisy crowd.
choices.B: he was swimming out in the deep end, far from all of the lifeguard chairs.
choices.C: he was not splashing or calling out, so he looked almost like someone who was fine.
choices.D: the pool was nearly empty that day, so no one was looking at the water.

questions.stem: The exchange between Mara and her brother in paragraph 5 mainly serves to:

choices.A: show that Mara's brief answer ends the teasing that had become a routine.
choices.B: reveal that Mara's brother had watched the rescue from the pool deck.
choices.C: suggest that Mara is ashamed of what happened at the pool that day.
choices.D: explain why Mara decides not to return to the pool the next summer.

questions.stem: According to the passage, who reached Mara and the boy first after she set him on the deck?

choices.A: The other guards
choices.B: Mara's brother
choices.C: The woman who had been laughing with a friend
choices.D: The boy's mother

questions.stem: The statement in paragraph 4 that Mara "could not remember deciding anything" most strongly suggests that:

choices.A: she was too frightened to act until the other guards arrived.
choices.B: her response came automatically, without a conscious decision.
choices.C: she later forgot the rescue entirely and had to be told about it.
choices.D: someone else made the decision and told her to enter the water.

questions.stem: The passage is told from the point of view of:

choices.A: a narrator outside the story who reports Mara's thoughts and memories.
choices.B: Mara herself, describing the events in the first person many years later.
choices.C: Mara's younger brother, who describes his sister's job and the rescue.
choices.D: the boy's mother, who watched the whole rescue from her seat by the fence.

questions.stem: The detail that the boy was "lighter than any of the teenagers she had practiced on" mainly emphasizes:

choices.A: that the boy was too small to be allowed in the pool without an adult.
choices.B: that Mara was stronger than the other guards at the pool.
choices.C: that the teenagers in training had been pretending to be heavier than they were.
choices.D: how the real rescue differed from the practice rescues Mara had done in training.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Laws and dictionaries have proven to be the most effective ways to save endangered languages around the world.
choices.B: Some communities have shown that endangered languages can gain new speakers, mainly by reaching young children, though the work is hard.
choices.C: Most of the world's endangered languages will disappear within a decade no matter what communities attempt.
choices.D: The Māori language was never truly endangered, since many adults continued to speak it throughout the twentieth century.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a language is described as endangered when:

choices.A: it has no written alphabet or dictionary.
choices.B: its speakers have moved from rural areas to cities.
choices.C: it is no longer taught in any school.
choices.D: fewer and fewer children are learning it.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 1, which of the following can disappear when the last speakers of a language die?

choices.A: songs, stories, and knowledge of local plants and places
choices.B: the written records kept by linguists who studied the language
choices.C: the laws that once protected the language in schools
choices.D: the dictionaries and recordings made during revival efforts

questions.stem: According to the passage, kōhanga reo were:

choices.A: adult evening classes that taught Māori grammar.
choices.B: government offices that recorded the speech of elders.
choices.C: preschools in which elders spoke only Māori with young children.
choices.D: primary schools that taught partly in English and partly in Māori.

questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 5, the word "decisive" most nearly means:

choices.A: quick to make up one's mind and act.
choices.B: most important in determining the result.
choices.C: final and impossible to change later.
choices.D: easy to identify or point out.

questions.stem: The mention of Hawaiʻi at the end of paragraph 4 mainly serves to:

choices.A: prove that Hawaiian is now spoken by more children than Māori is.
choices.B: explain why Māori families moved to cities in the twentieth century.
choices.C: suggest that the Hawaiian language had already disappeared by 1980.
choices.D: show that the language-nest approach was used beyond New Zealand.

questions.subskill: Applying a claim to a case
questions.stem: Based on paragraph 5, a child who studies an endangered language at school but never hears it at home would most likely:

choices.A: become a more fluent speaker than a child who hears it only at home.
choices.B: refuse to learn the language because it is taught only at school.
choices.C: know a good deal about the language without using it in everyday life.
choices.D: lose the ability to speak the community's other languages.

questions.stem: According to the passage, one reason revitalization is difficult is that:

choices.A: many parents must first learn the language themselves as adults.
choices.B: children learn new languages less easily than adults do.
choices.C: many communities lack enough elders to staff language nests.
choices.D: governments have refused to allow the languages to be taught in schools.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following contributed to the decline of the Māori language in the twentieth century?

choices.A: The closing of the kōhanga reo and of the Māori-language primary schools
choices.B: A law that made Māori the only language allowed in New Zealand's schools
choices.C: A decision by many elders to speak only English with their grandchildren
choices.D: Families moving to cities and children being discouraged from speaking it in school

questions.stem: Within the passage as a whole, the example of Hebrew in paragraph 3 mainly serves to:

choices.A: explain why Hebrew is far more widely spoken today than either the Māori or the Hawaiian language is.
choices.B: provide an established case showing that the assumption described in paragraph 2 can be wrong.
choices.C: argue that language revitalization can succeed only when a new country is founded.
choices.D: show that languages used mainly in prayer are much less likely to become endangered.

questions.subskill: Main idea of a literary passage
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the main focus of the passage?

choices.A: A narrator explains how to paint letters on glass, step by step, for readers who want to learn the craft.
choices.B: A narrator describes a rivalry between an aunt's sign shop and a print shop across the highway.
choices.C: A narrator recalls a summer job in which an aunt's trade changed how the narrator sees handmade work.
choices.D: A narrator regrets having spoiled a store's window and losing a customer for an aunt's business.

questions.stem: When Rosalind says, "That depends on the O" (paragraph 2), she most nearly means that:

choices.A: she has not yet decided which letter of the alphabet the narrator should practice next.
choices.B: the number of letters needed depends on the size of the sign that the shop is currently painting.
choices.C: some O's are much harder to paint than others because of differences in their size and shape.
choices.D: the narrator will keep practicing until the letters are acceptable, however long that takes.

questions.stem: The statement that the owner "seemed to decide that he had been admiring it all along" (paragraph 5) most strongly suggests that the owner:

choices.A: had noticed the uneven letters on the window before Rosalind or the narrator did.
choices.B: changed his view of the S after hearing Rosalind's explanation.
choices.C: wanted the narrator to scrape off the whole sign and then repaint it carefully.
choices.D: had never looked closely at the new sign on his window until Rosalind spoke.

questions.stem: In the last paragraph, the narrator's comment that Rosalind "scraped her own mistakes off without a second look" mainly serves to:

choices.A: suggest that her remark to the owner may have been partly a kindness rather than a fixed belief.
choices.B: prove that Rosalind never made mistakes in her own work.
choices.C: show that the narrator's letters were better than Rosalind's.
choices.D: explain why Rosalind eventually decided to scrape off the hardware sign.

questions.stem: The last sentence of the passage mainly indicates that by the end of the summer the narrator:

choices.A: had decided to become a professional sign painter like Rosalind someday.
choices.B: had learned to notice a difference that had been invisible to the narrator before.
choices.C: had come to prefer cut vinyl signs to the painted signs Rosalind made.
choices.D: felt embarrassed by the poorly made signs along the bus route home.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Experiments suggest that some night-active dung beetles hold a straight course by the glow of the Milky Way, though the findings have limits.
choices.B: Dung beetles are able to find their way back to their nests at night by memorizing the positions of the brightest stars.
choices.C: Dung beetles roll their balls in straight lines mainly because doing so uses less energy than rolling them in circles.
choices.D: Planetariums have become the most important tools that researchers now use to study the behavior of insects.

questions.subskill: Purpose of a behavior (cause and effect)
questions.stem: According to the passage, a dung beetle benefits from rolling its ball in a straight line because doing so:

choices.A: allows the beetle to keep the sun or moon directly in front of it as it walks.
choices.B: moves the beetle away from other beetles that might steal the ball.
choices.C: helps the ball keep its round shape over long distances on rough ground.
choices.D: lets the beetle return later to the same pile to make another ball more easily.

questions.stem: The main function of the third paragraph ("By day ... steering by?") is to:

choices.A: describe how the beetle uses its hind legs and front legs to push the ball backward.
choices.B: argue that earlier researchers in South Africa had misunderstood how the beetles use moonlight.
choices.C: present the results of the planetarium experiments and the researchers' explanation for them.
choices.D: explain an earlier finding and the unanswered question that led to the planetarium study.

questions.stem: The researchers most likely fitted some beetles with transparent visors in order to:

choices.A: give those beetles a clearer view of the Milky Way than beetles without visors had.
choices.B: protect those beetles' eyes from the bright light inside the planetarium dome.
choices.C: rule out the possibility that wearing a visor, rather than losing sight of the sky, caused the wandering.
choices.D: test whether beetles could see individual stars through a thin layer of material.

questions.stem: Which of the following results described in the passage most directly supports the claim that the beetles do not need to see individual stars?

choices.A: The beetles rolled almost as straight under a full starry sky as they did outdoors.
choices.B: The beetles kept a steady course when the dome showed only a diffuse band of light.
choices.C: The beetles wandered when the planetarium dome was completely dark.
choices.D: The beetles with cardboard visors wandered while those with transparent visors did not.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the researchers argued that steering by the Milky Way made sense for the beetles because:

choices.A: the Milky Way is the only part of the night sky that stays in one place.
choices.B: the moon is rarely bright enough to be seen from the ground in South Africa.
choices.C: the beetles need to know where they are going before they begin rolling.
choices.D: the beetles' eyes are probably too weak to pick out most individual stars.

questions.stem: The comparison to migrating birds in the last paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: clarify that the study showed holding a direction, not traveling to a particular place.
choices.B: suggest that dung beetles and migrating birds use the same parts of the night sky.
choices.C: show that migrating birds are better than dung beetles at seeing individual stars.
choices.D: argue that dung beetles will probably be found to migrate long distances as well.

questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 2, the word "fix" most nearly means:

choices.A: repair.
choices.B: arrange.
choices.C: establish.
choices.D: attach.

questions.stem: Based on the last paragraph, which of the following outcomes would be most consistent with the researchers' caution?

choices.A: A later study finds that the beetles cannot hold a straight line under any night sky.
choices.B: A later study finds that the beetles travel to the same distant location every night.
choices.C: A later study finds that the beetles use the Milky Way only when they are inside a planetarium.
choices.D: A later study finds that, when the moon is up, the same beetles steer by moonlight rather than by the Milky Way.

questions.stem: According to the passage, while rolling its ball, a dung beetle:

choices.A: walks on its front legs with its head down, facing away from its direction of travel.
choices.B: walks forward on all six legs while pushing the ball ahead with its head.
choices.C: rides on top of the ball and steers it with its front legs as it rolls.
choices.D: stops every few steps to climb on top of the ball and check the sky.

questions.stem: The narrator's description of how the mother referred to Rosalind's shop (paragraph 1) mainly suggests that the mother:

choices.A: was proud of her sister's success and liked to boast about the shop to her friends.
choices.B: regarded the business as an odd and somewhat unserious pursuit.
choices.C: did not really know what kind of work Rosalind's shop actually did each day.
choices.D: hoped that the narrator would someday take over the business from Rosalind.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following was a reason customers came to Rosalind instead of the print shop?

choices.A: They wanted gold leaf, which the print shop could not imitate.
choices.B: They needed their storefront signs finished in less than a single afternoon.
choices.C: They wanted to be able to choose from hundreds of different typefaces.
choices.D: They wanted to pay less for a sign than the print shop charged them.

questions.stem: In the passage, the detail that Rosalind "studied them the way other people read letters" (paragraph 3) mainly serves to suggest that she:

choices.A: treated the old signs as personal records worth close and careful attention.
choices.B: was trying to copy exactly the typefaces used by the painters who had died.
choices.C: preferred reading old letters to painting new signs for her customers.
choices.D: kept the photographs because she had painted many of the old signs herself.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following happened first?

choices.A: The narrator painted the name of a hardware store.
choices.B: The narrator was promoted to the rest of the alphabet.
choices.C: The narrator's O's stopped sagging.
choices.D: The narrator noticed the difference between cut and painted signs on the bus.

questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 2, the word "pooled" most nearly means:

choices.A: shared.
choices.B: thinned.
choices.C: dried.
choices.D: collected.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Kintsugi was invented in the fifteenth century after a Japanese tea bowl was poorly repaired in China.
choices.B: Kintsugi kits sold online have replaced the traditional method in most Japanese households.
choices.C: Kintsugi deliberately makes a repair visible, a choice whose meaning popular accounts can oversimplify.
choices.D: Kintsugi teaches that broken objects are more valuable than objects that have never been damaged.

questions.stem: The first two sentences of the passage ("Most methods ... damaged") mainly serve to:

choices.A: present a usual goal of repair that kintsugi rejects.
choices.B: criticize museum restorers for hiding the history of damaged objects.
choices.C: explain the steps a museum restorer follows when matching the glaze of a broken bowl.
choices.D: argue that thin glue lines are stronger and longer lasting than thick glue lines.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, the author's view of the story about the stapled tea bowl is best described as:

choices.A: convinced that it accurately records how and when kintsugi first began in Japan.
choices.B: skeptical of its accuracy but appreciative of its point.
choices.C: dismissive of it as a popular story that misleads readers about what kintsugi is.
choices.D: uncertain whether kintsugi ever used lacquer before the fifteenth century.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the traditional kintsugi method is slow mainly because:

choices.A: the gold powder must be ground by hand from solid pieces of metal before each new repair.
choices.B: craftsmen must first study the history of each bowl before beginning a repair.
choices.C: the broken pieces must first be soaked in water for several weeks to remove any old glue.
choices.D: each layer of lacquer must cure for days before the next is applied.

questions.subskill: Comparing two positions in a debate
questions.stem: The defenders of kintsugi kits described in the third paragraph would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

choices.A: Most admirers care more about the gold seam than about the lacquer.
choices.B: The quick-setting epoxy in the kits is stronger than traditional lacquer.
choices.C: The traditional method's patience is what gives a kintsugi repair its meaning.
choices.D: Kits should be sold only to people who have studied the traditional method.

questions.stem: In the fourth paragraph, the statement "No restorer smashes a bowl in order to mend it" mainly serves to:

choices.A: show that kintsugi restorers are more careful than other restorers.
choices.B: support the claim that kintsugi does not celebrate breakage.
choices.C: suggest that the fifteenth-century origin story is unlikely to be true.
choices.D: explain why kintsugi bowls are rarely displayed as curiosities.

questions.stem: As it is used in the first paragraph, the word "conspicuous" most nearly means:

choices.A: expensive.
choices.B: fragile.
choices.C: noticeable.
choices.D: traditional.

questions.stem: The author suggests that comparing kintsugi to recovering from personal loss can be a problem because such comparisons:

choices.A: are never made by people who practice kintsugi themselves.
choices.B: encourage people to break objects so that they can repair them.
choices.C: are based on a mistranslation of the term "golden joinery."
choices.D: may hide what the craft actually involves.

questions.stem: According to the last paragraph, a mended kintsugi bowl in a tea room is typically:

choices.A: still used for serving tea.
choices.B: displayed behind glass as a curiosity.
choices.C: retired from use once it is repaired.
choices.D: sold to collectors who value the gold.

questions.subskill: Relationship between the conclusion and an earlier claim
questions.stem: The last sentence of the passage most directly develops which earlier idea?

choices.A: A good glue line is a thin one, so that visitors cannot tell where an object was damaged.
choices.B: The lacquer hardens only in warm, humid conditions, and each layer must cure for days.
choices.C: The practice values the object's whole history, including the accident.
choices.D: A cheaper method has simply brought the idea of kintsugi to more households.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Offering shoppers fewer products is always the best way for stores to increase sales.
choices.B: A famous finding about too many choices has turned out to depend on circumstances.
choices.C: The jam study was flawed and should be ignored by researchers who study choosing.
choices.D: Economists have proved that more options can only help shoppers make better choices.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the 24-flavor display, compared with the 6-flavor display:

choices.A: attracted fewer shoppers but led to a larger share of them buying.
choices.B: attracted the same number of shoppers and led to the same share buying.
choices.C: attracted fewer shoppers and led to a smaller share of them buying.
choices.D: attracted more shoppers but led to a much smaller share of them buying.

questions.stem: The "common assumption" mentioned in the second paragraph is best described as the belief that:

choices.A: having more options cannot make a shopper worse off.
choices.B: shoppers prefer stores that offer fewer products.
choices.C: tasting booths increase sales of the products they display.
choices.D: upscale grocery stores attract shoppers who buy more.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, the finding that the average effect across fifty experiments was "close to zero" most likely means that:

choices.A: most of the fifty experiments were poorly designed and should not be counted.
choices.B: larger assortments had no effect on choosing in any of the fifty experiments.
choices.C: effects in opposite directions across studies largely canceled out.
choices.D: the original jam study could not be repeated by any later researchers.

questions.stem: The main purpose of the fourth paragraph is to:

choices.A: reconcile the mixed results with the original study.
choices.B: report the design of the jam study in more detail.
choices.C: argue that the original study was conducted incorrectly.
choices.D: describe how companies responded to the idea of choice overload.

questions.subskill: Applying a stated condition to a new case
questions.stem: Based on the conditions described in the fourth paragraph, which shopper would be LEAST likely to be discouraged by a large assortment?

choices.A: A shopper choosing a first laptop who must compare dozens of models with different features.
choices.B: A shopper who has bought one brand of tea for years and spots it at once.
choices.C: A shopper in a hurry who must pick one of forty unfamiliar sauces before a store closes.
choices.D: A shopper who has never tried any of the cheeses at a counter offering sixty varieties.

questions.stem: As it is used in the last paragraph, the word "striking" most nearly means:

choices.A: hitting.
choices.B: aggressive.
choices.C: final.
choices.D: remarkable.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the later, less dramatic findings about choice overload is best described as:

choices.A: approving, because they make the idea more useful.
choices.B: disappointed, because they disproved an important discovery.
choices.C: indifferent, because they did not change how stores sell products.
choices.D: suspicious, because they relied on too many different experiments.

questions.stem: According to the passage, after the jam study, some companies:

choices.A: stopped using tasting booths in their stores.
choices.B: raised the prices of their most popular products.
choices.C: reduced the number of products they offered.
choices.D: began conducting their own studies of shoppers.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: The narrator argues that subtitles, although they lose much of the original, are the most faithful kind of translation.
choices.B: The narrator explains how a supervisor's criticism taught the narrator to translate jokes rather than insults.
choices.C: The narrator came to see subtitling as choosing what serves viewers, not as a translation with parts left out.
choices.D: The narrator contends that viewers understand foreign films better from actors' faces than from any subtitle.

questions.stem: The narrator's view of subtitling during the first year on the job was most similar to the view held by:

choices.A: the people who ask whether it is frustrating to throw so much away.
choices.B: the supervisor who reviewed the subtitle for the grandmother's speech.
choices.C: the test audience that laughed at the joke about in-laws.
choices.D: the readers who believe that nothing has been lost in a translated novel.

questions.stem: The supervisor's remark "They need to know that she won" most strongly suggests that a subtitle for the speech should:

choices.A: summarize each of the insults briefly so that viewers can still follow all of them.
choices.B: be left out entirely, since viewers can follow the scene from the actors alone.
choices.C: make the grandmother's victory more obvious than it was in the original dialogue.
choices.D: convey the outcome and force of the speech rather than its full content.

questions.stem: The main function of the third paragraph is to:

choices.A: describe the training that the narrator received from the supervisor.
choices.B: explain why adding words to a subtitle can reduce what viewers understand.
choices.C: argue that actors' gestures matter more than any film's spoken dialogue does.
choices.D: introduce the comedy about the family running a failing restaurant.

questions.stem: As it is used in the third paragraph, the word lives most nearly means:

choices.A: is found.
choices.B: survives.
choices.C: grows.
choices.D: is recorded.

questions.stem: Based on the fourth paragraph, the narrator would most likely consider a subtitle for a joke successful if it:

choices.A: kept the literal meaning of every word in the original line of dialogue.
choices.B: was shorter than the line of dialogue spoken by the original character.
choices.C: had the same effect on its audience that the original line had on the original audience.
choices.D: replaced the original pun with a joke about in-laws or about some other family topic.

questions.stem: The narrator mentions the long, formal blessing mainly to illustrate that:

choices.A: a brief subtitle can be enough when the actor's delivery conveys the rest.
choices.B: formal greetings are especially difficult to translate into any other language.
choices.C: subtitles often need to contain more information than the original dialogue.
choices.D: neighbors in films usually greet one another more warmly than they do in life.

questions.stem: According to the narrator, subtitles are a "more honest" kind of translation than printed translations of novels because:

choices.A: subtitles usually keep more of the original words than printed translations do.
choices.B: subtitle writers must show each of their choices to a test audience before release.
choices.C: translators of novels are usually less careful than the people who write subtitles.
choices.D: the original remains audible, so viewers can sense where the subtitle departs from it.

questions.stem: The narrator's attitude toward what is lost in subtitling is best described as:

choices.A: resigned, because the narrator believes nothing can be done to save what is lost.
choices.B: accepting of such losses while redefining the job as choosing what matters.
choices.C: dismissive, because the narrator denies that subtitling loses anything at all.
choices.D: anxious, because viewers can easily notice what the subtitles have left out.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the way the passage is organized?

choices.A: A problem in film translation is described, several solutions are compared, and the best one is recommended.
choices.B: A common belief is stated, an experience that challenged it is recounted, and a revised view is explained.
choices.C: Several films are described in the order the narrator translated them, followed by a general conclusion.
choices.D: Two kinds of translation are defined at the start and then compared point by point throughout the passage.

questions.stem: The main purpose of the passage is to:

choices.A: argue that sand termites are the most likely cause of the fairy circles in the Namib Desert.
choices.B: describe how the fairy circles of Australia differ in shape and size from those in Namibia.
choices.C: explain why mathematical models of patterns are more reliable than digging into the ground.
choices.D: present two competing explanations for a natural pattern and the evidence bearing on each.

questions.stem: According to the termite explanation, the taller grass at the edge of each circle is supported mainly by:

choices.A: nutrients left in the soil by the termites' colonies.
choices.B: rainwater stored beneath the bare sand inside the circle.
choices.C: roots that the termites leave alone because they are too deep.
choices.D: moisture drawn from neighboring grasses outside the circle.

questions.stem: Based on the third paragraph, supporters of the water-competition explanation would most likely account for finding sand termites in nearly all of the circles by saying that the termites:

choices.A: settle in circles that already exist because water is stored beneath them.
choices.B: were probably misidentified by the researchers who dug into the circles.
choices.C: help the surrounding grasses compete with one another for scarce water.
choices.D: create new circles only in years when rainfall is unusually heavy.

questions.stem: In the fourth paragraph, the phrase beginning "though some insects do keep their distance" mainly serves to:

choices.A: provide direct evidence that sand termites fight neighboring colonies in Namibia.
choices.B: explain why researchers did not find termites in the circles of Western Australia.
choices.C: acknowledge a way that the termite explanation might account for regular spacing.
choices.D: show that the water-competition explanation cannot account for the circles' spacing.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings, if true, would most directly weaken the termite explanation?

choices.A: Sand termites were found in a circle that researchers had not excavated before.
choices.B: Individual circles were found to persist in the same spot for several decades.
choices.C: Grass at the edges of the circles grew taller in wet years than in dry years.
choices.D: New bare patches were seen forming and widening where no termites were present.

questions.stem: As it is used in the second paragraph, the word survived most nearly means:

choices.A: outlived.
choices.B: withstood.
choices.C: recovered from.
choices.D: continued after.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how do supporters of the termite explanation respond to the report of circles in Western Australia?

choices.A: They argue that the reports of Australian circles were mistaken.
choices.B: They argue that termites were in fact present in the Australian circles.
choices.C: They argue that a similar pattern in two places need not have the same cause.
choices.D: They argue that regular spacing proves the circles share a single cause.

questions.stem: According to the passage, experiments that remove termites from circles would be slow because:

choices.A: individual circles can remain in place for several decades.
choices.B: termites quickly return to circles from which they were removed.
choices.C: rain falls in the Namib Desert only once every several years.
choices.D: the circles are spread over a very large area of desert.

questions.stem: The final sentence of the passage most strongly suggests that:

choices.A: only mathematical models can reveal what caused a natural pattern.
choices.B: irregular patterns in nature are easier to explain than regular ones.
choices.C: the cause of the fairy circles will probably never be fully understood.
choices.D: very different processes can produce the same kind of regular pattern.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the two explanations is best described as:

choices.A: dismissive of the termite explanation, which the author regards as disproved.
choices.B: open-minded, treating both as serious and allowing that each may play a part.
choices.C: convinced that water competition alone explains every circle in Namibia.
choices.D: doubtful that the fairy circles have any natural cause at all.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best summarizes the passage?

choices.A: A teenager finally masters the chess strategy a grandfather taught and wins a local tournament.
choices.B: A teenager's pride in beating a grandfather gives way to uncertainty about what the wins really mean.
choices.C: A grandfather admits to his grandchild that he has been losing their chess games on purpose.
choices.D: A grandchild decides to stop playing chess with the grandfather after discovering a painful truth.

questions.stem: The details in the first paragraph mainly establish that, when the narrator was younger, the narrator's grandfather was:

choices.A: a strict teacher who expected the narrator to learn from mistakes.
choices.B: an impatient player who rarely explained his moves.
choices.C: a gentle player who often let the narrator take back bad moves.
choices.D: a distant relative the narrator saw only on a few special occasions.

questions.stem: The narrator is troubled by the bishop move described in the third paragraph mainly because the move:

choices.A: costs the narrator a valuable piece early in the game.
choices.B: shows that the grandfather has learned a new strategy.
choices.C: breaks a rule the grandfather had long insisted on.
choices.D: lets the grandfather win the game in only twenty minutes.

questions.stem: As it is used in the seventh paragraph, the word plain most nearly means:

choices.A: simple in style.
choices.B: obvious.
choices.C: unattractive.
choices.D: level and flat.

questions.stem: Based on the sixth paragraph, the narrator's view of the grandfather's response to the unguarded queen is best described as:

choices.A: uncertain, since the response could reflect either kindness or confusion.
choices.B: relieved, because the grandfather clearly saw the mistake and chose mercy.
choices.C: alarmed, because the grandfather clearly failed to see the queen at all.
choices.D: annoyed, because the grandfather refused to take the game seriously.

questions.stem: The fourth paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: describe the game in which the narrator first beat the grandfather.
choices.B: explain why the grandfather stopped playing in chess tournaments.
choices.C: lay out the two possibilities that the narrator then sets out to test.
choices.D: reveal that the narrator's friends doubted the narrator's claims about chess.

questions.stem: The narrator describes being "more grateful for that loss than for any of my wins" most likely because the loss:

choices.A: proved that the grandfather had been letting the narrator win all spring.
choices.B: showed that the narrator had finally become the better of the two players.
choices.C: meant that the narrator could stop bragging to friends about chess.
choices.D: let the narrator avoid a feared answer and keep their games going.

questions.stem: The detail that the narrator set the pieces back "the way he had taught me, white on the right" mainly serves to:

choices.A: show the narrator honoring the grandfather's lessons and their routine.
choices.B: suggest that the narrator has forgotten some of the basic rules of chess.
choices.C: reveal that the grandfather is unable to set up the board himself.
choices.D: indicate that the narrator plans to stop playing chess after this game.

questions.stem: The passage is told from the point of view of:

choices.A: the grandfather, explaining why he began to lose on purpose.
choices.B: an outside narrator who knows what both characters are thinking.
choices.C: the grandchild, looking back on events from the spring of turning fifteen.
choices.D: one of the narrator's school friends who heard about the games.

questions.stem: The main claim of Passage A is that parking minimums:

choices.A: should be raised in neighborhoods where streets are already crowded with parked cars.
choices.B: impose hidden costs and encourage driving, so builders should decide on parking.
choices.C: are necessary in suburbs but should be removed in city centers with frequent transit.
choices.D: have caused builders to stop providing parking in most new apartment buildings.

questions.stem: According to Passage A, after several cities eliminated parking minimums, builders:

choices.A: stopped providing parking in nearly all of their new buildings.
choices.B: built more parking than the old minimums had required.
choices.C: provided less parking where residents could walk or use transit.
choices.D: asked the cities to restore the old parking requirements.

questions.stem: Passage A suggests that a tenant who does not own a car is affected by parking minimums because the tenant:

choices.A: must pay a separate monthly fee for a parking space in the building's garage.
choices.B: cannot find a space on the street because the building's garage is full.
choices.C: is required by the city to buy a car in order to rent an apartment.
choices.D: pays rent that includes the cost of building parking the tenant does not use.

questions.stem: The author of Passage B regards the critics of parking minimums as:

choices.A: persuasive about transit-rich neighborhoods but wrong to apply their view everywhere.
choices.B: wrong about every point, since minimums protect all neighborhoods equally well.
choices.C: correct in every respect, so that minimums should be eliminated immediately.
choices.D: uninterested in the problems that cars cause in crowded city neighborhoods.

questions.stem: In Passage B, the statement that a household without parking at home "is not a household without a car" mainly serves to:

choices.A: explain why suburban households prefer to live near train and bus stations.
choices.B: challenge the assumption that removing required parking will reduce car ownership.
choices.C: show that suburban residents are unwilling to use public transportation.
choices.D: suggest that builders in suburbs should provide fewer parking spaces.

questions.stem: As it is used in Passage B, the word spill most nearly means:

choices.A: pour.
choices.B: drop.
choices.C: spread.
choices.D: waste.

questions.stem: Which of the following does the author of Passage B propose?

choices.A: Lowering minimums where transit is strong and linking the rest to bus frequency.
choices.B: Keeping existing parking minimums because they were designed for good reasons.
choices.C: Eliminating parking minimums in every city at once, as several cities have done.
choices.D: Requiring new suburban buildings to provide more parking than current codes do.

questions.stem: Both authors would most likely agree that:

choices.A: parking minimums should be removed in every type of neighborhood.
choices.B: suburban residents will give up their cars if parking is not provided.
choices.C: builders cannot be trusted to decide how much parking to provide.
choices.D: many codes require amounts of parking that do not match actual need.

questions.stem: The author of Passage B would most likely respond to Passage A's claim that builders should decide how much parking to provide by pointing out that:

choices.A: builders always provide more parking than their customers want.
choices.B: builders rarely build housing on small or oddly shaped lots.
choices.C: builders may not bear the cost when tenants' cars crowd nearby streets.
choices.D: builders cannot estimate how many of their tenants will use buses.

questions.stem: The narrator leaves the queen unguarded in the fifth paragraph mainly in order to:

choices.A: give the grandfather a win to make up for the earlier losses.
choices.B: show the grandfather that the narrator no longer needs lessons.
choices.C: test a sacrifice of the queen that the narrator had read about.
choices.D: see whether the grandfather would notice and punish the mistake.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Learning to improvise required absorbing a tradition and, eventually, departing from it.
choices.B: Improvisation in jazz is mostly memorized material that is made to sound spontaneous.
choices.C: The narrator's teacher was mistaken to require students to transcribe recorded solos.
choices.D: Jazz is easier to learn than other kinds of music because it has fewer fixed rules.

questions.stem: When Mr. Okafor says, "That was free. It was not improvised," he most likely means that:

choices.A: the narrator had played too loudly to be heard over the recording.
choices.B: improvising requires the musician to plan every note in advance.
choices.C: ignoring the music's structure is not the same as improvising.
choices.D: the narrator should have played exactly what was on the recording.

questions.stem: The comparison between a jazz solo and a conversation in the second paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: suggest that jazz solos are usually prepared in advance like speeches.
choices.B: show how a performance can be unrehearsed and still follow shared rules.
choices.C: explain why some musicians deliberately clash with the chords in a song.
choices.D: argue that listeners should talk with musicians during a performance.

questions.stem: According to the passage, transcribing a solo involved:

choices.A: memorizing a solo from sheet music written by the original musician.
choices.B: playing along with a recording until the solo felt natural.
choices.C: inventing new solos over the chords of a famous recording.
choices.D: slowing a recording down and writing out every note by ear.

questions.stem: Mr. Okafor's reply that "nobody ever learned to speak by inventing words" most strongly suggests that he believes:

choices.A: a personal style grows from what a musician learns from others.
choices.B: students should give up on trying to find a voice of their own.
choices.C: learning to speak is more difficult than learning to play music.
choices.D: copying the solos of great musicians is the final goal of study.

questions.stem: When the narrator says Mr. Okafor "was right, though not entirely," the narrator most likely means that:

choices.A: transcription took too long to be worth assigning to most students.
choices.B: absorbing other players' phrases alone did not produce a personal style.
choices.C: the narrator had already found a personal voice before transcribing.
choices.D: great saxophonists never learned by transcribing other musicians.

questions.stem: As it is used in the fourth paragraph, the word collages most nearly means:

choices.A: paintings made by gluing paper to canvas.
choices.B: exact imitations of a single musician.
choices.C: assemblages of pieces from other sources.
choices.D: brief summaries of longer pieces of music.

questions.stem: The narrator describes the solo played after forgetting a memorized phrase as "mine" mainly because the narrator:

choices.A: played it more smoothly than any of the solos learned by transcribing.
choices.B: received praise from Mr. Okafor for playing it at a performance.
choices.C: had stopped transcribing other musicians' solos some time before.
choices.D: had to find a way back to the chord without relying on a borrowed phrase.

questions.stem: The last sentence of the passage mainly serves to:

choices.A: suggest that students should try to make as many mistakes as possible.
choices.B: argue that personal expression requires departing from learned material.
choices.C: explain why the narrator stopped assigning transcriptions to students.
choices.D: argue that learned material is more important than personal expression.

questions.stem: The narrator's current attitude toward transcription is best described as:

choices.A: treating it as the only reliable way for students to learn.
choices.B: regretting the years spent on it as largely wasted effort.
choices.C: valuing it as necessary, though not enough by itself.
choices.D: doubting whether it helps students who want to improvise.

questions.stem: The main purpose of the passage is to:

choices.A: explain how fireflies produce light from chemicals inside their bodies.
choices.B: show how firefly flash signals serve courtship and are exploited by predators.
choices.C: argue that Photuris fireflies deliberately choose which species to imitate.
choices.D: describe the many birds and spiders that hunt fireflies on summer nights.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, a Photuris female's imitation succeeds mainly because males:

choices.A: cannot see females who are perched on leaves below them.
choices.B: are attracted to any flash they see at night, regardless of its pattern.
choices.C: rely on a species-specific reply pattern and delay to recognize a mate.
choices.D: prefer Photuris females to females of their own species.

questions.stem: According to the passage, besides food, Photuris females gain from eating other fireflies:

choices.A: the ability to produce flash patterns of other species.
choices.B: bright pigments that make their own flashes easier to see.
choices.C: eggs that the males were carrying to their own mates.
choices.D: chemicals that make them distasteful to their own predators.

questions.stem: The detail that Photuris females "cannot make these chemicals themselves" mainly serves to:

choices.A: explain why eating other fireflies is an important source of protection for them.
choices.B: suggest that Photuris females are easier for birds and spiders to catch.
choices.C: show that Photuris females are less closely related to other fireflies than once thought.
choices.D: indicate that Photuris females are unable to produce their own flashes of light.

questions.stem: In the fourth paragraph, the biologists who "prefer more cautious language" differ from the others mainly in their view of:

choices.A: whether Photuris females switch reply patterns at all during an evening.
choices.B: whether the females' switching reflects deliberate choice or a simple rule.
choices.C: whether Photuris females eat the males that they attract with their flashes.
choices.D: whether male fireflies can tell different reply patterns apart.

questions.stem: As it is used in the third paragraph, the word exploited most nearly means:

choices.A: explored.
choices.B: destroyed.
choices.C: manipulated.
choices.D: explained.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that males who approach answering females more slowly and flash more times before landing are most likely:

choices.A: unable to recognize the flash patterns of their own species.
choices.B: trying to imitate the replies of Photuris females themselves.
choices.C: less interested in mating than males that approach quickly.
