questions.stem: The narrator's statement "Fixing a thing properly seemed like the respectful choice" (paragraph 4) suggests that at that point the narrator believed:

choices.A: Mr. Pellerin would be offended by a choice of the cheaper option.
choices.B: the cleaning option would damage the typewriter further.
choices.C: the narrator's mother expected a costly repair.
choices.D: a full repair would best honor the typewriter and its former owner.

questions.stem: In the passage, the line Mr. Pellerin types before the repair serves mainly to:

choices.A: provide a sample the narrator later matches to Vesna's letters.
choices.B: show that Mr. Pellerin doubted the narrator would pay for the repair.
choices.C: prove that the machine could no longer type legible letters.
choices.D: demonstrate the speed at which Mr. Pellerin could type.

questions.stem: Mr. Pellerin's reaction when the narrator calls the shop suggests that he:

choices.A: was disappointed to lose the more expensive repair.
choices.B: believed cleaning would not fix the machine at all.
choices.C: had expected the narrator might keep the quirk.
choices.D: had already started replacing the linkage.

questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 4, the phrase "come home" most nearly means:

choices.A: return to its owner.
choices.B: settle back into place.
choices.C: arrive at a house.
choices.D: strike the paper harder.

questions.stem: In the final sentence, the narrator suggests that replacing the linkage would have:

choices.A: insulted Mr. Pellerin by doubting his skill at cleaning.
choices.B: made Vesna's letters impossible for anyone to read.
choices.C: destroyed the carbon copies found in the box.
choices.D: erased a trace of the great-aunt that survived in the machine.

questions.stem: The passage indicates that the letters at the bottom of the box were:

choices.A: letters the narrator had once written to Vesna.
choices.B: copies Vesna had kept of letters she sent.
choices.C: drafts of letters Vesna never mailed.
choices.D: notes Mr. Pellerin had left in the machine.

questions.stem: In the first paragraph, the narrator's feelings about having asked for the typewriter are best described as:

choices.A: regretful, since the narrator's mother wanted it.
choices.B: proud, since it matches the laptop.
choices.C: uncertain, since the narrator cannot explain why.
choices.D: indifferent, since it was never meant for use.

questions.stem: The main idea of the passage is that the archerfish:

choices.A: hunts more successfully than any other fish in mangrove waters.
choices.B: relies mainly on instinct and cannot improve its aim over time.
choices.C: is studied mostly because its jet could inspire new engineering designs.
choices.D: shows complex hunting and learning abilities despite a modest brain.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the water in the archerfish's jet gathers into a single large drop:

choices.A: just before it reaches the target.
choices.B: as soon as it leaves the fish's mouth.
choices.C: only when the target is very close.
choices.D: after it bounces off the leaf.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the archerfish's ability to correct for the bending of light is at least partly learned because:

choices.A: adult fish hit targets from directly below without any correction.
choices.B: fish that watched a skilled shooter aimed better at moving targets.
choices.C: young fish miss often but become more accurate with practice.
choices.D: light bends whenever it passes from air into water.

questions.stem: In the context of the passage, the sentence "This is harder than it sounds" (paragraph 2) mainly serves to:

choices.A: suggest that the archerfish often fails to catch insects.
choices.B: introduce the problem that refraction poses for the fish's aim.
choices.C: signal that the author doubts the accuracy of earlier reports.
choices.D: shift the focus from the fish's hunting to its learning by watching.

questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 1, the word snaps most nearly means:

choices.A: breaks suddenly.
choices.B: speaks sharply.
choices.C: photographs.
choices.D: closes quickly.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the fish that watched a skilled shooter in the experiment:

choices.A: improved at hitting moving targets without practicing on them first.
choices.B: hit moving targets less often than fish that had not watched.
choices.C: had already practiced extensively on moving targets.
choices.D: learned to recognize the skilled shooter's face.

questions.stem: The author mentions that fish "lack the part of the brain that primates use to recognize faces" (paragraph 5) mainly to emphasize that:

choices.A: primates are poor at recognizing the faces of other species.
choices.B: the archerfish recognized faces without the brain structures primates use.
choices.C: the fish probably memorized the screen's position rather than the face.
choices.D: scientists have discovered the brain region fish use for faces.

questions.stem: Based on the last paragraph, the author would most likely agree that:

choices.A: only animals with large brains can solve difficult problems.
choices.B: the archerfish is more intelligent than most primates.
choices.C: complex skills can arise in animals with simple nervous systems.
choices.D: scientists should stop comparing fish with other animals.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, if an archerfish fired at a target farther away than usual, it would most likely:

choices.A: fire the jet at a steady speed so the water would not break apart.
choices.B: swim directly beneath the target so the light would not bend.
choices.C: wait for another fish to fire so it could learn the correct aim.
choices.D: adjust its jet's timing so the drop forms near the farther target.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the order in which the passage presents the archerfish's abilities?

choices.A: Aiming, shaping the jet, learning by watching, and recognizing faces
choices.B: Recognizing faces, aiming, learning by watching, and shaping the jet
choices.C: Shaping the jet, aiming, recognizing faces, and learning by watching
choices.D: Aiming, learning by watching, shaping the jet, and recognizing faces

questions.stem: The main idea of the passage is that:

choices.A: Ebbinghaus proved that nonsense syllables are harder to remember than real words.
choices.B: the study methods that feel most effective are not always the ones that last.
choices.C: rereading is useless, and students should never reread what they study.
choices.D: students forget most of what they learn because they do not study enough.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Ebbinghaus chose nonsense syllables so that:

choices.A: he could memorize the lists more quickly.
choices.B: other researchers could easily repeat his experiments.
choices.C: meaning or associations could not help him remember them.
choices.D: the lists would be the same length each time.

questions.stem: The main function of the third paragraph is to:

choices.A: explain how Ebbinghaus measured forgetting over a month.
choices.B: argue that rereading should be banned from classrooms.
choices.C: introduce a new experiment that contradicts the one in paragraph 2.
choices.D: describe a gap between students' confidence and their results.

questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 4, the word fluency most nearly means:

choices.A: skill at speaking a language.
choices.B: speed of reading aloud.
choices.C: ease of processing.
choices.D: accuracy of memory.

questions.stem: The author mentions "attempting a test on material one has never seen" (paragraph 5) mainly to:

choices.A: show that not every kind of effort helps memory.
choices.B: suggest that students should test themselves before studying anything.
choices.C: prove that rereading is more effective than recall in every case.
choices.D: describe a method that Ebbinghaus used in his experiments.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Ebbinghaus found that lists he relearned on several separate days:

choices.A: were forgotten more quickly than lists he learned once.
choices.B: outlasted lists he crammed in a single sitting.
choices.C: took less time to learn than lists of real words.
choices.D: were remembered perfectly after a month.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, a student preparing for an exam a week away who feels frustrated while trying to recall notes without looking at them should most likely conclude that:

choices.A: the method is not working and rereading would be better.
choices.B: the frustration proves the material has been fully learned.
choices.C: recall is useful only for tests given within five minutes.
choices.D: the frustration does not mean the method is failing.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward students' preference for comfortable study habits is best described as:

choices.A: cautious, because comfort may be a poor guide.
choices.B: approving, because comfort shows the habits are working.
choices.C: dismissive, because students never know how they learn.
choices.D: neutral, because the passage does not discuss study habits.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the organization of the passage?

choices.A: A theory, several objections to it, and a rejection of the theory
choices.B: A personal story, a definition, and a list of study tips
choices.C: An early study, a modern experiment, an explanation, and a qualification
choices.D: A problem, a proposed solution, and evidence that the solution failed

questions.stem: The main idea of the passage is that John Cage's 4′33″:

choices.A: was a joke that Cage later admitted had confused his audience.
choices.B: proves that a composition must contain musical notes to count as music.
choices.C: was meant to redirect listeners' attention to sounds they usually ignore.
choices.D: was the first piece of music ever performed without a piano being played.

questions.stem: According to the passage, during the performance David Tudor marked the three movements by:

choices.A: opening and closing the lid over the keys.
choices.B: playing a single note at the start of each one.
choices.C: announcing each movement to the audience.
choices.D: turning his stopwatch on and off.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, Cage would most likely say that the audience members who talked and walked out during the third movement:

choices.A: ruined the performance by interrupting its silence.
choices.B: proved that the piece had failed as a joke.
choices.C: should have been asked to leave before it began.
choices.D: became part of the sounds the piece was framing.

questions.stem: The main function of the third paragraph is to:

choices.A: describe how anechoic chambers are built and used.
choices.B: recount an experience that shaped Cage's view of silence.
choices.C: show that the audience in 1952 misunderstood the piece.
choices.D: present a critic's argument against 4′33″.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the two sounds Cage heard in the anechoic chamber came from:

choices.A: equipment inside the chamber.
choices.B: traffic outside the building.
choices.C: his own body.
choices.D: the engineer standing nearby.

questions.stem: The statement that "true silence does not exist for a living listener" (paragraph 3) most nearly means that:

choices.A: a living person always hears some sound, if only their own body.
choices.B: a listener can learn to hear perfect silence with enough practice.
choices.C: anechoic chambers do not work as designed.
choices.D: people dislike silence and avoid it whenever possible.

questions.stem: The two critical views described in the fourth paragraph differ mainly in whether 4′33″:

choices.A: was performed by David Tudor or by Cage.
choices.B: contains three movements or one.
choices.C: should be performed in a concert hall or outdoors.
choices.D: is a genuine musical work or mainly an idea.

questions.stem: In the final paragraph, the author suggests that both critical views:

choices.A: are wrong because 4′33″ is clearly a joke.
choices.B: miss how the piece changes the way people listen.
choices.C: are correct and cannot be reconciled.
choices.D: depend too heavily on the details of the 1952 performance.

questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 2, the word frame most nearly means:

choices.A: set off for attention.
choices.B: build a structure around.
choices.C: falsely accuse.
choices.D: put into words.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, a researcher who tested the students in paragraph 2 only five minutes after studying would most likely have mistakenly concluded that:

choices.A: rereading a passage produces better memory than practicing recall.
choices.B: practicing recall produces better memory than rereading after a week.
choices.C: students forget most of what they learn within the first day.
choices.D: students who practice recall feel more confident about remembering.

questions.stem: The main purpose of the passage is to:

choices.A: trace how the idea that Earth once froze over grew out of a model that seemed to rule it out.
choices.B: argue that the snowball Earth hypothesis has now been proven beyond reasonable doubt.
choices.C: explain why most geologists rejected Budyko's climate model as too simple to be useful.
choices.D: compare the evidence for glaciers near the equator with the evidence for a tilted axis.

questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, Budyko concluded that runaway freezing had never occurred because he assumed that:

choices.A: ice reflects less sunlight than ocean water or bare land does.
choices.B: ice sheets could never have spread far from the poles.
choices.C: a completely frozen Earth would have been unable to thaw.
choices.D: Earth's climate had always been warmer than it is today.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Kirschvink proposed that a frozen Earth could eventually thaw because:

choices.A: heat from volcanoes would gradually melt the ice from below the surface.
choices.B: the weathering of rock beneath the ice would release large amounts of heat.
choices.C: Earth's axis would slowly tilt until the tropics were facing the sun again.
choices.D: carbon dioxide released by volcanoes would build up with little to remove it.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that once melting began, the thaw would have sped up mainly because:

choices.A: exposed darker surfaces would absorb more sunlight than the ice had.
choices.B: volcanoes would release more carbon dioxide once the ice was gone.
choices.C: carbonate rock forming in the oceans would trap additional heat.
choices.D: rain would return and quickly remove carbon dioxide from the air.

questions.stem: The passage presents the carbonate layers in Namibia as support for Kirschvink's scenario mainly because the layers:

choices.A: prove that the oceans froze completely all the way to the equator.
choices.B: show that photosynthetic organisms survived the long period of glaciation.
choices.C: suggest that warm conditions quickly followed a period of glaciation.
choices.D: formed before the glacial deposits that lie beneath them in the rock.

questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 6, the phrase "a one-way door" refers to the idea that:

choices.A: Earth's climate can change only gradually over long periods of time.
choices.B: a scientific theory cannot be revised once it has been widely accepted.
choices.C: ice can spread from the poles toward the equator but not in the other direction.
choices.D: a frozen Earth, once formed, could never return to a warmer state.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements would the author most likely agree with?

choices.A: Even if the oceans never froze completely, Earth's climate can reach extremes once thought impossible.
choices.B: The slushball proposal has replaced the snowball Earth idea among most scientists.
choices.C: Budyko was mistaken in claiming that ice reflects more sunlight than ocean water does.
choices.D: Since life survived, the claim that the oceans were ever completely frozen must be false.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 5, critics point to the survival of photosynthetic organisms because these organisms:

choices.A: first appeared only after the glaciations had already ended.
choices.B: release carbon dioxide that would have melted the ice too early.
choices.C: depend on sunlight, which thick ice over the oceans would have blocked.
choices.D: can survive only in warm water near hot springs or volcanic islands.

questions.stem: Compared with the "slushball" proposal, the original snowball Earth idea differs mainly in claiming that:

choices.A: the glaciations were caused by a steeply tilted axis.
choices.B: the oceans were frozen over even near the equator.
choices.C: volcanoes played no part in ending the glaciations.
choices.D: glacial deposits formed only in regions near the poles.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the passage as a whole?

choices.A: A narrator describes the many difficulties of running a small piano-tuning business.
choices.B: A narrator who starts a summer job reluctantly comes to understand and share in the work.
choices.C: A narrator recalls a conflict with an aunt that ends when one of them apologizes.
choices.D: A narrator explains, step by step, the technical process of tuning an old piano.

questions.stem: In the first paragraph, the narrator's statement "I let everyone know it" mainly suggests that the narrator:

choices.A: openly complained about having to spend the summer working.
choices.B: was proud of being trusted with Ines's tools.
choices.C: had already told friends about Ines's skill.
choices.D: stopped complaining once the job had begun.

questions.stem: Ines's reaction after playing a chord in the church basement (paragraph 2) most strongly suggests that she:

choices.A: was in pain from carrying the heavy tool bag down the stairs.
choices.B: disliked having to work on pianos that belonged to churches.
choices.C: doubted that the old piano could be repaired at all.
choices.D: could hear flaws in the piano's sound that the narrator could not.

questions.stem: Ines's explanation for tearing the covers off her books (paragraph 3) is most similar to which of her other actions in the passage?

choices.A: Eating the same sandwich of cheese and pickles at lunch every day
choices.B: Spending nearly two hours tuning a piano that no one in Mr. Okafor's house ever played
choices.C: Leaving the narrator to hear the beats without explaining what they would sound like
choices.D: Using only one of the dozen tuning forks that she owned

questions.stem: Mr. Okafor's statement "I like to know it's ready" (paragraph 4) most nearly suggests that he:

choices.A: values having the piano cared for even though he does not play it.
choices.B: plans to begin taking piano lessons soon.
choices.C: expects guests who will want to play it.
choices.D: is preparing the piano to be sold.

questions.stem: When Ines says "That's someone playing it" (paragraph 5), she most nearly means that:

choices.A: Mr. Okafor secretly plays the piano when he has no visitors.
choices.B: Mr. Okafor's careful listening gives the piano a use worth her full effort.
choices.C: the piano is still played by students of Mr. Okafor's wife.
choices.D: the narrator should learn to play the piano before tuning one.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the narrator first heard the beats when:

choices.A: Ines struck two keys together on the piano in the church basement.
choices.B: Ines played a slow piece for Mr. Okafor after finishing her work.
choices.C: handing Ines mutes and felt strips during the first two weeks.
choices.D: striking a tuning fork and a key on the practice piano in Ines's garage.

questions.stem: The comparison of the pulse to "two people walking almost but not quite in step" (paragraph 6) mainly serves to:

choices.A: suggest that the narrator and Ines have begun to work together as equals.
choices.B: show that the old practice piano had been badly damaged by the damp.
choices.C: describe the slight mismatch between two sounds that the narrator can now hear.
choices.D: explain why Ines preferred to work alone rather than with an assistant.

questions.stem: The final sentence of the passage most strongly suggests that Ines:

choices.A: was paying closer attention to the narrator's tuning than she seemed to be.
choices.B: had lost interest in her book because she had guessed its ending.
choices.C: disapproved of the way the narrator had turned the tuning pin.
choices.D: wanted the narrator to stop working so that she could read quietly.

questions.stem: Compared with the narrator in paragraph 3, the narrator in paragraph 6 is more:

choices.A: eager to rejoin friends at the community pool.
choices.B: critical of the methods Ines uses in her work.
choices.C: impatient with Ines's habit of saying little.
choices.D: engaged in the work of tuning a piano.

questions.stem: The main function of paragraph 2 is to:

choices.A: show that geologists had already confirmed Budyko's model using evidence from ancient rocks.
choices.B: present geological evidence that the explanations offered at the time did not convincingly explain.
choices.C: explain why most geologists came to accept the idea of a steeply tilted axis.
choices.D: describe the methods geologists use to determine how old a layer of rock is.
